0.p: When companies use AI systems that share a backbone model but each company trains only their own small adaptations, an attacker stealing the small adaptations can recover the actual training data, breaking privacy promises.
0.a: Watch the attention signals in the frozen layers to spot individual words, then reconstruct sentences using the small adaptation data, guided by what makes grammatical sense.

1.p: Systems that organize graph data by similarities often fail because they mix structural connections (how things link) and semantic meaning (what things mean) without truly balancing both, and pick bad negative examples.
1.a: Use a strategy that progressively picks harder negative examples and scores node reliability by combining how well they fit their cluster with their consistency across different views.

2.p: When recommending products, combining images and text usually gives little new insight, and the system misses that collaborative meaning (what users typically buy) differs from visual meaning, confusing the recommendation.
2.a: Learn three separate views—collaborative purchase patterns, item links, and visual patterns—then align them by maximizing how consistent they are with each other.

3.p: Emotion support chatbots either follow pre-written logic (stiff and hard to adapt) or rely on AI reasoning (unstable and hard to understand why they chose that response).
3.a: Blend both: use logic-based reasoning for strategy selection and neural learning for empathetic tone, so the system balances explainability with emotional responsiveness.

4.p: People's personal data—calendars, purchases, emails, fitness—holds answer to complex time-based questions like 'How many weekends did I stay home last month?', but no benchmark exists to test if systems answer accurately.
4.a: Build a test dataset of realistic questions over synthetic personal timelines, where questions need to aggregate many events and often require specific dates.

5.p: Online learning platforms try to diagnose what a student doesn't understand, but current methods freeze student-and-question identifiers even when AI language systems could recognize semantic meaning more deeply.
5.a: Use a trained language model to enrich the standard identifier approach with semantic understanding of questions and students, while keeping the system's existing strengths intact.

6.p: Image classification on the web fails when it sees new categories or when the data distribution shifts, because learned search instructions overfit to training categories and don't generalize.
6.a: Extract knowledge from descriptions of each image using an AI system and teach the model using two teacher signals that guide how text and images align together.

7.p: Websites share login cookies across subdomains for convenience, but if a hacker breaks into any subdomain, they steal the cookie and hijack the user's account on all other services.
7.a: Detect which domains leak cookies by simulating a hijacked subdomain and recording what gets stolen, then check darknet data for real leaked credentials from this flaw.

8.p: AI systems that look up external facts before answering sometimes pull contradictory information, and the system has no way to recognize conflicts or pick the trustworthy source.
8.a: Train the system in stages to detect when it senses conflicting information by comparing confidence across sources, use that signal to select better training examples and prefer robust choices.

9.p: Engineers parse massive log files to find errors, but AI systems focus only on the fixed parts and ignore the changing parts, wasting computation and losing visibility into what actually varied.
9.a: Flip to focus on the changing parts, use them to group logs more efficiently, and avoid redundant AI calls by remembering past decisions on the same changing parts.

10.p: Systems that flag unusual graphs (frauds, botnets) train only on normal examples, but in reality the training data contains anomalies anyway, creating a gap between theory and practice.
10.a: Model uncertainty as a distribution over predictions so anomalies have less influence during training, and iteratively separate normal from abnormal without expert filtering.

11.p: Using AI language systems to understand graphs either requires heavy computation or loses the ability to transfer what it learned to graphs from different domains.
11.a: Pre-train an AI language system on multiple types of graphs at once using two types of similarity to handle both local structure and cross-domain consistency, then adapt it per task.

12.p: Answering factual questions using organized knowledge fails because systems ask the knowledge system to find facts for only one interpretation of the question, missing complementary angles.
12.a: Detect multiple distinct angles in the question using topic modeling and sample from all of them, then train on which angles actually helped the final answer.

13.p: Cities collect enormous amounts of data from IoT sensors and AI systems, but don't yet have integrated frameworks to turn that data into better decisions and services.
13.a: A workshop series exploring how web technologies can help cities use data more effectively to improve decisions, services, and citizen experience.

14.p: Graph classification systems fail on rare categories because they train on balanced data and become biased toward common categories, plus they can't admit when they're uncertain.
14.a: Use multiple experts with evidence-based beliefs (modeled as probability distributions) and uncertainty estimates, so the system combines their views robustly for both common and rare categories.

15.p: Online shopping has become overwhelming because there are too many choices, and websites struggle to show you products you actually want.
15.a: Build a test system that measures how well AI agents can filter products for specific shoppers, rather than just showing the same items to everyone.

16.p: Websites collect messy data where things are connected in many different ways, making it hard to sort them into meaningful groups.
16.a: Develop a mathematical technique that groups these mixed connections faster and more accurately than older methods.

17.p: When extracting facts from web pages, current systems miss conditional details—like when a rule only applies in certain situations.
17.a: Use a noise-removal technique that treats facts and their conditions as connected parts, then gradually refines messy guesses into clean answers.

18.p: Marketplace platforms like Amazon profit by copying successful products from sellers, but nobody understands the game-theory dynamics of when they'll do it.
18.a: Model this as a strategic contest where the platform decides when to enter a market, and use both math and machine learning to predict what sellers will do.

19.p: New AI systems pre-trained on simulated data show promise for predictions, but their fairness—whether they treat all groups equally—remains a mystery.
19.a: Test one such system on real data, measure whether it discriminates against certain groups, and identify where the fairness breaks down.

20.p: AI systems that write text have two contradictory needs: generating varied, interesting text versus producing reliable, consistent answers.
20.a: Identify two model types—one favoring variety, one favoring stability—and explain when each is better for real jobs like code-writing or shopping advice.

21.p: Online rumors spread fast because fact-checkers struggle to find good supporting evidence and often miss important details in their final claims.
21.a: Filter out bad evidence before checking, then have an AI system debate both sides of a claim and teach a smaller model to decide if it's true.

22.p: Predicting what people will do online requires capturing both immediate events and distant past patterns, but most systems can't handle both efficiently.
22.a: Treat event patterns as waves and run calculations in frequency space, so distant patterns influence predictions without expensive computing.

23.p: Shopping sites use purchase rate to rank products, but they ignore refunds—missing the fact that some items get bought then returned constantly.
23.a: Build a public dataset and a system that predicts net purchases after refunds, modeling the two-step delay from click-to-buy to buy-to-return.

24.p: When learning from data spread across devices without gathering it centrally, shared skills can clash with personal preferences, hurting predictions.
24.a: Share only part of a system's learned features, keeping each device's personal layers separate, so global knowledge doesn't override individual needs.

25.p: AI systems now explain shopping recommendations in plain language, but real browsing histories are messy—they include accidents and outdated clicks.
25.a: Test whether these AI explanations stay consistent when you add realistic noise to browsing records, revealing weaknesses in explanation stability.

26.p: AI systems route work to specialized modules, but recalculating routes for similar questions wastes time and produces inconsistent results.
26.a: Store which module combinations worked before, then reuse them for similar questions while letting live decisions keep things current.

27.p: E-commerce systems predict purchase rates at the product level, missing fine details like size or color that strongly influence buying decisions.
27.a: Group product variations by price to capture crucial details without creating too much data sparsity, then train a system aware of these groupings.

28.p: Selling data privately requires adding noise to hide personal information, but existing methods either reveal the data or fail when dealers are dishonest.
28.a: Use distributed computation where computers work together to add noise without any single party seeing the raw data, even if some computers are corrupted.

29.p: Systems that look up facts before answering often get irrelevant results, which then get included in the final answer alongside good information.
29.a: Evaluate how relevant each retrieved fact is and give that score to the AI answering system, so it knows which sources to trust.

30.p: Recommendation systems show users the best 10 results, but training them to get those top 10 right is computationally expensive and breaks when user tastes suddenly shift.
30.a: Replace the expensive ranking math with simpler comparisons between scores and learned thresholds, then stabilize against sudden changes in what users want.

31.p: Quantum computers are coming and will crack the encryption that protects blockchain transactions and cryptocurrencies, but no one knows how to build practical quantum-safe systems yet.
31.a: Teach how quantum computing works, show new cryptography that computers cannot break, and explain how to rebuild blockchain security for the quantum era.

32.p: In remote areas without good maps or GPS, tracking where people go is nearly impossible, yet this data matters for everything from planning roads to tracking disasters.
32.a: Use web data that volunteers share to fill gaps in location history, starting with rough patterns from far away, then zooming into local details.

33.p: Cryptocurrency investment pools favor big players because larger pools earn better returns, locking out regular people even when they combine their money.
33.a: Show mathematically why pooling money together actually does make economies of scale, but design a protocol where many small investors share the benefits fairly.

34.p: Cloud networks struggle to give some services priority without slowing others down, wasting bandwidth and hurting video quality when lots of users log on.
34.a: Build a system that watches which tasks need bandwidth most right now and splits it intelligently between high-priority and regular traffic.

35.p: Video sites keep recommending the same creators and videos you already know, hiding new voices even though you might love them if you tried them once.
35.a: Estimate how much you already know each creator, then adjust the ranking to push newer, unfamiliar videos higher without losing what you already enjoy.

36.p: Group chats stall out without a moderator because no one speaks up, and managing hundreds of people manually is impossible.
36.a: Drop in AI agents that understand the chat's topic, jump in when things slow down, and coordinate with each other so they do not all talk at once.

37.p: A system that learns from how things connect works best when connected items are similar, but it breaks on networks where connected items are often different.
37.a: Look at connections between individual features—not just whole items—to adapt to networks where similar things connect or opposite things connect equally often.

38.p: When complex apps crash or slow down, engineers manually dig through logs to find the cause, which is slow and requires deep expertise.
38.a: Train an AI system on examples of what broken versus working logs look like, so it can automatically find and explain faults in new traces.

39.p: Recommending videos across many platforms fails because past data ignores the real rhythm of when people watch—sometimes bursts, sometimes nothing for weeks.
39.a: Track when interactions actually happened, use that timing to guess what someone wants, and borrow hints from the person's behavior on other platforms.

40.p: Cryptocurrency fraud spreads across multiple blockchains in complex ways, and catching it is hard because blockchain text, timing, and network structure matter together.
40.a: Combine graph structure, time patterns, and text metadata to spot when fraud tactics learned on one blockchain apply to a new one.

41.p: Cloud apps crash or slow unpredictably because microservices depend on each other in tangled ways, making it hard to predict when something will break.
41.a: Map out how services depend on each other and model what causes what inside each service, then predict problems by looking at workload flow.

42.p: New traders copy expert trades in meme coins but lose money because bots secretly rig prices, hide positions, and fake sentiment to trap followers.
42.a: Use an AI with reasoning skills to spot fake trading signals and choose which trades are real, so followers copy winners instead of schemes.

43.p: Web databases are everywhere but wildly different, and no single model can classify their rows without retraining from scratch each time.
43.a: Borrow an AI system that already reads text, use it to understand table rows, then tweak one setting to work with any database type.

44.p: Teachers spend hours planning lessons by hand in ad-hoc ways that miss pedagogy, and adapting lessons to different student needs is painful.
44.a: Use multiple AI agents with different expertise—novice, veteran, master—to collaborate on lesson plans and refine them step by step like real teachers do.

45.p: Cities need to predict many connected things at once—traffic, pollution, population—but most tools only predict one thing, missing how they actually affect each other.
45.a: Route different types of city data through specialized sub-systems that each focus on one prediction, then combine them to capture the full picture.

46.p: AI can now create convincing fake text, images, and videos at scale, overwhelming both people's ability to spot fakes and experts' ability to track what's real.
46.a: Track where information came from and demand proof of its source, instead of trying to spot fakes after the fact.

47.p: When many organizations share learning without sending raw data to one place, they must balance general knowledge everyone needs with keeping their own personal adjustments.
47.a: Each organization keeps two models—a large one for shared general knowledge and a small one for its own adjustments—then blend both at decision time.

48.p: Live-streaming chats have toxic behavior mixed with thousands of messages per minute, and human moderators can't keep up or handle the abuse themselves.
48.a: Teach an AI system to notice toxic messages by reading both the text and the emotes alongside them, combining that with traditional filtering.

49.p: AI systems trained on web data may have memorized private information like passwords or medical details, but detecting what they've learned is nearly impossible.
49.a: Feed the AI system slightly reworded versions of suspected sensitive content and watch its attention patterns to tell if it actually memorized the original.

50.p: Ride-hailing services struggle to forecast demand because locations behave differently and unexpected events like weather or protests throw predictions off.
50.a: Learn what makes each neighborhood special by studying maps and how people move through them, then use that knowledge to adjust predictions when events happen.

51.p: When creating new medicines, the same chemical structure changes can work differently depending on the context, and models trained on old data fail in new situations.
51.a: Separate the core rules of how molecules work from the changeable details, then assign each rule to a specialist system that handles its own piece.

52.p: Finding photos from hand-drawn sketches is nearly impossible because sketches are rough and sparse while photos are detailed and exact.
52.a: Convert rough sketches into plain-English descriptions of what they show, then use those descriptions as hints to match against photo collections.

53.p: Blockchain networks split work across many shards for speed, but when a transaction touches multiple shards, they conflict and slow things down dramatically.
53.a: Each shard predicts which other shards it will interact with soon and shares simple hints, so all shards can schedule their work together.

54.p: When an AI system generates text, it often gets distracted by common filler words like punctuation instead of focusing on what actually matters.
54.a: Identify which words are genuinely important, reduce or remove the noisy ones, and make sure the AI still understands the meaning correctly.

55.p: Recommendation systems using connection graphs struggle when two sessions end with the same product—they can't tell the sessions apart even if users want different things.
55.a: Build similar and different versions of sessions through graph processing, then use comparison learning to push apart sessions that truly differ.

56.p: Personalizing AI assistants requires expensive human feedback and on-device tuning that drains batteries and memory on phones and small devices.
56.a: Choose which user interactions are worth sending for feedback and update only the most important layers of the model to save power and data costs.

57.p: Shopping sites use multiple signals—clicks, cart adds, purchases—but clicks are noisy and often misleading about what someone actually wants to buy.
57.a: Ensure the system keeps secondary signals aligned with purchase decisions, while staying stable when different signals disagree with each other.

58.p: Training one model to work across wildly different graph databases fails because the data types and structures are completely different between domains.
58.a: Project all domains into a shared semantic space by learning what features matter in each, then use a shared hidden distribution to guide training.

59.p: Fake videos spread on platforms faster than humans can verify them, and current tools can't combine outside fact-checking with the video's own content.
59.a: Find real and fake videos that match the suspect video's claims, compare them through attention, then fuse all the evidence to judge if it's fake.

60.p: Shopping sites push popular items and bury niche products, making it hard for people to discover what they actually want because the systems ignore why popularity bias exists in the first place.
60.a: Use an AI system that reads and writes language to break down popularity bias into parts—what items are popular and what each person actually prefers—and ask the AI specific questions to understand the root causes.

61.p: AI systems that learn from what users click and engage with want to collect that feedback, but doing so reveals personal behavior data and violates privacy, creating a catch-22 between learning and protecting people.
61.a: Process feedback in split pieces across different devices without gathering it in one place, add mathematical noise to hide individuals, and use an AI judge to guide the system's choices without leaking private data.

62.p: Ads placed next to inappropriate content can wreck a brand's reputation, but checking stories by hand is slow and costs a fortune, and today's automated systems miss subtle harms.
62.a: Build a test set of 435 story chapters labeled by humans for 9 types of safety problems, then train language systems on that data so they can spot where ads shouldn't go.

63.p: When a product photo has a main item and background decorations, recommendation systems get confused and treat both equally, so they guess wrong about what the user really cares about.
63.a: Split photos and product text into individual objects, use an AI system to spot which one is actually the product, then focus the recommendation on that one thing only.

64.p: AI systems that answer complex questions can only search web pages, but the real deep knowledge is locked in research papers, reports, and spreadsheets where text and images live together.
64.a: Parse scientific papers and reports to preserve tables, charts, and equations as meaning-preserving chunks, then search across both text and visuals to gather evidence and build answers step by step.

65.p: Squeezing videos and sensor data to fit on phones and cloud storage is slow because different data types need different methods, and no single approach works when some pieces are easy to compress and others are hard.
65.a: Deploy multiple specialized compressors as a team, automatically pick how many compressors to use based on how hard each chunk is to squeeze, and use high precision only on the parts that matter most.

66.p: When a computer tries to spot patterns in a network diagram, the way the diagram is drawn hugely changes what the computer can see, but today's methods use the same fixed layout for everything.
66.a: Build a system that automatically draws network diagrams in different ways for different networks, showing each network's unique structure, so the computer can spot properties like whether you can visit every node exactly once.

67.p: AI systems answering medical questions often make up diseases and treatments that sound real, which is dangerous in a health context where wrong answers can hurt people.
67.a: First use a knowledge base of disease facts to plan safe answers to each question, then ask the AI to only use those approved facts, and finally check that the answer only includes facts from the plan.

68.p: Online learning platforms guess what a student will forget next, but they use one rigid method that misses how learning happens across fast and slow timescales in real students.
68.a: Combine four different types of learning models, each tuned for different time patterns, and automatically pick which mix works best for each individual student's history.

69.p: Social networks and transaction graphs with billions of connections are too huge to train AI systems on, but shrinking them loses directional meaning (like who paid whom) that matters for fraud detection.
69.a: Split a giant directed graph into smaller independent pieces using community detection, train on the pieces separately, then merge them into a tiny synthetic graph that keeps the original's direction and structure.

70.p: Makers of self-driving cars must prove their tests are real, but sharing raw test logs leaks trade secrets and raises questions about whether anyone tampered with the data.
70.a: Use cryptographic proof (a math trick that proves something is true without showing the evidence) so a company can show its test met safety rules without revealing the actual data or methods.

71.p: AI systems treat emojis of people with different skin tones as if they carry the same meaning, but some systems actually feel more positive or negative about one skin tone versus another, reinforcing bias.
71.a: Test AI systems to see how they feel about emoji skin tones and what meaning they assign, exposing hidden biases so platforms can fix the underlying systems to be fair.

72.p: Social platforms deploy filtering and recommendation rules to fix bad outcomes, but they only know if a rule works after it harms real people, and they can't test risky ideas before going live.
72.a: Simulate a social network where AI bots act like real users and the platform makes decisions, train the bots on real platform data, then test new policies in this safe sandbox before launch.

73.p: Pre-trained AI systems that learn from networks often discriminate against people with multiple overlapping identities (like race plus gender), but fixing this requires retraining the whole system which costs too much.
73.a: Add small adjustable components to the pre-trained system and inject fairness hints at the start, tuning only those small pieces to reduce bias against underrepresented groups while keeping the main system frozen.

74.p: People's tastes change over time, so recommender AI systems built on language need updates, but retraining everything causes the system to forget what it knew about other users and breaks old recommendations.
74.a: Divide the representation space into clusters of similar preferences, update each cluster separately with its own lightweight adapter, and route each user to their cluster at decision time.

75.p: AI systems trained on text from different languages absorb unfair biases about groups of people, just like systems trained only on English do, making them unsafe when used worldwide.
75.a: They reviewed how researchers test for unfairness across languages and cultures, and catalogued what kinds of testing are missing or broken in each region.

76.p: When a shopping site learns recommendations from multiple sites at once, it often applies rigid rules that treat all scenarios the same, leading to bad suggestions or even making things worse.
76.a: The system learns flexible rules on its own by studying which parts of different sites overlap, then carefully replays past user actions to avoid broken recommendations.

77.p: Finding missing connections in medical databases is hard because no link might mean either they don't interact or we just haven't discovered it yet, making it tough to know what to test.
77.a: They tried different strategies for choosing which non-existent connections to call false when training the model, and found some choices lead to far better predictions than random guessing.

78.p: Recommendation systems that keep data on each user's phone instead of sending it to one server struggle to learn good suggestions because everyone's data looks too different and too sparse.
78.a: They use a technique that finds flatter, more stable paths through the learning process, so the system can learn consistent suggestions despite each user having wildly different data.

79.p: Websites and apps change constantly, and crawlers that copy them lose track of what changed when, so people can't stay up-to-date on news that matters to them.
79.a: They mapped which websites link to or reference each other, then used a trial-and-reward algorithm to decide what to crawl next instead of treating each site alone.

80.p: AI chatbots can correct false beliefs people have, but they work much better on some topics like health than others like politics, and we don't know why or how to fix it.
80.a: They tested the same chatbot correcting misinformation across three domains and found big differences in how well it worked depending on whether the lies were about health, science, or politics.

81.p: When an AI system looks up facts before answering complex questions, it often forgets or misuses the facts it found, and it wastes time searching for redundant information.
81.a: It breaks questions into a tree of smaller sub-questions, only explores confident branches, and anchors searches to specific names and dates instead of vague ideas.

82.p: Fraud and crime networks in the real world have many different types of actors, but systems that learn from connections struggle when some actor types are much sparser or more important than others.
82.a: They align how suspicious patterns spread across different actor types, then use separate learning streams that protect each type's distinct task without conflicting with the others.

83.p: Students in poor areas or developing countries can't access good tutoring or immersive lessons because hardware is limited and systems are too heavy to run on weak devices.
83.a: They built a lightweight web classroom that combines question-answering, animated human characters, and attention tracking to work even on old phones or slow connections.

84.p: Most AI systems require retraining from scratch for each new dataset, but spreadsheets and databases are everywhere; we need one model that works across all kinds of structured data instantly.
84.a: They explore how large AI models trained on mixed data and generated examples can learn to guess well on new spreadsheets or tables without any prior training.

85.p: AI helpers that listen to people's emotional problems over weeks can't remember what was said before, hallucinate facts, or track how someone's feelings have changed over time.
85.a: They tested long-memory AI systems on scenarios where a person's needs shift and problems are hidden in old messages, and measured what memory tricks actually stopped false answers.

86.p: Tools that edit photos can change colors or objects but ignore how the picture *feels* or makes the viewer *feel*, so emotional tone gets lost even when details stay the same.
86.a: They taught an AI to shift a photo's emotion while keeping objects and facts intact, by first understanding what emotion words mean together, then carefully protecting what shouldn't change.

87.p: Recommendation systems built on user-item connections fail when most users haven't interacted with most items, and the system can't guess what hidden need or interest a user actually has.
87.a: They added invisible nodes that represent shared interests and patterns between users and products, making more bridges and anchors so the system learns better despite sparse data.

88.p: When you ask a search engine follow-up questions in a conversation, noise in old context confuses it, and you can't see why it picked the results it did, so you don't trust it.
88.a: They use an AI that cleans up confused context with logic, then explains results using readable text instead of hidden math, and checks answers via two different search paths.

89.p: Websites force you through menus and clicks to do simple tasks, overloading your brain, but a chatbot alone can't remember layouts or let you see what's possible at a glance.
89.a: Developers describe what their app can do in plain language, then the AI picks the relevant buttons and builds a simple, focused interface on the fly for what you asked.

90.p: When using AI systems on websites, people worry about privacy leaks, bad outputs, and whether the results are safe to publish.
90.a: They teach a step-by-step workflow to add safeguards to AI instructions, test outputs with tricky cases, and decide when answers are good enough to use.

91.p: The web changed from a library of documents to a place where what matters is how satisfied users feel over weeks or months, not just whether one search worked.
91.a: They trace how web designers shifted from counting matches to measuring if people keep coming back, especially as AI systems got better.

92.p: When you search by photo on shopping sites, you often get items that look similar but are actually different, wasting your time.
92.a: They built a system that understands both images and product categories, learning to spot the real differences between a leather belt and a rope.

93.p: Fake reviews and click fraud happen in organized gangs that hide their abuse by acting collectively, evading normal detection.
93.a: They treat spam as a group problem, not individual behavior, and use a single learning process to catch the coordinated patterns.

94.p: When data is stored separately (no single company holds everything), it's vulnerable to saboteurs who poison part of the data.
94.a: They show how to attack those systems and then defend them by spotting when one location's data looks wrong compared to the others.

95.p: Recommendation systems trained on past data fail when the world changes (like a pandemic) because they learned fake patterns that don't hold anymore.
95.a: They use geometry to separate which features matter from which are just coincidences, so recommendations work even when circumstances shift.

96.p: Small AI models can't answer questions that need knowledge from databases unless they're trained to use those sources well.
96.a: They teach smaller models to search a knowledge database for the right facts, organize them, and reason through the facts step-by-step.

97.p: When a sudden crisis (war, pandemic) appears, old fake-news detectors fail because they never saw that topic before.
97.a: They use AI to understand the meaning of news and how people react to it, making those patterns transfer to brand-new situations.

98.p: Most websites skip basic security steps like encryption, leaving data vulnerable to hackers and eavesdropping.
98.a: They measured which security practices are deployed across German websites to show where defenses are weakest.

99.p: Fake content on social media mixes false images, false captions, and mismatches between them—but testing treats it all as one blob.
99.a: They map all eight possible combinations (real/fake image, real/fake text, match/mismatch) and built an AI checker for each part.

100.p: AI models learn shortcuts (a word that happens to go with anger) instead of learning why a phrase is actually negative about a topic.
100.a: They create fake examples showing what happens if a shortcut word changes, then train the model to ignore those shortcuts.

101.p: Misinformation spreads through networks because people share posts; stopping it means cutting certain nodes to break the chain.
101.a: They designed fast algorithms that run in minutes on networks with tens of millions of connections.

102.p: As the web adds AI and decentralized systems, devices need new ways to prove they're trustworthy without leaking private information.
102.a: A workshop explores zero-knowledge proofs (ways to prove facts without showing the data) and blockchain for secure, decentralized identity.

103.p: Internet standards are written in dense specs, but nobody explains why designers made the choices they did—only the decision itself.
103.a: They built a system that searches old email records between standard-makers and rewrites their reasoning in plain language.

104.p: Traders in crypto markets can't find the best arbitrage paths fast enough because the search space is huge and time is milliseconds.
104.a: They used a learning algorithm to pick profitable trading paths in milliseconds instead of seconds, trading some profit for speed.

105.p: AI agents can now automatically do tasks on the web using tools, but attackers can trick those tools into giving wrong answers, and systems today only catch the mistake without fixing it.
105.a: Automatically detect when a tool misbehaves by watching attention patterns, then rewind to before the bad action and ask the AI to try again with that path blocked.

106.p: Companies claim their products are eco-friendly, but often these claims are false or exaggerated, misleading consumers and investors who want to support genuinely sustainable businesses.
106.a: Build a tool that checks whether sustainability claims match real facts from reliable reports, either by searching documents or by linking claims to an organized database of true ESG data.

107.p: When you show a shopping app an image plus instructions for what to change, it struggles to pick the right details from the photo that match your request, getting confused by irrelevant visual clutter.
107.a: Use reasoning about what you want to guide the system on which parts of the image are relevant, then carefully combine information from different levels of detail.

108.p: Child protection experts need to quickly tell if material shows adults or children, but faces are often not visible, slowing down their work to remove harmful content from the internet.
108.a: Learn to judge age from body shape and relative proportions alone, using a strategy where the system handles different ages at once and learns by comparing pairs of people.

109.p: Phone networks rely on SIM cards to verify who you are, but SIM data has been stolen at massive scale, creating a huge security hole for billions of users.
109.a: Replace SIM verification with mathematical proofs that you own a secret key, where no personal data is ever shared or stored centrally.

110.p: Detecting how groups evolve in networks is crucial for safety in hospitals or traffic, but today's systems are black boxes that give no explanation for why groups formed.
110.a: Teach an AI system to explain clustering by first mapping nodes to five named human-like roles—like hubs or bridges—then using an AI to reason about those roles in plain language.

111.p: When a group votes based on private hunches about the truth, some will strategically vote against their actual preference if they can coordinate with others, but we don't know how many allies they need to succeed.
111.a: Analyze voting mathematically to find when the majority's true answer wins no matter which group sizes can secretly coordinate together.

112.p: AI systems can hallucinate false facts, and while adding knowledge bases helps, they often lose information by turning structured facts into text, or the system ignores the knowledge.
112.a: Inject mathematical vectors representing connections from a structured database directly into the AI's processing, without changing the AI itself or converting data to text.

113.p: Explaining why a system makes decisions on messy real-world networks is hard because noise in the data distorts every reason the system gives.
113.a: Use a statistical method to clean noisy network structure, then explain decisions by filtering which connections matter most while respecting that nodes have different types.

114.p: New products that people haven't rated yet are nearly invisible in recommender systems, so new item launches fail and users miss out on fresh choices.
114.a: Use a technique that smooths out uneven training across new and popular items so the system generalizes better, sharing lessons across related categories.

115.p: In a barter swap between people with different opinions on what items are worth, the middleman struggles to make a fair deal that gives everyone a real win.
115.a: Design a mathematically optimal algorithm that maximizes total value gained, guarantees no one loses money, and can work when people don't reveal their true valuations.

116.p: Recommendation systems focus only on showing people what they want most, but this creates bubbles where users see only one viewpoint and never encounter diverse ideas.
116.a: Let each user set their own priorities for accuracy versus diversity versus fairness, then automatically balance the AI's choices to meet those personalized goals.

117.p: AI models run in web browsers for speed and privacy, but a visitor can easily steal the model's code or weights by reading the browser's memory or JavaScript.
117.a: Scramble the model code so deeply inside the browser's efficient execution layer that reverse-engineering it becomes far harder, with no loss in accuracy or speed.

118.p: AI systems that rank search results can only see a sliding window of a few documents at a time, so they miss important connections and waste money on repeated calls.
118.a: Build a system that reads all results at once by inventing a clever position encoding for long lists and pruning which documents the AI actually needs to pay attention to.

119.p: Building better short-video recommendations is held back because there are almost no large real-world datasets that show actual user behavior on video platforms.
119.a: Release a public dataset with 40 billion real user interactions from a major platform, so researchers can build and test new recommendation ideas fairly.

120.p: Cryptocurrency systems that use proof-of-stake rely on validators to honestly create new blocks, but dishonest pools can secretly build their own chain to earn more coins than their share.
120.a: They showed that Polkadot's system, which picks validators ahead of time, lets a bad actor with one-third of the validators earn extra rewards without risk of being caught or punished.

121.p: AI systems that fetch facts from the internet before answering questions are slow and expensive, making them vulnerable to attackers who can slow them down on purpose.
121.a: Insert fake documents into knowledge sources that look relevant so the AI fetches and processes them, forcing the system to waste computing power.

122.p: Networks change constantly over time, and we need to find small sets of points that can monitor all connections even though those monitoring points only work for a limited time.
122.a: Develop algorithms that choose which points to activate and when, considering that each point stops working after a set lifespan.

123.p: You have a limited number of tools or items you can rent out repeatedly, and people ask for them at unpredictable times with varying rental lengths.
123.a: Design pricing rules that decide whether to rent each item, making decisions in real-time without knowing future requests, while mathematically guaranteeing competitive profit.

124.p: Historians want AI systems to roleplay as historical figures, but there's fragmented information scattered across different sources that needs organizing.
124.a: Build a platform with nearly 20,000 AI agents representing Chinese historical figures, combining their biographies, writings, families, and events into coherent personas.

125.p: Published research code usually fails when others try to rerun it due to missing parts, outdated software versions, or logical gaps in the analysis steps.
125.a: Test whether AI systems can automatically fix broken code by either asking it many clarifying questions or having it inspect files and apply fixes until the analysis works.

126.p: When AI systems answer questions by pulling from fact databases, they often mix up directions or reverse relationships, like saying Microsoft bought Activision instead of the truth.
126.a: Check answers by converting text back into graph structures and verifying that relationships point the right way without needing to generate new text.

127.p: When opinions spread online, we focus on predicting what will happen next but rarely explain why and how the spreading actually works beneath the surface.
127.a: Create a dataset with detailed opinion threads and apply a mathematical model that shows which emotions spread fastest, how replies trigger reactions at each level, and what people remember.

128.p: Tabular foundation models for structured data have different interfaces and preprocessing rules, making it hard for practitioners to compare and adopt them.
128.a: Build a unified library that standardizes how to load, run, fine-tune, and evaluate multiple tabular models through a single consistent interface.

129.p: When finding images using text or vice versa, most systems compare one photo to one description, missing the reality that many images and texts can share the same meaning.
129.a: Use a structure that links multiple images and texts together when they mean the same thing, then enhance both directions so images and text understand each other equally.

130.p: AI language systems struggle to find the right tool in enormous toolkits because tool descriptions don't match how users naturally phrase their questions.
130.a: Use reward-based learning to teach the AI to rewrite user questions to match tool descriptions better and discover which tools actually work for similar problems.

131.p: News recommendation algorithms show people more of what they already like, trapping them in bubbles and missing chances to shift public opinion toward stability.
131.a: Guide users toward target stories gradually by recommending intermediate articles that match their current interests while slowly steering them toward the final goal.

132.p: Customer support AI struggles because users ask vague questions like 'my app is slow' without knowing what the system can actually diagnose or fix.
132.a: Reason through competing explanations for the problem, asking targeted questions to rule out possibilities until one clear path to the solution remains.

133.p: Graph-learning systems work well in training but fail suddenly when data shifts slightly, giving wrong answers where they used to give right ones.
133.a: Study how the loss landscape becomes sharper during training and boost generalization by augmenting data in ways that prevent answers from flipping under small changes.

134.p: Data visualizations aim for clarity but often fail to engage people or spark new thinking because designers ignore subtle visual choices that matter psychologically.
134.a: Design visualizations with hidden visual properties like color emotion and filtering options that help people notice patterns, create ideas, and decide faster.

135.p: E-commerce sites run campaigns with vague creative themes, making it impossible to know which customers bought because of which ads.
135.a: Use an AI system that reads each campaign, guesses what product types it promotes, then matches actual purchases to those types to train ranking models.

136.p: Web services need different team structures for different tasks, but training one custom design per task wastes effort and doesn't transfer knowledge.
136.a: Built a single universal system that reads a task description and auto-generates the best team structure, reusing shared patterns across all tasks.

137.p: When different offices cluster the same data privately, they disagree on how many clusters exist, breaking the ability to combine their results fairly.
137.a: Separate each office's data into public patterns everyone agrees on and private details that stay local, then align only the public parts.

138.p: Social networks spread rumors fast, but finding where a rumor started requires trial-and-error testing of thousands of possible sources in real time.
138.a: Pre-train a lightweight model on simulated rumor paths, then use brief prompts to instantly pinpoint likely source nodes without full retraining.

139.p: Time series forecasting relies on collecting everyone's data in one place, but companies won't share private data like power grids or hospital records.
139.a: Each company keeps data local and trains only its own patterns, while sharing just enough information to learn shared low-frequency trends without exposing private details.

140.p: Recommendations fail because user-item networks have wildly different local structures, but current systems assume the same geometry everywhere.
140.a: Treat learning as a physical process unfolding on a shape that bends and adapts to match each region's local topology, enabling better long-range connections.

141.p: Medical AI needs to spot tiny visual abnormalities in tissue samples, but generic vision-language models miss fine details that don't fit their broad training.
141.a: Make vision and language work together: vision provides region details, then language describes exactly what to look for, then vision re-focuses on those clues.

142.p: AI systems that read and write language can't easily understand graphs, so researchers tokenize graphs into text, but this loses explicit graph structure clues.
142.a: Add a step that reconstructs the graph from the AI's output, forcing the system to keep graph information intact alongside text, not just inside text tokens.

143.p: Expert screeners need to know when to stop reviewing documents, but without checking every one, true progress stays invisible and further checking is expensive.
143.a: Combine a ranking model's confidence scores with a small random sample of actual judgments to estimate recall early via statistics, then set a stopping rule.

144.p: AI search engines must retrieve facts from huge knowledge graphs, but they check only shallow connections, missing the rich multi-step relationships that explain answers.
144.a: Dynamically find self-contained clusters of connected facts based on each question, then look up the most relevant chunk at each detail level, cutting waste.

145.p: Data marketplaces struggle to set fair prices: data isn't like physical goods (one buyer means less for others), yet everyone wants a simple price tag.
145.a: Use economic theory of supply-and-demand balance to compute prices where all buyers get fair value and sellers' data is fully allocated, even though each buyer gets their own copy.

146.p: Deepfakes spread on video and audio across cultures and languages, but detection methods ignore how content meaning shifts while the fake technique stays the same.
146.a: Separate what makes something look fake from what the content means, and split the 'Fake' label into subtypes for different generation methods.

147.p: Unsafe C/C++ code runs in browsers via WebAssembly and crashes memory without harming the rest, but existing fixes need source code or slow down the program.
147.a: Rewrite the compiled WebAssembly binary to split memory into isolated regions, like a software memory manager, catching buffer overflows with no source code needed.

148.p: Self-driving cars drain 12V batteries unpredictably because heater and AC loads jump based on driver behavior, making planning ahead nearly impossible.
148.a: Use the past 60 seconds of power draw to predict the next draw via statistics, cutting uncertainty by 40% even during sudden temperature swings.

149.p: Scammers hide by doing normal-looking actions (like adding friends), making it hard to spot fake accounts without knowing the hidden intent behind each action.
149.a: Learn typical behavior patterns for each account type, then spot when the same action serves different hidden purposes depending on surrounding context.

150.p: When AI assistants look up facts online, they use old index snapshots and give you no say in which sources they trust, mixing reliable and dubious information.
150.a: Let users pick their trusted sources beforehand, then automatically re-check those pages for new information when they ask a question.

151.p: Forecasting what thousands of variables will do next month takes massive computing power because tracking how each variable affects all the others scales up quadratically.
151.a: Rearrange variables so that local clusters and global patterns are separate, then process them in groups instead of all together, cutting computation costs.

152.p: When training AI systems on images and text together, most feature dimensions fill with noise while a small subspace holds the actual meaning, making the system poorly generalize.
152.a: Identify which dimensions matter for the task versus which are noise, then selectively boost the important ones while filtering out junk.

153.p: Recommendation systems have lots of product data but struggle to understand what users actually want because user history is sparse or missing entirely.
153.a: Use an AI system that reads language to infer user interests from their past activity, then blend that with product data to make better guesses.

154.p: To use an AI assistant for quick answers, users waste time copying text into a chat window and retyping the same kinds of questions.
154.a: Detect what you're reading anywhere on your screen, add a keyboard shortcut, and get instant AI explanations or summaries without leaving the app.

155.p: Networks of connected data (like social graphs) confuse AI systems when friends aren't similar, and systems that work on training data fail when test data has different connection patterns.
155.a: Create a codebook of connection patterns during training, then during testing combine them flexibly to handle rare or new patterns the model never saw.

156.p: Social platforms remove content manually, but humans make mistakes—citing the wrong policy—leading to wrongly deleted posts and wrongly-kept harmful content.
156.a: Use AI to spot when a moderator probably got it wrong, diagnose whether the rule itself was unclear, and write clearer guidelines.

157.p: Detecting depression from social posts is hard because mental health data is scarce and different AI systems understand symptoms differently.
157.a: Find the most relevant past posts about depression symptoms, then pick the right reasoning strategy and AI system for each person's unique situation.

158.p: Online game studios need to predict how much money each player will spend to decide who to advertise to, but spending patterns have many peaks and zeros.
158.a: Model the realistic, messy spending distribution for each game separately, then share cross-game patterns to predict lifetime value better.

159.p: AI systems are tested under relaxed conditions, but real-world decisions happen under time limits and pressure, when AI reliability matters most.
159.a: Systematically test AI against harder scenarios, measure how much accuracy drops as tasks get tougher, and report robustness scores.

160.p: Current tests for AI that turns text into human movement are flawed: one assumes distributions have specific shapes, the other misses the big picture.
160.a: Create two new tests: one treats text-motion matching as a transport problem to see the whole picture, one uses an improved motion-reading tool to measure similarity fairly.

161.p: When users ask AI multi-step questions in a chat, the system must understand their changing intent across turns to find relevant information.
161.a: Combine AI's ability to read instructions and reason with systems that plan retrieval steps, adapting strategy dynamically as conversation evolves.

162.p: Workplaces are using AI assistants but nobody knows what tasks are actually getting done with them, making it hard to measure impact.
162.a: Summarize multi-turn conversations automatically, cluster them into work topics, then let people refine the groupings to get real insights.

163.p: Privacy law now requires deleting a user's data from models without retraining everything, but ransomware detection systems must stay accurate and fast.
163.a: Split the ransomware detector across separate shards so you only retrain the affected shard instead of the whole system when deleting data.

164.p: Predicting drug side effects from chemical structure is hard when you only have examples of bad effects, not confirmed safe drugs.
164.a: Reweight the model's focus at two levels: emphasize useful structural patterns and downgrade uncertain cases, so it spots rare true positives.

165.p: Computers struggle to understand how things connect in networks because they see patterns at only one level, missing both tiny local details and the big picture.
165.a: Build a system that looks at networks from three different angles at once—close-up, medium, and zoomed-out—so the computer learns richer patterns of what belongs together.

166.p: When a shopping site tries to guess what you want based on your entire past history, the weight of all that old data makes it too slow to answer quickly.
166.a: Compress your long history into a few smart summaries, keeping only the moments that truly shaped your tastes, so the computer can guess fast without throwing away what matters.

167.p: Video streaming often pauses even when your internet is fast enough, because the app misreads your connection speed when video frames arrive in bursts.
167.a: Measure your connection speed frame-by-frame instead of packet-by-packet, so the app sends video at the right pace and avoids stalls.

168.p: Spotting saboteurs inside a company is nearly impossible because their bad acts hide in mountains of normal work and happen slowly over time.
168.a: Look at many clues from different angles—emails, files, keystrokes—using an AI system to weigh which signals matter most for finding hidden threats.

169.p: When an AI system misbehaves or does something unsafe, there's no clear way to prove what happened or rebuild the chain of events.
169.a: Record and replay all questions asked to an AI system like investigators do at a crime scene, so you can audit who asked what and when.

170.p: Finding clothes online is hard when you describe a change to an image you like—say, 'make it red instead'—because systems don't grasp the visual-plus-words mix.
170.a: Deploy multiple specialized robots that imagine the target look, filter possibilities by what they see, and double-check the answers make sense.

171.p: Search engines can extract answers written in documents, but struggle when the answer must be figured out by connecting clues that are never stated directly.
171.a: Build a test set of questions that need real reasoning from hints, so AI systems can learn to spot the unstated answers hiding in the facts.

172.p: AI agents that search the web waste time doing too many searches or stop too soon because they cannot tell when they have enough facts to answer.
172.a: Use logic to find when the agent's stopping point is wrong, then retrain it to know the right moment to answer instead of searching more.

173.p: Finding groups of related items in a network is unreliable when the connections are messy or when positive and negative ties mix together.
173.a: Clean up the group edges by testing each member's fit, then teach the system to spot which connections truly matter for grouping.

174.p: Wearables and phones send time-series data from different users that shifts over time, so AI trained on old phones struggles on new ones.
174.a: Generate synthetic sensor patterns that cover frequencies you haven't seen, so the AI learns to handle data shifts across different devices.

175.p: Shopping sites use AI trained on general images to pick what to show you, but the AI doesn't know your taste, so it shows everyone the same items.
175.a: Group shoppers by interest and give each group its own tiny AI tuning, so the image AI can highlight aspects of a product your group cares about.

176.p: Gig platforms pay workers based on guesses of how much a task is worth, exploiting the fact that workers don't know their own value.
176.a: Show how a small group of workers who commit to a price floor can force the platform to pay fairly, instead of just lowering wages.

177.p: Fake claims spread online for different reasons—clickbait, distraction, ideology—but tools that spot fakes ignore these hidden motives.
177.a: Train a system to discover what goal each fake claim really serves, then use those goals to predict and stop false stories.

178.p: Adapting AI from one network dataset to another fails when one source alone doesn't capture all the real-world patterns in the target network.
178.a: Use knowledge from several source networks at once and simplify the AI design to focus on the key steps that move information through the graph.

179.p: Mental health chatbots today are black boxes that don't follow the real stages of therapy or explain their choices to the person seeking help.
179.a: Build an AI counselor that mirrors how real therapists work—explore the issue, build insight, plan action—while recording every step so it stays honest and clear.

180.p: Scientists writing papers need to find real sources to back up claims, but AI can invent fake citations, and researchers worry their work will be copied or exposed.
180.a: Built a tool in the writing software itself that finds real academic papers from trusted sources and checks if they actually support the claim—without sending data anywhere.

181.p: Photos on the internet come with hidden bias—most cat photos show striped ones, making AI learn that cats are striped—so image classifiers become unfair without anyone meaning them to be.
181.a: Detect what the bias actually is by looking at patterns, then fix photos by changing just the biased part, creating a balanced mix for the AI to learn from.

182.p: When Kubernetes hosting clusters break, IT teams spend hours guessing what went wrong, and each fix is forgotten when the next problem hits.
182.a: Created an AI system trained on thousands of past fixes that remembers patterns and suggests solutions faster, improving from failing half the time to succeeding 90% of the time.

183.p: Online advertisers have tiny budgets to test where to spend money, but standard AI learning methods need huge amounts of historical data to work well.
183.a: Used AI trained on human feedback to make smart guesses from just a few examples, then used those guesses to tweak spending decisions with numerical precision.

184.p: AI can now create fake versions of people's faces, opening doors to fraud and impersonation, so researchers built defenses—but attackers can break those defenses.
184.a: Showed that a face-cleaning algorithm designed for old, blurry photos can actually undo the anti-fraud defenses, exposing a new attack weakness.

185.p: In online chats and videos, people use sarcasm to hide their real meaning, and AI systems that spot sarcasm often can't explain why, making it hard to trust the answer.
185.a: Built a system that learns how text, tone, and facial expression work together to spot sarcasm, while also showing readable explanations of why it detected it.

186.p: The web is moving to a future where AI agents write most content, but when agents copy content from other AI systems, false claims and license violations spread.
186.a: Attach a detailed record to AI-written content showing exactly what was asked, when, and by what model—like a receipt that agents can check before reusing it.

187.p: Web recommenders learn from real data, but real data is messy—users change their minds, hackers add fake reviews, trends shift—so recommendations become unreliable.
187.a: Guide researchers through the sources of error on the web and show methods that make systems survive messy data, sudden changes, and deliberate manipulation.

188.p: Training AI on sensitive human feedback like medical records or engineering designs is risky—experts won't share raw data due to privacy laws and trade secrets.
188.a: Use cryptographic math that proves whether feedback is correct without revealing the underlying data, so sensitive information never gets shared.

189.p: Building searchable databases of scientific facts requires either expensive manual work with lots of errors or AI that misses important details from research papers.
189.a: Combine AI writing prompts with a standardized dictionary to extract facts consistently from papers, matching how humans would describe the research.

190.p: Different research databases each cover different parts of the world and time, making predictions about things like traffic or epidemics inaccurate when data is sparse.
190.a: Generate new data variants from what's available using a statistical model, combining hints from other databases to fill in missing information.

191.p: Cities and phones generate huge amounts of location and movement data, but we lack simple ways to turn that data into answers that non-experts can understand.
191.a: Survey how modern AI systems can read and explain location data at three levels: individual places, individual people's paths, and whole-city traffic patterns.

192.p: When AI systems look up facts before answering questions, they confidently give wrong answers if the facts they found are incomplete or unreliable.
192.a: Ask the AI what would change if the facts were different, then combine those answers to get a realistic confidence score instead of false certainty.

193.p: AI models are shrunk down to run on phones and cheap devices, but attackers can sneak in hidden changes during shrinking that cause the AI to refuse valid questions or ignore safety rules.
193.a: Show how to inject hidden commands during shrinking that survive even after the optimization process, causing the model to misbehave in specific ways.

194.p: Predicting which ideas will spread online usually means one-by-one checks of who influences whom, which is too slow to handle large conversation threads and misses group effects.
194.a: Group people by shared interests instead, then model how groups influence groups, making predictions 100x faster while handling videos and chains with tens of thousands of people.

195.p: Video apps show you shorts one after another, but guessing which ones will keep you watching long-term is harder than predicting what you'll click on right now.
195.a: Account for where videos sit in your feed (top looks better), learn which parts of the video matter most, and model how creators re-engage viewers over days or weeks.

196.p: Tor hides which websites you visit, but if attackers watch your traffic pattern while you open many tabs at once, they can still guess which sites you're on.
196.a: Treat mixed traffic like a cocktail party where you need to pick out one person's voice from the crowd, separating each tab's signal and identifying websites by their unique patterns.

197.p: Small banks need fraud detection to protect vulnerable customers, but they don't have much data, and hackers can sneak poison into the shared learning system without being caught.
197.a: Build fraud detection without gathering all banks' data in one place, and defend against hidden attack triggers by modeling how attackers probe and how defenders adapt.

198.p: In crisis response, AI must quickly sort social media into damage reports, missing persons, and other needs, but people don't trust AI they can't understand the reasoning for.
198.a: Pull key phrases from text and key image patches side-by-side, so the AI explains in words and pictures why it sorted a post the way it did.

199.p: Shrinking AI models to fit on phones or watches still burns tons of power doing math, even after compression, and scaling down the numbers clips important details.
199.a: Mimic the brain's spike-based neurons, storing only what matters most and replacing heavy multiplication with simple addition, so a watch runs the AI without draining the battery.

200.p: Search engines give everyone the same results for a query, but what one person needs is different from what another person needs, and rewriting queries for each person is too slow.
200.a: Train the AI to reason about what a person wants, then hide that reasoning from the output so search stays fast but gains the accuracy of deep thinking.

201.p: Scammers now mass-produce fake ads using AI voice and images, and checking each ad one-by-one to stop them is impossible when they pump out thousands of near-copies.
201.a: Study how scammers work as organized campaigns—same tricks repeated with slight tweaks—and block at the campaign level rather than chasing individual ads.

202.p: When you fine-tune an AI model with only a few extra parameters, starting from scratch and how wide the model is makes learning slow and choppy.
202.a: Use smarter starting numbers and a different math procedure to train the extra parameters so the AI learns faster and steadier with less tweaking.

203.p: AI systems must spot both categories they saw during training and completely new categories they've never seen, but bias toward the old categories makes it guess wrong on new ones.
203.a: Use statistics to softly guess which samples are new categories, then use paired comparisons to pull similar new items together and push confusing ones apart.

204.p: Security analysts must match AI vulnerabilities to attack methods and fixes, but this info lives in different systems with different formats and languages, so it's slow and error-prone.
204.a: Build a shared knowledge machine that speaks all the security vocabularies, so tools can automatically link a vulnerability to what attacks could cause it and how to stop them.

205.p: AI that reads text about products misses the hidden signals in how people buy—which items are similar, which go together—because text and purchase links don't naturally fit together.
205.a: Feed the AI both product descriptions and a map of who bought what together, then align the two using math so it learns from both at once.

206.p: Learning from graphs without labeled examples is hard because standard shortcuts for learning break the structure, and single-level learning misses how items group into bags.
206.a: Build a two-level system that learns at both the item and bag level, tweaking data safely to keep the structure whole, and align the levels with paired comparisons.

210.p: Shopping sites struggle to predict what new customers want because they have no history of their tastes to learn from.
210.a: Use quantum computers to speed up the process of finding patterns in how millions of customers bought things, then use those patterns to make better guesses for newcomers.

211.p: Tracking giant social networks and websites that change daily burns enormous amounts of electricity and computing power, much of it wasted on repetitive patterns.
211.a: Identify the core stable patterns that repeat in the network and throw away the rest, keeping the important structure while shrinking the data size dramatically.

212.p: Systems that learn from how things connect in networks work well when similar things cluster together, but fail when the network's structure is the opposite.
212.a: Use curved geometry to let the system adjust its learning method depending on the local area, working equally well whether similar or dissimilar things sit next to each other.

213.p: A blockchain must guarantee that once a transaction is approved, no one can erase or reverse it, but VeChain's system has a security flaw that breaks this guarantee.
213.a: Show through math and experiments that an attacker can flip the outcome of approved transactions by controlling enough of the network's validators.

214.p: When training AI across many devices without sharing raw data, blindly shuffling or mixing data hurts the final model because each device's data is different in unique ways.
214.a: Each device learns its own custom rules for how to shuffle its data to match the others, and uses a smart shortcut to reduce the amount of back-and-forth communication.

215.p: Systems that look up facts from the internet before answering are vulnerable to attackers poisoning the lookup database with fake image-text pairs, making the system give wrong answers.
215.a: Check for poisoned content by finding contradictions across multiple retrieved items and isolating suspicious sources, then rebuild clean answers from trusted sources.

216.p: Restaurants fail or thrive based partly on their place in the web of customer reviews and connections, but most survival models ignore this network altogether.
216.a: Build a system that watches how each restaurant's position in the review network changes over time and uses that to forecast whether it will stay open.

217.p: AI systems that answer medical questions sometimes make up false information because they don't distinguish between facts they actually know and plausible-sounding guesses.
217.a: Connect the AI to an organized web of medical facts instead of loose documents, so it only builds answers from proven relationships between diseases, treatments, and evidence.

218.p: Website designers don't know how much battery their sites drain on phones because existing tools only measure speed, which doesn't always match energy use.
218.a: Analyze a page's visual structure and layout to predict its energy cost directly, and show developers exactly which design choices waste the most power.

219.p: When organizations keep their data private and train AI together, missing pieces in each organization's data and incomplete connections between datasets cripple the shared learning.
219.a: Privately figure out what data is missing from each organization, fill in likely missing connections, and train the system to be robust to these gaps.

220.p: Security teams have to manually rewrite threat-detection rules for each vendor's platform because every company uses completely different rule languages and syntax.
220.a: An AI agent translates rules from one platform to another by converting to a vendor-neutral middle layer, looking up official documentation, and testing both versions to catch mistakes.

221.p: Automated systems that detect hateful memes fail badly when text is missing or blurry because they rely too heavily on words and ignore what the image alone shows.
221.a: Train the system to find one shared pattern language that both images and text can map to, so it works even when text is garbled or gone.

222.p: Documenting how AI models and datasets work requires time-consuming manual writing, and automated methods use rigid templates that miss important context.
222.a: Automatically hunt through papers for details by asking more specific follow-up questions, and borrow information from similar models to fill in gaps and complete the documentation.

223.p: Fact-lookup systems that improve at finding relevant passages don't always help the AI reason better because retrieved passages often contain noise or contradictions.
223.a: Retrieve chains of evidence where each fact explicitly supports the next, ensuring every passage added actually helps the AI's reasoning, not just boosts search numbers.

224.p: Grouping customers or users into clusters often unfairly leaves out certain races, genders, or income groups, and traditional algorithms don't enforce fair representation.
224.a: Select representative people from each group so that every demographic is included fairly, while still keeping the cluster centers as close as possible to all the data.

225.p: AI systems that understand images and text run slowly on phones or cost too much in data centers, forcing a choice between speed and quality.
225.a: Split the work: run simple tasks on your phone and send hard ones to the cloud, using a smart cache to remember which tasks you've seen before.

226.p: When companies run massive AI systems, small changes to settings like batch size or how data flows through computers can mean the difference between fast and slow service.
226.a: Automatically try different setting combinations and pick the best one, testing many in parallel across multiple computers to find what works fastest.

227.p: Law enforcement needs to identify victim ages in abuse materials to prioritize investigations, but AI systems that do this are hard to trust or explain.
227.a: Build a system that copies how human experts think by looking at multiple clues—face, body shape, and other markers—instead of one black-box guess.

228.p: Online stores spend money on ads and need to decide how much to spend, but they can't know in advance whether spending more will actually work.
228.a: Let the budget grow or shrink based on how well ads are performing in real time, treating it like a learning problem instead of a fixed choice.

229.p: AI systems are good at explaining things in words, but they struggle to predict when you might buy something again based on your past patterns.
229.a: Test whether giving AI systems more details about your history actually helps them predict, rather than just assuming more information is always better.

230.p: Shopping recommendation systems update daily but lose track of what your older purchases meant, treating everything as if it happened right now.
230.a: Remember the full history of when you bought things and use that timing to understand your tastes better when suggesting what to buy next.

231.p: Recommendation systems trained by one expert are weaker than they could be, and student models just copy teachers instead of learning to think differently.
231.a: Learn from multiple teacher systems at once, picking the best ideas from each, so the student model becomes stronger and more clever than any single source.

232.p: Social media platforms spread text, images, audio, and video together, but no one evaluates AI systems that understand all these types together for safety.
232.a: Bring together researchers to test how well multi-type AI systems work on real social media, measuring both quality and risks like misinformation.

233.p: When AI systems look up facts online to answer questions, they sometimes pick up false or misleading information that hurts the final answer.
233.a: Balance the goal of finding true facts with the risk of picking up bad ones, measuring both when choosing which sources to use in the final answer.

234.p: Hackers can spy on which websites you visit just by watching your internet traffic, even if your connection is private, because each site leaves a fingerprint.
234.a: Predict exactly which page on a website someone visits when multiple tabs are open, learning the hierarchy of site structure to make the attack more precise.

235.p: Time series data changes over time in unpredictable ways, and old methods fail to spot unusual patterns as the normal behavior shifts.
235.a: Keep a small, smart summary of past data that updates itself, using it to spot what's unusual without needing to remember everything forever.

236.p: Harmful content like misinformation, hate speech, and lies spreads across different websites and languages, but researchers study each type in isolation.
236.a: Bring together experts who study different kinds of harmful content across platforms and languages to share methods and find common patterns.

237.p: Network graphs where connected nodes are different types create problems for systems that assume connected nodes are similar, so existing solutions throw away those differences.
237.a: Measure how bent the network is using geometry and combine multiple clues to decide how much each neighbor should influence a node's behavior.

238.p: Time series prediction systems miss weak but important signals buried in noise and distort strong patterns when converting data between formats.
238.a: Split the job: one path focuses on small signals using adaptive methods, another preserves strong repeating patterns, then merge both results.

239.p: Companies want to learn patterns from data they own without sharing it, but secure privacy-keeping methods to do this are extremely slow.
239.a: Use secret-sharing math to let multiple companies do manifold learning together while keeping data private, optimizing the parts that were slowest before.

240.p: Finding patterns in huge databases of connected facts is too slow—the number of possible patterns explodes exponentially, making current systems crawl through them painfully.
240.a: Cut down what patterns to look for by ignoring less useful ones, then estimate key statistics quickly instead of computing them exactly, trading some accuracy for dramatic speed.

241.p: Travel sites lose money when rooms show sold-out but aren't, and adding inventory carelessly might not actually boost revenue—it might just steal bookings from other hotels on the same platform.
241.a: Use statistical causality math to predict which inventory additions would genuinely increase the platform's total revenue, and check hotel acceptance odds and room scarcity before acting.
