242.p: Finding suspicious groups of connected accounts in fraud and security requires understanding how they work together, not just spotting odd individual accounts.
242.a: Train a system that learns multiple types of connections—path, tree, cyclic—between accounts, then identifies groups whose pattern of connections doesn't match normal behavior.

243.p: AI systems need corrections when they're wrong or outdated, but making those fixes one at a time often breaks earlier fixes, causing knowledge to get tangled up.
243.a: Before editing, measure which edits conflict with each other and adjust which parts of the model to change, then carefully tune only the neurons that matter for that specific knowledge.

244.p: Cloud services need to send urgent control orders fast to millions of containers, but existing methods either overload the control system or bog down the machines doing the actual work.
244.a: Use two delivery paths—direct remote calls for urgent messages and a message queue for others—and automatically switch between them based on which is faster right now.

245.p: Quantum computers will break the cryptography protecting blockchains and crypto wallets, but decentralized systems can't flip a switch globally to adopt new math—they need to coordinate upgrades across thousands of independent nodes.
245.a: Create a checklist that maps exactly which cryptographic components in your blockchain need upgrading and in what order, so you can plan the migration without guessing.

246.p: AI now generates convincing fake news faster and better than ever, and people are getting worse at spotting it—we need tools to study this arms race and find ways to fight back.
246.a: Build platforms that measure how humans react to AI-generated fake news and generate controlled examples for research, then test whether detection tools and teaching people to be skeptical actually help.

247.p: Communities on social media form around shared grievances and moral beliefs, but traditional ways of spotting communities only look at who talks to whom, missing these deeper currents.
247.a: Add the emotional language and moral values people use in their posts as extra layers to the network, then find communities again—this reveals tighter-knit groups that last longer.

248.p: Shopping and video sites want to predict what you'll click next based on your entire history, but handling long sequences of your past behavior bogs down computers with too much math.
248.a: Group your old behaviors into chunks, then use a specialized fast attention system that separately captures your overall tastes, how they're shifting, and your immediate interests.

249.p: Dividing up tasks or resources fairly between people at different roles is hard—a task might require different effort from someone in marketing versus operations.
249.a: Design algorithms that assign jobs or resources so everyone gets a fair minimum share and no one is jealous, even when valuations change based on job title.

250.p: Smart sensors on phones and devices need AI to work without draining batteries, but current AI models require too much memory to run when storage space fluctuates wildly.
250.a: Automatically shrink which parts of the model run in memory based on what's available, skip redundant calculations when possible, and manage memory fragmentation to fit tighter.

251.p: Picking the best features from data spread across hospitals or labs is hard when each site has different patients—current methods miss real cause-and-effect links and chase coincidences.
251.a: Use a method that learns which features matter across all sites by fixing hidden biases, finding true causal links instead of coincidences, and separating shared importance from site-specific quirks.

252.p: Reasoning techniques that make AI systems better at thinking also accidentally make them more biased and less trustworthy—the more steps they take, the more bias creeps in.
252.a: Test popular reasoning methods on fairness tests and show where they amplify stereotypes and harmful beliefs across different languages.

253.p: Recommending things to you should respect your privacy and adapt as your tastes change, but existing privacy-preserving learning systems ignore how your preferences evolve over time.
253.a: Keep historical tastes alive during model updates through a self-teaching trick, and borrow successful patterns from similar users to guide your recommendations without sharing personal data.

254.p: Foundation models and learning without gathering everyone's data in one place are two major trends in AI, but researchers haven't connected them yet.
254.a: Host a workshop where researchers share ideas about combining these two approaches and figure out promising directions for the field.

255.p: Smart home devices accidentally reveal their location through public control interfaces, letting attackers pinpoint where millions of IoT devices are deployed worldwide.
255.a: Analyze what shows up on the device's web page, search for clues about location, and ask an AI system to guess the exact GPS coordinates and city.

256.p: Scientists designing new plastics struggle with predicting what the material will actually do, because doing so requires both chemistry expertise and heavy software skills.
256.a: Build a conversation tool that scientists can talk to in plain language, which automatically runs data pipelines and predicts plastic properties without coding.

257.p: Shopping apps struggle to suggest your next purchase because they treat your click history as one flat list, missing the fact that you shop in waves and care about some items more than others.
257.a: Remember which items in your history matter most and group your clicks into shopping sessions, so recommendations focus on truly relevant products.

258.p: Talking-head videos—realistic faces that sync with speech—are getting better, but researchers don't agree on what 'better' means or how to measure real progress.
258.a: Catalog 100+ research papers, create a shared vocabulary, and track how evaluation methods have changed over five years to show what the field actually cares about now.

259.p: AI language systems trained on billions of web pages must purge sensitive user data and copyrighted text when requested, but existing methods are slow and fragile.
259.a: Tweak only the AI's final output layer to block unwanted concepts while keeping all general knowledge, so forgetting is quick and doesn't affect other abilities.

260.p: Figuring out which people or accounts are hubs in networks that change over time is expensive to compute, and most of those hubs turn out to be nobody.
260.a: Use a system that learns from how things connect and groups similar nodes together, so it recognizes the rare truly important people without getting confused by noise.

261.p: AI systems that learn from connected knowledge graphs make predictions, but you can't tell why or trust that they're using real knowledge versus coincidences.
261.a: Trace the actual knowledge connections the AI used to make its prediction, separate real patterns from flukes, and show which facts really mattered.

262.p: Researchers writing papers must hunt through millions of recent publications to find references, wasting time on searches that leave them missing relevant work.
262.a: Give an AI system a paper excerpt and a database of 500k papers, and have it fetch the relevant ones first before suggesting which to cite.

263.p: Blockchain miners can team up with just a few users to cheat transaction fee systems, creating an arms race in auction design.
263.a: Prove mathematically that defending against tiny collusions is the same as defending against any size collusion, so builders only need one simple solution.

264.p: New AI models that work on spreadsheets perform well without training, but when you teach them on your own data, they often get worse instead of better.
264.a: Compare zero-shot, meta-learning, and fine-tuning approaches across many datasets to find when training helps and when it hurts.

265.p: Recommender systems need to store individual profiles for billions of users and IDs for millions of items, eating up enormous amounts of memory.
265.a: Use words from a language AI to represent items and compute preferences on-the-fly without storing user profiles or graph networks.

266.p: After floods, drones collecting images across disaster zones must send massive data back to servers, overwhelming networks when quick decisions are needed.
266.a: Have each drone process its images locally and send only high-level summaries to a central server, cutting data transmission by 99% while staying accurate.

267.p: Millions of people in Southeast Asia can't get good machine translation because training AI on massive datasets burns energy and requires data they don't have.
267.a: Use an AI agent to pick the small, culturally perfect training set of real dialogues, then teach a language model just on that smart selection.

268.p: Systems that detect websites by watching network traffic patterns stop working after weeks or months as websites change and network conditions vary.
268.a: Teach an AI system on millions of diverse real-world traffic patterns so it learns patterns that stay reliable even as websites evolve.

269.p: AI systems struggle to tell similar-looking things apart—like different dog breeds or car models—which is crucial for trustworthy applications.
269.a: Combine vision models, text descriptions, and diverse datasets to train systems that can distinguish subtle visual differences and explain their reasoning.

270.p: Recommendation systems treat products as isolated tokens instead of whole items, missing the connections between what people actually buy together.
270.a: Focus the AI's attention separately on what's inside each product and on how products relate to each other, so it understands both item details and buying patterns.

271.p: Translating TV and movie subtitles into other languages breaks sentences apart, mangles names and repeated terms, and loses the feeling and tone of what actors say.
271.a: Use an AI system that reads dialogue in context, keeps track of who's speaking, and knows which words should stay consistent throughout the whole show.

272.p: Powerful AI systems that understand images and text are too slow for real-time shopping and search, where users expect answers in milliseconds.
272.a: Distill the reasoning from slow, powerful models into a lightweight text-only system that keeps 98% fewer parameters but stays nearly as smart and fast enough for live use.

273.p: When searching huge datasets by both content and date, systems either give back wrong results or waste time searching through everything to avoid missing items.
273.a: Split data by date ranges, build an index within each chunk, then search only the relevant chunks to find matches correctly without wasted effort.

274.p: When ads appear inside AI-written articles instead of sidebar slots, their value depends on where they land and what surrounds them, breaking old auction math.
274.a: Model how readers choose among options and whether they stop after seeing each ad, then design auction rules that maximize revenue or overall value under these new conditions.

275.p: Web advertising secretly drains your device's battery and uses extra electricity through trackers and ad calls, but nobody measures or talks about this hidden tax.
275.a: Track CPU activity across hundreds of thousands of real website visits to measure how much power ads, consent banners, and trackers actually burn on user devices.

276.p: Online shopping platforms are moving from one central recommendation engine to dozens of AI agents negotiating with each other, but there's no way to see how or why they coordinate.
276.a: Create a workshop space to share research on building agent teams that coordinate transparently, handle failures gracefully, and measure success beyond just sales.

277.p: Large AI systems struggle to find relevant documents from huge collections even in theory, but nobody knew if the problem was math or the sheer number of dimensions involved.
277.a: Test whether squashing high-dimensional search spaces into fewer dimensions helps, and combine multiple smaller searches instead of one big one to get better results.

278.p: Image watermarks that bind themselves to the picture's meaning get broken when AI systems make tiny, clever edits that keep the image looking right but erase the mark.
278.a: Use an AI system that reasons about image meaning to find edits that destroy watermarks while keeping the image visually consistent and human-recognizable.

279.p: Writing software requires jumping between coding, testing, reviewing, and debugging; one AI model alone can't handle the whole loop or remember context across steps.
279.a: Team up multiple AI agents in specialized roles using memory systems, tool access, and human feedback to plan, write, test, and review code as a group.

280.p: Personalizing what users see online requires learning from their behavior, but privacy rules forbid gathering everyone's data in one place, and users change what they like constantly.
280.a: Use short-term memory for today's interests and long-term memory anchored to shared patterns learned across users, updated privately without collecting individual profiles.

281.p: Product recommendations based on descriptions miss that the same item appeals to different people for different reasons, and what the AI learns doesn't match how people actually shop.
281.a: Have the AI imagine each product's ideal customer from its description, then tweak that understanding by watching actual buying behavior to close the gap between theory and reality.

282.p: When AI systems look up facts to answer questions, bad actors can poison those facts to make the system lie, and no one checks whether the sources are trustworthy.
282.a: Score documents for reliability by analyzing how they connect to other sources, then reject suspicious facts while keeping the system honest and factual under attack.

283.p: Generative AI models trained on one kind of data often fail catastrophically when you try to use them on new situations, genres, or combinations they didn't see before.
283.a: Teach AI models techniques to adapt after training so they handle new concepts and unfamiliar combinations of text and images without forgetting what they knew.

284.p: Recommendation systems juggling multiple goals (search relevance, clicks, engagement) have expert submodels working together, but weak ones hold back results even though they hold useful knowledge.
284.a: Identify which experts lead versus support each task by measuring their impact, then reuse supporting experts' knowledge to strengthen the leader experts for real gains.

285.p: Cities trying to go green need to predict how today's building and transportation choices affect tomorrow's air quality and livability, but cities struggle to track and connect scattered data about energy, traffic, and weather.
285.a: Build a map of how city systems will change over time by pulling together information from different sources—satellite imagery, traffic counts, weather forecasts, and input from residents—to test scenarios before committing to policy.

286.p: People trying to spot false news can look for emotional language as a clue, but bad actors now use AI to swap emotions while keeping false stories intact, making the news harder to fact-check.
286.a: Train a detector that ignores emotional tone and focuses on what's actually said, so it won't get fooled when liars swap angry news for sad news but keep the same lies.

287.p: 3D models of objects made from point clouds can be tricked by tiny, invisible changes that make them misidentify what they're looking at, and current defenses require slowing down or redesigning the whole system.
287.a: Filter out the noise by analyzing the model's mathematical fingerprint, removing outlier points, then smoothing the rest to strip away hidden attacks without touching the model itself.

288.p: AI agents crawling the web for information are breaking the economics of online news and content—publishers can't control what bots see, and current blocking is too crude and fragmented across countries.
288.a: Set transparent rules that work worldwide so AI bots can access content fairly, and make sure news sites stay profitable through clearer agreements on how content is used.

289.p: AI is making fake news, deepfakes, and phishing easier to scale, yet the same AI tools could catch these attacks and protect privacy, so we need to understand when AI helps versus harms.
289.a: Examine real examples of AI being weaponized and defended against, then debate what rules and safeguards tech companies should follow to keep the web trustworthy.

290.p: Medical AI often gets confused when patients ask questions that could mean many different things, and poor answers can be dangerous—but doctors need to spot when the AI is unsure before giving bad advice.
290.a: Detect unclear questions by checking patterns inside the AI's decision-making, then pause and ask the patient to clarify before answering, without slowing down or needing to retrain the AI.

291.p: Construction workers need to exchange detailed building specs across firms, but the standard format is so technical and rigid that even experts find it hard to use, keeping smaller firms out.
291.a: Let workers type what they need in plain language, and let an AI system automatically translate it into the official technical format, making the process fast and natural.

292.p: Cloud data centers waste computing power on temporary jobs because they can't predict how much memory or CPU each job will need, driving up electricity bills and operational costs.
292.a: Watch overall cluster load trends to make rough resource guesses, then fine-tune for each task using a sliding window of recent history, without needing predictive models.

293.p: Cities need to predict traffic flow to avoid congestion and accidents, but existing models miss patterns in how traffic changes over time and space, and treat road networks too rigidly.
293.a: Convert traffic time-series into images so visual models can spot trends, cluster nearby roads by similarity instead of geography, then blend temporal and spatial patterns together.

294.p: Graph systems that learn from web data break when encountering new situations or users outside their training set, because they latch onto shortcuts that worked before but fail on fresh data.
294.a: Spot hidden sub-patterns within the graph that cause false correlations, then blend multiple experts to find rules that hold true across different situations and data sources.

295.p: GPS tracks from delivery trucks and rideshare cars are often gappy and jumpy because of weak signals, and apps need smooth routes to route drivers efficiently and show riders the truth.
295.a: Use a generative model that remembers earlier steps while filling in gaps, so it can reconstruct full, smooth paths from scattered GPS pings without losing realism.

296.p: Machine learning systems work well on training data but fail in the real world when conditions shift, and data experts struggle to spot and explain what went wrong to non-technical users.
296.a: Build a conversational AI tool that walks users through finding the problem, explaining why it happened, and suggesting fixes in plain language, adjusting to their expertise level.

297.p: Customs officers must classify imported goods into thousands of categories from messy, handwritten descriptions in different languages, and getting it wrong costs money and delays shipments.
297.a: Train an AI system on a few hundred examples to read messy descriptions and output clean, structured data, then let officers review and correct the AI's guesses before approving shipments.

298.p: Video platforms need to catch harmful content fast, but their current AI models are updated slowly and only look at the video itself, missing when users flag problems or when the creator's history matters.
298.a: Build a lightweight model that updates daily, pulling in viewer reports and video metadata alongside AI scores, so harmful content gets caught and removed quicker.

299.p: Graph-based clustering methods treat node-level and graph-level grouping as separate problems, missing chances to use insights from one level to improve the other and wasting compute.
299.a: Learn both node and graph clusters at the same time in two connected branches that push the same information back and forth, so local patterns guide global grouping and vice versa.

300.p: When you try to predict future data like weather or stock prices, some of your training examples are too noisy or messy to learn from, making the whole model confused and unreliable.
300.a: The system learns to spot which training examples are hard-to-predict mess and gradually punishes them less, while still extracting whatever value they hold.

301.p: A small city needs to predict traffic or bike usage, but has barely any historical data; a big city nearby has tons of it, but their patterns might not match or even mislead.
301.a: An AI system selectively pulls helpful patterns and knowledge from the big city's data and reads them aloud as instructions to guide the small city's forecasting.

302.p: Running AI language systems on phones and cheap devices without draining battery and exploding latency is hard; each device has different hardware and unpredictable resource availability.
302.a: Find the most impactful settings, borrow what worked on similar devices before, and pick the best one dynamically based on what resources are available right now.

303.p: When you have facts organized as networks with text and images mixed in, answering questions like 'find me something like this' is tough because images lie sometimes but text is vague.
303.a: Score each piece of data by how much it looks and sounds like the question, separately for each type of information, then blend them smarter based on context.

304.p: Attackers hide secret web control panels inside smart home and IoT devices to steal data or hijack them, and today's scanners miss most of these hidden doors.
304.a: Reverse-engineer the device's wiring map to find all hidden buttons, then use an AI system to automatically send test requests and check if they work.

305.p: Social networks and sensor readings change over time, and odd behavior that deviates from normal patterns hides in that change; old static methods can't catch it.
305.a: Build a model that remembers important details from the past and spots weirdness by measuring similarity across multiple time scales at once.

306.p: Simulating how diseases spread or ideas go viral through billions of social connections is too slow, even with powerful computers, for practical use.
306.a: Combine fine-grained step-by-step updates with fast statistical sampling, split the network smartly to cut talking between computers, and run it all in parallel.

307.p: Spotting dangerous fake accounts in social networks when you only have a handful of labeled examples is nearly impossible; real patterns hide under noise.
307.a: Extract stable causal patterns by filtering out random noise, then ask the model which unlabeled accounts matter most to label next.

308.p: AI systems often pick between good and bad choices, but in real life, nobody agrees on what good means—utilitarians want happiness, others want duty or fairness.
308.a: Give the AI competing moral frameworks with adjustable weights, and let it learn from experience which balance works best in each situation.

309.p: When you search the web, your search tool was trained on full articles, but at runtime it has to work with computer-written summaries that look and sound different.
309.a: Train a summarizer to write summaries the search tool loves, and retrain the search tool on those summaries, swapping back and forth until they fit.

310.p: E-commerce merchants have to decide when to raise bids in ads and when to offer discounts, but need to make both decisions together so one doesn't break the other.
310.a: Teach an AI to make both decisions in sequence, tweaking its choices so it maximizes profits while staying within a budget that only comes from commission.

311.p: Online retailers with billions of customer records and hundreds of raw measurements need fast predictions for recommendations, but the data is skewed and messy.
311.a: Use a specialized math network to automatically learn good transformations of each raw measurement, then feed those into a fast neural network that spots patterns.

312.p: Running image-recognition models while keeping user data completely private on a web server requires so much communication and time that it kills the service.
312.a: Redesign the neural network to work well with privacy-protecting math, reuse data across layers to save bandwidth, and swap out expensive operations for simpler ones.

313.p: AI systems are great at reasoning, but can they write down clear, step-by-step proofs that humans can read and verify, using formal logic instead of just yes-or-no?
313.a: Build a framework to test how well an AI extracts, simplifies, and explains logical proofs from structured knowledge, and measure where it breaks down.

314.p: AI language systems recommendation systems ignore the long tail problem: they work great for popular items but fail on niche ones that users actually want.
314.a: Tweak the model's loss function item-by-item to penalize overconfident bad predictions on rare items, keeping the math efficient enough for huge systems.

315.p: Shopping bots ask questions but struggle to learn which questions worked best when answers come back many steps later and across many different interactions.
315.a: Measure three human motivations—feeling in control, doing well, and being heard—and use those to give the bot constant internal feedback as it learns.

316.p: Security filters on websites try to block attacks in data streams, but can be fooled by how different systems order and process that same data differently.
316.a: Rearrange the order of data in legal ways that trick security filters into missing attacks while real servers still process them correctly.

317.p: Devices checking for illegal radio broadcasts can only listen to tiny slices of frequencies at once, so they miss most of what's happening and can't learn properly.
317.a: Let devices share what each one hears, so they learn from each other's partial views using a system that understands how frequency bands connect.

318.p: Open-source code repositories get poisoned with malicious packages that rule-based detection misses, yet dangerous code keeps sneaking through.
318.a: Build a library of known malicious code and reasons why it's harmful, then check new packages against that library using an AI that reads like an expert.

319.p: Multiple recommendation services want to learn together without sharing user data, but AI systems encode what they know invisibly and inconsistently across domains.
319.a: Share only the direction of learning changes, not the full magnitude, so each service adapts without dominating the joint learning.

320.p: Learning from graph-shaped data relies on subtle local patterns, but the model overfits to those patterns and can't generalize to new graphs.
320.a: Corrupt the data strategically to hide some patterns, forcing the model to learn both local details and broad principles that work anywhere.

321.p: Online ad platforms must split budgets across channels with different behavior, but markets change fast and past methods either can't adapt or forget history.
321.a: Use a system that plans budget changes from historical patterns, then adjusts moment-by-moment when reality shifts from the plan.

322.p: Cities and governments make big decisions based on data and algorithms, but nobody fully understands how that data actually reshapes what gets discussed and decided.
322.a: Survey research across disciplines to map where and how data and AI shift the balance of power among people negotiating policy.

323.p: The web has evolved through many choices about ranking, openness, and scale, yet we keep repeating old tensions with each new technology like AI.
323.a: Trace the web's history of ranking and knowledge systems to spot which problems keep returning and what genuinely changed with modern AI.

324.p: Quantum computing services need to fix errors but can't see the actual circuits without risking that companies steal each other's secret designs.
324.a: Use cryptographic proofs to let the service fix errors using only aggregate statistics without ever seeing the full circuit itself.

325.p: Assigning papers to conference reviewers means balancing effort fairly when some reviewers volunteered for certain papers and others didn't.
325.a: Assign papers so no reviewer feels cheated, everyone gets roughly equal work, and total effort stays as low as possible.

326.p: AI agents shopping online make choices in ways humans don't, and those choices can be biased or random in ways that break how marketplaces are supposed to work.
326.a: Test AI agents on a mock marketplace to see which product features and page positions actually drive their choices versus what we assumed.

327.p: Graph-based AI systems learn from one area but forget or do poorly when learning in a new, different area afterward.
327.a: Keep separate skill modules for each new area that don't interfere with old skills, letting knowledge from all areas boost performance together.

328.p: Finding which friends form a tight group is hard when you start from just one person and early wrong guesses derail the whole search.
328.a: Model community groups as flows through geometric space, pick better starting people, and use anchors to guide the search to the right group.

329.p: Images with text, fake videos, and memes spread fast online and mislead people, but understanding them fully requires reading text and images together.
329.a: Bring together researchers across image analysis, text analysis, and social science to build tools that analyze text-and-image content as one thing.

330.p: AI systems that suggest products read your browsing history, but struggle to blend two different strategies: learning from what similar people liked, and understanding what actually makes you personally interested.
330.a: Convert the signals from what-similar-people-did into the same format the AI uses for word prediction, then train both together so neither strategy drowns out the other.

331.p: When you mix text, images, and structured facts into a giant web of connections, different tasks want different pieces of information, but one-size-fits-all systems throw everything at every problem.
331.a: Build a system that learns to route different information pieces to different tasks, so each one gets only what it actually needs.

332.p: AI systems that learn from how things connect to each other are vulnerable to poisoned training data hidden in those connections, and today's defenses only stop specific known attacks.
332.a: Spot suspicious nodes in the network first, then automatically pick defense strategies without knowing what attack was used.

333.p: Web search evolved from just matching keywords, to understanding meaning, to AI systems that guess answers for you—but we haven't asked if this is actually better or if we're losing something important.
333.a: Walk through the technical steps behind modern search and ask hard questions: What are we losing when machines guess? Are we widening inequality? Eroding skills?

334.p: AI systems that answer by first looking up facts work well for simple questions, but they retrieve information only after they finish drafting an answer, missing chances to fill in holes mid-thought.
334.a: Break complex questions into small steps, measure the AI's doubt at each step using three different signals, combine them, and trigger fact lookups when doubt is high.

335.p: Cryptocurrency mixing services hide money flows to protect privacy, but criminals use them too, and security researchers can't test detection techniques without good data.
335.a: Automatically run fake mixing transactions in a test blockchain to create a large realistic dataset, then use it to show which existing detection methods actually work.

336.p: People running their own AI systems on their own servers to keep data private often don't know those systems are exposed to the internet with no password, inviting attackers in.
336.a: Automatically scan public AI deployments to find and test common security holes—then tell people how to fix them.

337.p: When you ask an AI a complex question with many parts, it asks clarification questions one by one, but doesn't realize some questions need to be answered before others to actually help.
337.a: Identify which questions logically depend on each other, ask them in the right order, and teach the AI which question paths work best.

338.p: AI systems for tracking how things move and change over time usually flatten everything into a single geometry, but real networks have natural curves and folds that get distorted.
338.a: Build a system that changes and learns while respecting the actual geometric shape of the network itself, not forcing it into flat space.

339.p: When high-stakes AI systems (medical, legal, scientific) make mistakes, we need to know if they're likely wrong, but word-confidence scores are fragile and fail when topics are unfamiliar.
339.a: Look at how the AI's inner states change during generation; if they're wobbly and unstable, the answer is probably wrong, and this works without running it twice.

340.p: AI systems that learn from examples in a chat prompt can be fooled by attackers who slip in fake examples or bury real instructions, but it's hard to test these vulnerabilities.
340.a: Design attacks that slip past without querying the AI, prove they work, and create automatic defenses that harden the chat prompts against them.

341.p: When dividing unpleasant tasks (like chores) fairly among many people, mathematical fairness is impossible, and real-world systems have to decide who gets unfairly burdened.
341.a: Guarantee all but one person gets their fair share, while the last person gets almost-fair, so most users stay happy—the right tradeoff for real platforms.

342.p: Recommendation systems that predict what you'll want next have to juggle what similar people liked, what the words mean, and how you rated things before, but mixing these signals well is hard.
342.a: Use an AI that reads text to understand what things mean, mix that with collaborative and rating signals, and train on softer targets to capture richer behavior patterns.

343.p: Recommendation systems need compact, fast numeric fingerprints for searching millions of items, but compact usually means less expressive—creating an impossible tradeoff in production systems.
343.a: Train on sparse numeric fingerprints instead of dense ones, cutting size 10x with zero accuracy loss, and the sparse patterns reveal how items naturally cluster.

344.p: News on YouTube reaches millions, and channels use emotional framing to drive engagement, but we don't know which emotions work across different cultures or how deep that engagement really goes.
344.a: Analyze images and titles together to measure moral emotion in 400,000 videos across Korea and the US, then test whether outrage-based framing drives passive views or active arguing.

345.p: Medical image analysis systems trained on clean data fail in reality because actual doctors disagree on what they see, yet we still need a fair way to measure if new systems work.
345.a: Built a dataset of cell images where four pathologists labeled each one, plus one senior expert's definitive answer, so researchers can test both how well systems match the gold standard and how well they resolve expert disagreement.

346.p: AI systems that look up facts before answering perform worse when the facts keep changing—new articles appear daily, old information becomes outdated—because retraining the search engine costs too much.
346.a: Update only a tiny fraction of the search engine (0.64% of parameters) using a layered learning method that makes retrieval decisions align with the AI's final answers, not just raw similarity.

347.p: We treat data as infinite and free to reuse, but every time someone analyzes personal data, private information leaks out, and these leaks add up when the same data is used repeatedly.
347.a: Recognize data as a consumable resource like fuel—privacy loss accumulates with each use—and design systems and policies that budget how many times overlapping datasets can be analyzed.

348.p: Social networks are messy privacy problems: protecting one person without leaking information about their friends is hard, because everyone's data is tangled up with everyone else's.
348.a: Weight the connections between people carefully without cutting them off, so sensitivity calculations stay tight and tight privacy noise doesn't destroy the network's usefulness.

349.p: Wikipedia and GitHub now mix human knowledge with AI-written text, but feedback loops could dilute quality—if people learn from AI instead of the archive, AI then trains on both, and quality spirals down.
349.a: Built a mathematical model tracking how archive size, human skill, AI skill, and platform rules all interact, then tested it on real Wikipedia data to predict when systems stay healthy or collapse.

350.p: Finding dense clusters in two-sided networks (users and items, buyers and sellers) is slow because existing methods enumerate all possible dense cliques, which explodes in cost.
350.a: Count connections cleverly instead of listing them all, so clustering runs fast, and then prune edges that can't possibly matter to shrink the problem before you start.

351.p: Finding and separating closely related topics in a narrow domain is hard: off-the-shelf search systems are too generic, but hand-labeling every article is expensive.
351.a: Use an AI system to label a small random sample, then teach a cheap local model to cluster the rest, keeping the interpretability of traditional methods without labeling thousands of articles.

352.p: Journalists can't track shifts in social movements fast enough to report on real links between activism and events like elections or policy changes.
352.a: Collect posts and news, extract emotional themes, then predict future emotion patterns so journalists spot discourse shifts early and understand what external events shaped the movement.

353.p: People using AI chatbots trust them blindly because the system hides how it makes decisions and what reasoning tricks it uses to give answers that please users.
353.a: Show hidden signals and reasoning patterns through visual dashboards, so users see when the AI is reasoning versus conforming, and learn to evaluate and trust it appropriately.

354.p: When a model sees images and text together from new distributions, performance drops because it learned features that work in training but break when the real world shifts.
354.a: Automatically gate which features get used at prediction time, keeping only those stable across environments, combined with adversarial training to find truly causal patterns.

355.p: Researchers cite papers in ways that contradict them, or cite claims those papers never actually made, and today's methods can't detect this subtly wrong citation because they ignore the broader network.
355.a: Use an AI to reason through multi-step citation chains and spot contradictions, then shrink that expensive reasoning into a faster system that learns graph patterns to flag miscitations at scale.

356.p: Real-world data like finance or health arrives as tangled multi-dimensional time series where hundreds of variables interact, and tracking which ones influence which is computationally impossible.
356.a: Estimate separate dependency networks for each dimension using a Kronecker product structure, which breaks the explosion in complexity and stays fast even as new data arrives.

357.p: Cloud-based AI systems personalized at the edge can't be private: the cloud can reconstruct users' raw prompts from the intermediate data sent to it before processing.
357.a: Split intermediate numeric fingerprints into public and private parts, send only the public part to the cloud, then perfectly restore the private part's effect through compensation—lossless and secure.

358.p: Internet traffic gets hijacked, censored, and redirected in the DNS layer, but the scale and methods of these attacks are invisible because domains bounce between thousands of edge servers dynamically.
358.a: Analyze how domain names resolve through chains of redirects to link results, then measure manipulation across thousands of popular domains on global DNS systems to reveal attacker patterns.

359.p: Websites change their layouts constantly, breaking old analysis tools and making it hard to study long-term patterns in how web design evolves.
359.a: Archived over 246 million HTML structure snapshots from 223 popular sites, each precisely timestamped, so researchers can study layout changes and build tools that survive web evolution.

360.p: When edge devices like drones and base stations train AI models together, they must share data or models to learn from each other, but this creates huge communication costs and privacy problems.
360.a: Instead of sharing raw data or models, send only small summaries of learned patterns that are mixed with slight variations, letting each device learn without exposing private information.

361.p: City planning today relies on slow, expensive expert committees, but people who actually live in cities have no say in what gets built in their neighborhoods.
361.a: Let residents describe what they want in plain language, use an AI system that learns from trying different plans and rewards, and simulate resident satisfaction to pick the best design.

362.p: Recognizing emotions in videos requires understanding both what people say and how they look, but audio and visual data are very different and hard to combine at deep levels.
362.a: Build a system where sound and images take turns guiding each other at every stage of analysis, so they gradually learn how to coordinate across their differences.

363.p: Recommendation systems that learn from who-buys-what sometimes fail because the web of connections between users and items is weak or disconnected in certain regions.
363.a: Automatically identify and strengthen the weakest connection links in the network by learning which edges matter most, using mathematical properties of how information flows.

364.p: Most AI systems controlling what you see online hide how they work, what data they used, and what decisions they made, making it impossible to audit or appeal.
364.a: Create a transparent ledger system similar to certificate transparency that records proof of every AI decision and its sources, verifiable by anyone without revealing private details.

365.p: Detecting hateful meme comments requires both images and text, but online systems often break when one source is missing, forcing companies to build separate backup systems.
365.a: Train one flexible system that projects both images and text into a shared safety score, so it works with just one type of data without needing to rebuild.

366.p: Current building layout systems require users to write very formal instructions and give no way to see and adjust the design before final rendering.
366.a: Break natural language instructions into simpler tasks, show a 3D model users can edit interactively, and render photorealistic views from any angle they choose.

367.p: There is no standard way to fairly test if AI systems work well on legal tasks, so researchers cannot compare results or check if new methods actually help.
367.a: Build a toolkit that bundles many legal task tests, lets researchers run experiments flexibly with a web interface, and makes results reproducible for everyone.

368.p: Starlink satellites provide internet globally, but nobody outside SpaceX knows how their ground network is organized, where security holes exist, or how they operate.
368.a: Use DNS records and network scanning to map Starlink's internal architecture, observe user behavior patterns, and identify vulnerable or exposed services.

369.p: Chinese idioms often mean something completely different from their literal words, and the same idiom shifts meaning depending on context, confusing AI systems reading text and images together.
369.a: Map out how each idiom's literal meaning relates to its true meaning, then train separate expert branches that specialize in literal versus metaphorical understanding.

370.p: When AI systems retrieve facts from organized knowledge before answering, attackers can inject fake information into those databases and trick the AI into giving harmful answers.
370.a: Plant poisoned facts that appear as a natural evolution from existing knowledge, so the reorganized structure makes the fake information seem to emerge correctly from history.

371.p: Networks like social graphs hide tree structures within them, but standard learning methods treat all connection patterns equally without exploiting this hidden hierarchy.
371.a: Extract the tree structure from the graph to identify important bridges and central nodes, then use this multi-level information to create smarter ways to modify the data for learning.

372.p: VTuber performers who create digital personas sometimes quit due to burnout or harassment, and when they start over with a new identity, both they and audiences lose money and trust.
372.a: Analyze 728,000 livestreams to measure exactly how much performers, companies, and communities lose financially and in viewership when someone starts fresh with a new avatar.

373.p: Classifying nodes in networks fails when test data contains completely new classes never seen during training, and models cannot cleanly separate known from unknown categories.
373.a: Mix training data with neighboring patterns in strategic ways and use cross-layer similarity matching to make the model tighter within classes and more confident rejecting unknowns.

374.p: Live streaming platforms must detect harmful content or social signals instantly from video, audio, and text together, but running AI on all frames costs too much compute.
374.a: Use a fast lightweight model for most moments and only send hard cases to a heavy vision-language model, deferring judgment when there is not enough context yet.

375.p: YouTube's algorithm shows people different videos depending on length, and nobody knows if short videos push viewers toward one political side more than long ones.
375.a: Compared recommendations for the same news story in both short and long form to see which version showed more political bias or diverse viewpoints.

376.p: When people ask AI systems questions about events that happened at specific times, the AI often forgets what time it is or mixes up the order of events.
376.a: Built a system that stores facts with exact dates and times, then checks each answer step-by-step to make sure the timeline makes sense.

377.p: Online businesses want to know which customers will spend a lot of money, but most customers spend very little, making the valuable ones hard to spot.
377.a: Created a system that first separates customers into groups by spending level, then predicts exactly how much each group will spend.

378.p: If AI systems write most of the content on the web, search engines might end up reading AI-generated answers instead of real information, breaking search itself.
378.a: Tested what happens when fake AI content floods search results to see how quickly search quality falls apart.

379.p: AI agents on the web must choose what to do next without perfect information, balancing trying new things against repeating what already worked.
379.a: Teaches AI agents how to make smart decisions by borrowing methods from gambling—knowing when to explore new options versus sticking with winners.

380.p: Ad-ranking systems trained on messy real-world data break when their inputs shift or contain bad numbers, costing money through pricing mistakes.
380.a: Watches for sudden changes in how ads are priced, then automatically fixes broken numbers before they cause expensive mistakes.

381.p: Chinese toxic language hides in deliberately scrambled spelling, fake characters, and shortcuts that traditional filters cannot recognize.
381.a: Built a connected map of toxic words and their disguises, then taught an AI system to spot hidden meaning by reasoning through the connections.

382.p: Dengue outbreaks spread in patterns through neighborhoods, and cities need to predict where the next cases will happen to stop the spread early.
382.a: Created a system that models how diseases flow between districts using weather and population data, producing weekly risk forecasts for each area.

383.p: Finding the exact style or color of a piece of clothing in photos is hard because standard methods get distracted by backgrounds and zoom too far out.
383.a: Looks at meaningful clusters of pixels rather than tiny patches, focusing attention only on the specific style details the user cares about.

384.p: Crowdsourcing platforms let bad workers produce garbage labels and good workers feel cheated, making it hard to get high-quality training data.
384.a: Pays workers based on whether their specific answers helped or hurt the final result, penalizing bad work without destroying worker motivation.

385.p: Recommender systems struggle when most users rate nothing and popular items get rated way more often than niche ones.
385.a: Transforms the user-item data into a different form where sparse and imbalanced problems become standard problems with known solutions.

386.p: Research papers about web systems spread across thousands of separate studies with no clear guidebook for what we've learned or what works best.
386.a: A workshop where experts gather to write surveys and reviews that pull together key lessons from many papers into actionable insights.

387.p: Industrial systems like power grids need lightning-fast real-time security, but new encryption methods are too slow and cause dangerous delays.
387.a: Uses lighter, faster cryptography for the speed-critical sensors and saves the heavier encryption for the slower, safer parts of the system.

388.p: New AI-powered search engines might be fooled by tricks that worked against older search engines, allowing scammers to hijack results.
388.a: Tested ten popular AI search engines with 1,000 real scam websites to find which tricks still work and which ones the AI blocks.

389.p: Training AI on many phones at once fails when different phones use different AI models that cannot learn from each other.
389.a: Uses a middle-layer server on each network that translates knowledge between different models so all phones can learn together.

390.p: Real estate listings lie constantly about being new developments, but spotting the lies requires checking text, images, and data sources together—which most systems do one at a time.
390.a: They combined weak signals from multiple sources and used a system that learns from how entities connect to each other, keeping answers consistent across linked projects and organizations.

391.p: Streaming platforms want to predict what shows will blow up next week, but AI systems struggle to learn from millions of past user choices and then rank every option fast enough.
391.a: They used a trained AI system to forecast which items will become hits tomorrow and explain why in simple language, pairing its predictions with real trend data to stay accurate.

392.p: Generated networks often have a tiny critical core that matters, surrounded by noise and clutter, but current systems treat all edges as equally important.
392.a: They learned to spot the critical edges first using topology math, then built the network layer by layer, adding the important bits early and filling in clutter later.

393.p: Factories using AI for safety rely on cameras, sensors, and human workers together, but failures happen at the seams—when a camera disagrees with a sensor or a human misreads the screen.
393.a: They surveyed real factory breakdowns and organized risks into five layers: data, models, systems, organizations, and rules, then matched each risk type to actual fixes that work across these boundaries.

394.p: Shopping recommendation systems learn from who bought what, and adding social network info helps, but storing one number per person costs too much memory and slows everything down.
394.a: They built user profiles from social signals without storing a unique number for each person, cutting memory in half while still beating existing systems at finding good matches.

395.p: Wikipedia editors must manually check that claims have citations, a constant chore, but doing this for all ten language editions is slow and misses the ones that need help most.
395.a: They built a machine learning system that flags claims needing citations in ten Wikipedia languages, tested it for both accuracy and speed, and put it to work in production.

396.p: Predicting tomorrow's traffic without sharing data between cities (for privacy) fails because each city's patterns are unique and messy, but they still need global knowledge.
396.a: They separated each city's unique traffic rhythms from shared patterns across cities, using math to keep these two parts from mixing, so knowledge transfers without leaking private data.

397.p: Banks have private tools for research and trades, but AI systems trained on generic data don't know how to call these tools or understand finance-specific quirks in real user questions.
397.a: They collected real finance questions, expanded the dataset to cover edge cases, and trained the AI system on two steps: understanding which tool fits and executing it correctly.

398.p: Browsers running AI agents in real-time face three walls: too little memory for instant context, network delays for each step, and no defense against malicious websites hijacking the agent.
398.a: They used WebAssembly (a sandbox inside the browser) to keep context fast, batch multiple steps to cut delays, and limit what untrusted websites can trick the agent into doing.

399.p: AI systems trained for one kind of network graph (like social networks) fail on another kind (like molecule structures) because features mean totally different things in each domain.
399.a: They identified what stays the same about node features across all graphs and trained a foundation model that transforms any graph into a shared format for knowledge transfer.

400.p: Graph AI systems are fragile—tiny tweaks to a few important nodes can fool the whole network—and defenses that work for one attack often fail on newer, sneakier attacks.
400.a: They designed a defense that watches if input features still carry the information needed for correct answers, filtering out junk while keeping the signal, and tested it on many attack types.

401.p: Predicting city traffic during storms is nearly impossible because storms are rare, messy, and weather's effect on traffic is subtle and varies across locations and times.
401.a: They split normal traffic patterns from weather effects into separate branches, added fake weather scenarios to training data while protecting real patterns, and tested on three cities during extreme weather.

402.p: AI answer engines like ChatGPT fetch pages fresh for every question instead of using cached results, burning far more electricity and internet bandwidth than a search engine does.
402.a: They measured what ChatGPT and Claude actually fetch on real queries and found both rely heavily on existing caches, suggesting shared caches and transparency standards could cut waste.

403.p: Short texts online are sparse and vague, making it hard to group them by meaning, especially when some topics are rare and skewed so the AI guesses wrong group labels.
403.a: They guessed which group each cluster belongs to at each training step, then fixed wrong labels and refined profiles, teaching the system to handle imbalanced, messy web data.

404.p: Memes with harmful intent hide in jokes and symbols, so spotting abuse requires understanding cultural knowledge and joking, but AI systems often miss the meaning or confuse satire with hate.
404.a: They enriched image and text understanding with knowledge from cultural databases, fine-tuned the AI to sharpen distinctions between satire and abuse, and made its reasoning transparent.

405.p: AI systems reviewing research papers make decisions based only on text, but papers contain tables and formulas too—so we never know if the AI would flip its opinion if the numbers changed.
405.a: Built a test box that rewrites parts of papers (text, tables, formulas) to see if the AI's review stays consistent, and shows which breakdowns happen.

406.p: Companies host many AI systems with different abilities and costs, but don't know which one to use for which question, so they waste money running expensive systems on simple tasks.
406.a: Learn what each AI system is good at and what it costs, then pick the cheapest reliable one for each question based on how hard it is.

407.p: Stores choose book covers and images randomly, but what a person sees first often decides whether they click—yet most recommendation systems ignore this entirely.
407.a: Use vision and language systems together to understand what pictures appeal to each person, then pick covers that fit their taste.

408.p: When a text talks about multiple topics at once, systems struggle to say which parts belong to which topic, confusing readers about what the text actually means.
408.a: Teach an AI to reason through each topic step by step, then highlight which words matter for each one.

409.p: Stores have limited coupons or inventory, so giving the best offer to today's customer might leave nothing for tomorrow's person who would pay more.
409.a: Pick items that give good value to current customers while saving the best items for future customers who might be willing to spend more.

410.p: AI systems recommend products but give no reason, so you can't tell if they understood your taste or just guessed based on your last purchase.
410.a: Train AI to explain its thinking first (why you might like this), then make the recommendation, so humans can judge if it makes sense.

411.p: E-commerce search is slow when AI tries to explain why it matched your search, but if we drop the explanation at serving time, all that thinking power is wasted.
411.a: Make one AI think through many angles of what you meant, then teach a fast AI to copy that thinking using the original reasoning as a guide.

412.p: When companies learn together without sharing raw data, their models latch onto local quirks instead of real patterns, and we can't tell which pieces of the model actually matter.
412.a: Find training examples where the models disagree, use those to fix shortcut learning, and add noise to features to make predictions depend only on true patterns.

413.p: Indoor 5G signal quality is hard to predict inside buildings because radio waves bounce off walls in complex ways—measuring from outside gives few clues about inside.
413.a: Use a system that learns how signals really spread through buildings, not just straight lines, to predict indoor quality from a few exterior sensor readings.

414.p: Graph systems often remove edges to go faster, but nobody explains which edges are useless and which are just quiet—you're guessing in the dark.
414.a: Use a fair scoring method to rank edges by importance, then remove the lowest ones, so you see exactly what was cut and why.

415.p: Social media floods us with posts about events, but sifting through millions to track what's happening and how it evolves is too slow and noisy.
415.a: Sample the most representative posts from the stream, then have an AI look up facts about the event to build an evolving map of what's going on.

416.p: System logs arrive at random times in bursts with different kinds of information, but most anomaly detectors assume steady, regular input—so they miss real problems.
416.a: Build a graph that tracks how log entries relate through time, content, and damage patterns, and adjust what you pay attention to as the flow changes.

417.p: Robots navigating unknown spaces need to find objects but training them takes huge amounts of data and computing power.
417.a: Use off-the-shelf vision systems trained on real photos to understand 3D spaces and match text descriptions, so robots can navigate without any training.

418.p: Using one AI system to recommend things limits what it can do—different systems are better at different kinds of reasoning, but companies pick just one.
418.a: Route each user or item to the AI systems that are best at handling it, combine their answers, and never retrain the underlying systems.

419.p: When AI systems generate answers by looking up facts, they sometimes make things up anyway, and existing methods waste time checking facts they'll never use.
419.a: Probe the AI's uncertainty at the word and fact level to know when to look up information, then rank results by how confident the system was.

420.p: When hiring one candidate from a random stream of applicants, you must decide now with no future information—but how do you avoid picking poorly?
420.a: Use a pricing strategy that balances waiting for better candidates against the risk of missing good ones, achieving 25% better decisions than the classic approach.

421.p: When attackers flip labels in training data to fool AI models, some categories get hurt much more than others, but nobody understood why until now.
421.a: Identify which class pairs are easiest to confuse, then train the AI to push them further apart in its internal thinking space, protecting vulnerable categories.

422.p: Creating a tiny dataset that trains AI as well as a huge one saves energy, but the tiny versions only work on the same type of AI they were built for.
422.a: Design synthetic data by making it forget which specific AI architecture created it, so the data teaches any model equally well, not just the original one.

423.p: Search engines and recommendation sites must be fair to all groups and businesses, but the rules for fairness are scattered and hard to compare.
423.a: Borrow three dimensions from economics—big-picture vs. individual, what people want vs. what's supplied, immediate vs. long-term—to organize all fairness rules in one framework.

424.p: Community fact-checking systems show helpful corrections, but after they go live, people with opposite views often vote them down and they disappear.
424.a: Analyze how ratings shift after a note becomes visible and show that polarized voting from people who disagree drives helpful corrections off the platform.

425.p: Factory machines send constant sensor data that could predict breakdowns, but sending it all to the cloud is slow, and keeping it local loses accuracy.
425.a: Scan sensor data at the factory for warning signs, send suspicious cases to the cloud for expert analysis, then use an AI assistant to explain findings in plain language.

426.p: Graphs where nodes have text descriptions (like social media or research papers) take huge memory and time to train, slowing down AI research.
426.a: Compress both the text and connections by picking key text pieces and matching similar connections, shrinking datasets to 1% size without losing learning accuracy.

427.p: In quiet search environments, emerging trends invisible in search data stay hidden until they're already mainstream and no longer news.
427.a: Generate search queries directly from news posts before users search, then continuously learn what's trending by adjusting the AI without forgetting past lessons.

428.p: Describing a video in natural language is hard because the visual and text must align, and the AI misses connections between what you see and what to say.
428.a: Build a graph linking visual concepts and text words, then generate captions while respecting what that graph suggests, filtering out weak connections.

429.p: Web3 platforms produce rich time-stamped records ideal for understanding user behavior and predicting churn, but shared standards for testing new methods are missing.
429.a: Create a public test set using real blockchain transactions where users predict who will stop using the platform, showing that domain-specific features beat generic ones.

430.p: Travel planning tools are either static listings or chatbots, but travelers need fresh itineraries tailored to their tastes and updated with new information.
430.a: Scrape live travel articles, summarize them, then use AI to compose itineraries right in your browser, with sliders to control preferences for history, nature, culture.

431.p: Spotting network attacks requires detecting computers talking to many others, but current methods miss that attackers often hit targets in the same neighborhood.
431.a: Estimate connections grouped by IP address subnet instead of full address, using clever hashing to stay fast and small while catching 8 times more attacks.

432.p: Adapting AI systems to spot misinformation on social networks needs thousands of labeled examples, but getting humans to label sensitive content is slow and costly.
432.a: Teach the AI on both labeled and unlabeled posts, letting it learn from connections between posts and refining its own labels as it sees more patterns.

433.p: NFTs promise to be permanent digital assets on the blockchain, but many actually depend on fragile centralized storage that can vanish or be tampered with.
433.a: Analyze 16 million real NFTs and map storage problems into eight vulnerability types—from access failures to forgeries—then score their real-world severity.

434.p: Ad blockers that use AI work well on test data but fail in the real world when attackers tweak ads, blockers drift over time, and new websites surprise them.
434.a: Extract stable features from code and URLs that are hard for attackers to disguise, then use cheap pseudo-labeling to keep accuracy high without constant retraining.

435.p: Social media and recommendation algorithms each push people into separate information bubbles, but nobody fully understands how these two forces work together to split us apart.
435.a: Built a computer simulation with artificial people connected like a social network, where algorithms feed them content in real-time, showing how the two effects combine to create stronger echo chambers.

436.p: AI systems now show their working thoughts to improve transparency, but we found that these reasoning traces accidentally reveal whether the AI has seen something before during training, leaking private information.
436.a: Created an attack that scores how familiar or uncertain the AI's reasoning looks, then maps that score onto an axis to guess whether something was in the training data.

437.p: In developing countries, people with low reading skills download loan and gambling apps, but predatory companies hide the real dangers in fine print they know people won't understand, causing massive financial fraud.
437.a: Tested whether AI-generated summaries, translations, and pictures can make privacy terms clear enough that ordinary people actually understand what they're signing up for.

438.p: Websites need to predict which items connect well together (products you might buy with another, people who might become friends), but they struggle when things have multiple kinds of relationships that help or hurt each other.
438.a: Built a system that learns which relationships boost each other and which clash, then uses that to better predict which connections matter most.

439.p: Drones fly and film fast, so lightweight AI models on the drone get confused by sudden changes, yet drones can't afford to retrain constantly or they fall behind.
439.a: Designed a system that detects when the drone's video has changed drastically, shares retraining across nearby drones, and reuses old models that performed well in similar conditions.

440.p: Cities need detailed demographic information to plan schools and services, but privacy rules block census data from being that specific, leaving huge blind spots at the neighborhood level.
440.a: Used what people search for on Yelp and which businesses they visit to infer fine-grained neighborhood wealth and demographics, bridging the gap between coarse public data and what planners need.

441.p: AI systems write so fluently now that fake AI text fools human readers the same way real human text does, but we don't yet understand why people fall for it or how to train them to spot it.
441.a: Tested hundreds of people on whether they could tell AI-written text from human text, then used statistical causal analysis to prove that exposure to fake news actually trains people to be better detectors, not worse.

442.p: Detecting fake news with both text and images is hard because labeled training data is scarce, messy, and imbalanced, so AI models can't learn reliably.
442.a: Built a generator-discriminator system that creates artificial text-image pairs for training while checking that fake and real are properly separated, letting scarce data stretch farther.

443.p: Sensors and IoT devices often miss readings because of network hiccups or breakdowns, and the gaps break downstream tasks like finding anomalies, but noise injection in standard fix methods doesn't adapt to how real data is actually shaped.
443.a: Instead of injecting noise uniformly, we adjust the noise strength separately for each frequency so it matches how energy is actually distributed in the real data.

444.p: Real-world web apps show you content from many sources but some views go missing, and they introduce new categories constantly, forcing models to learn under both problems at once.
444.a: Built a system that learns flexible patterns that work when views are missing and adapts to new classes without exploding in size, by compressing the learned patterns into atomic pieces.

445.p: Recommendation systems need to generate personalized suggestions using language AI, but the raw AI often misses what a customer actually wants because it doesn't use their personal history smartly enough.
445.a: Used customer-business relationships to build two-way signals (what items are popular vs. what is personally relevant) and kept the meaning intact when compressing the recommendation codes.

446.p: AI systems that look up facts before answering work well for trivia, but break down on tasks like recommendations where you need to guess what someone will like, not retrieve a known answer.
446.a: Designed a retrieval system that compares a customer's past behavior to candidate items using meaning-based similarity, then weights the AI's answer using that personalized signal.

447.p: When companies use fake AI-generated data to train new AI, the fake data gets worse at each step, losing rare details and diversity, until the AI collapses into speaking all the same way.
447.a: Found underrepresented regions in the data, then used structured instructions to steer the AI to generate more examples of those rare cases, keeping diversity alive without retraining.

448.p: Edge devices coordinating workflow tasks can't find services they need when networks cut out and devices drop offline, even though similar services are still available and could work just as well.
448.a: Built a resilient registry system where each device acts as an intelligent agent that learns which services are similar, shares that knowledge locally, and recovers gracefully when connections drop.

449.p: Modern image AI systems are huge and expensive to retrain for each new task, even though they already learned general image understanding from massive pretraining.
449.a: Surveyed methods that update only a tiny fraction of the model's knobs so tasks can adapt without the full computational cost, analyzing trade-offs between speed, accuracy, and parameter efficiency.

450.p: When someone describes a legal problem in a few sentences but searches a huge court document, the AI struggles because it learned to match similar-length texts together.
450.a: Find the most relevant parts of the legal document using a specialized scorer, then retrain the AI to understand legal writing better and match short descriptions to long documents accurately.

451.p: Online shopping sites struggle to guess whether you'll click an ad or product because predicting clicks requires understanding many overlapping features at once.
451.a: Use multiple separate neural networks that each learn different patterns, then have them teach and correct each other to work together and predict clicks better.

452.p: When a search engine knows facts through text and images about people and companies, it misses how those facts relate to each other within each type of information.
452.a: Build separate networks for text and images that learn relationships within each, then smartly combine what they learned, giving more weight to the most useful facts.

453.p: Recommendation systems measure success by clicks and time spent, ignoring whether users actually trust the suggestions or feel they had control over what they see.
453.a: Measure success by asking real people about trust, choice, and honesty instead of just counting clicks, then design systems around what actually matters to them.

454.p: Ads platforms predict how many people will buy, but their global predictions fail for some groups of people while overestimating for others, unfairly treating different audiences.
454.a: Frame prediction fairness as a balance problem and find the right mix of adjustments across different groups so no single group gets systematically over- or under-estimated.

455.p: Social networks influence recommendations in complex hidden ways, and current explainers only show which connections matter, not how they work together to influence the final choice.
455.a: Find small groups of connected people whose combined influence explains the recommendation, then show the actual path from you to the suggested item through that group.

456.p: Training powerful AI that handles both text and images requires gathering everyone's private data in one place, which companies cannot do for privacy and legal reasons.
456.a: Train lightweight add-ons to the AI at each person's device without sharing data, then combine only those add-ons at a central server to save privacy and communication.

457.p: To recommend products across very different marketplaces, systems must learn from each domain separately because features and product types don't carry over between them.
457.a: Use an AI that writes language to create universal descriptions that mean the same thing across all marketplaces, then learn patterns that transfer from rich to sparse domains.

458.p: Taiwan's land agency wastes time and money on fieldwork because scheduling is manual and forecasting how long each land survey will take is inaccurate.
458.a: Build a system that learns from maps and field data to predict survey time accurately, then intelligently assigns and schedules work to save time and labor costs.

459.p: Robots in labs need to understand what objects can do from lab photos found on the web, but those photos are messy and lack precise 3D measurements that robots need.
459.a: Convert web photos into structured 3D descriptions of objects, what they contain, and how hands interact with them, so robots can reason about safe liquid-handling tasks.

460.p: Training AI across many devices fails when some are weak phones and others are powerful servers, because traditional methods assume everyone trains the same model.
460.a: Let powerful devices train large models and weak phones train tiny models, then fuse their separate learned knowledge on the server to reach full model performance.

461.p: Crypto blockchains run slowly or unevenly because thousands of settings control performance, and changing them manually wastes time and performs poorly under changing demand.
461.a: Use trial-and-reward learning to automatically adjust the most critical settings in real time, watching performance at each stage to stay fast and stable under any load.

462.p: People checking if health rumors are true often read only sources that agree with them, but it's unclear whether looking at multiple sources actually helps them spot false claims.
462.a: Test real people fact-checking health rumors and measure how tab-switching and time off-site predict accuracy, finding that checking multiple sources cuts through bias.

463.p: Finding where a rumor or virus started in a network is hard because real spread happens over time and the network has messy noise that throws off AI systems.
463.a: Model spread as continuous-time changes, use a math process to track patterns, and filter out network noise to accurately pinpoint the original source.

464.p: Training AI across different companies' local networks fails because each company's data lives in different mathematical spaces, so global models don't fit all of them.
464.a: Give each company its own custom curved mathematical space tailored to its network shape, then combine learnings without sharing raw data between companies.

465.p: When AI systems pull facts from the web to answer questions, attackers can hide malicious instructions in that content, poisoning what the system retrieves and what it says.
465.a: Build a test suite that checks whether web-facing systems can resist hidden commands and biased content, using real social media posts and measuring how often attacks actually change the answer.

466.p: Learning AI models across millions of phones without sharing private data fails when some people's data is rare, causing the AI to forget how to handle those groups.
466.a: Adjust how knowledge flows from the global AI to each phone based on what data each person has, protecting rare groups by keeping their knowledge separate from common groups.

467.p: Shopping sites show stars for overall quality, but real people care about different things—some want durability, others fast shipping—and the site can't guess which matters to each customer.
467.a: Build a system that tracks what each person values on which issues, then ranks items by combining all those separate scores in a way that honors each person's priorities.

468.p: Governments need ways to let citizens participate in decisions without top-down control, but there's no clear framework for how that actually works in practice.
468.a: Create a visual toolkit that shows how direct democracy and liquid voting systems would play out in real government scenarios, making the mechanics concrete.

469.p: Academic peer review has grown so large and varies so much that editors can't tell which reviewers are doing good work or which reviews are actually helpful.
469.a: Build a platform that grades peer review quality using both structured checklists and AI judgment, so journals can spot excellent reviewers and catch poor ones.

470.p: When websites show new types of products or relationships that AI has never seen before, the AI fails to recognize them because it only learned from old categories.
470.a: Use a curved mathematical space that captures how categories are organized hierarchically, so the AI can reason about completely new types without retraining.
