471.p: Recommendation systems learn from multiple data sources to get smarter, but they accidentally copy unfairness from one source to another, hurting some customer groups.
471.a: Balance training data across customer groups and ensure that benefits from using multiple sources are shared fairly, not just going to already-favored groups.

472.p: Social networks and website services need to spot fraud or sabotage happening right now, but current detection methods are slow or hard to explain to security teams.
472.a: Track how surprising each new interaction is compared to normal behavior using a memory-efficient sketch, giving clear alerts with reasons why something looks wrong.

473.p: AI assistants that work with biology or finance data become expensive fast because long sequences of specialized information blow up how many tokens the AI must process.
473.a: Compress long biology or financial sequences into short summaries before sending to the AI, then use a gate mechanism to keep only the most relevant context as the AI reasons step by step.

474.p: Cybersecurity professionals use different words for the same attack, and can't connect low-level technical fixes back to the business threats they prevent.
474.a: Build a wiki-like system that maps those different terms to each other and traces the chain from business goal to security control to attack type to actual vulnerability.

475.p: AI systems that describe medical X-rays sometimes make up facts because they only see the image, not the subtle patterns across many similar cases.
475.a: When generating a report, pull similar past reports and images from a database, then teach the AI to look at both the new image and retrieved cases together to stay factual.

476.p: People on social media use metaphors to talk about depression in ways that algorithms don't catch, missing early warning signs that clinicians could spot.
476.a: Collect social posts about depression labeled with the metaphors people use, then train the AI on those real phrases so it learns to spot depression by recognizing the figurative language.

477.p: Videos and social posts have audio, text, and images, but when one piece is missing—or someone blocks it for privacy—the AI treats different people's incomplete data differently.
477.a: Build a graph of how the modalities relate to each other, use a single shared space for class prototypes, and train the AI to stay consistent whether data is complete or partial.

478.p: Privacy-protecting social networks that hide who is friends with whom still leak information to attackers who sneak in fake profiles to corrupt what the AI learns.
478.a: Spot abnormal submitted data and remove sophisticated fake profiles, then recover the AI's accuracy by filling in gaps the privacy protection created.

479.p: Foundation models need to turn real-world structures like knowledge networks into tokens like a language model does, but math on curved surfaces breaks current methods.
479.a: Design tokens that capture fundamental patterns in networks using curved geometry, then use a decoder that keeps tokens consistent across different types of structures.

480.p: Testing systems that organize information (facts and their connections) requires huge realistic datasets, but creating them by hand is impractical at web scale.
480.a: Build fake datasets by studying the deeper structure and shapes within existing data, then use those patterns to generate new ones that behave like the real thing.

481.p: Finding tight-knit groups within massive networks—like friend circles or biological connections—takes forever with current methods on graphs with millions of nodes.
481.a: Break the problem into smaller, solvable pieces that still preserve the key constraint, so you can cut away irrelevant parts much faster before they waste computation.

482.p: Events happen constantly in online stores, hospitals, and social media, but predicting the next one is hard because the timing and type of events depend on each other in ways that simple models cannot capture.
482.a: Watch what type of event just happened and what other types have occurred recently, then use that context to forecast what comes next and why it matters.

483.p: Web crawlers waste effort revisiting old pages or miss fresh content because humans manually pick which websites to check, often by guessing instead of data.
483.a: Use the history of what pages actually show up and stay live to automatically pick the best starting points that yield the most new finds in the least time.

484.p: AI systems that write code are overconfident about wrong answers and miss edge cases, creating insecure or buggy software that passes surface tests.
484.a: Have three virtual experts debate the code plan—one pushes hard to fix flaws, one stays practical, one optimizes—then stress-test the result with trick cases before delivering it.

485.p: Networks need to catch malicious traffic in real time, but decision trees deployed on high-speed switches either fail to catch attacks or use too much hardware to run multiple copies.
485.a: Split the decision tree into a critical branch (the one that catches most attacks) and simpler side branches, then place them efficiently on switch resources to save space without losing accuracy.

486.p: People constantly tweak hateful messages—using slang, misspellings, symbols—to trick content filters, and old detectors cannot adapt to these evolving tricks.
486.a: Teach the detector to learn continuously by using an AI to recover the real meaning from garbled text and update itself as new evasion tactics appear.

487.p: The web has exploded with technical reports, patents, and legal documents that machines cannot fully parse because they mix text, tables, diagrams, and structured facts.
487.a: Combine symbolic knowledge (organized facts in databases) with modern language AI to understand complex, messy documents and reason about their meaning accurately.

488.p: When you delete sensitive data from a trained model (for privacy or copyright), it is hard to verify it is truly gone rather than just hidden from the output.
488.a: Look inside the model's hidden layers using a specialized tool to detect whether deleted information was actually removed or just buried where output-level tests cannot find it.

489.p: Recommender systems that chat with you should use past conversations to improve suggestions, but sometimes old chat history actually makes recommendations worse by anchoring to stale interests.
489.a: Have two virtual debaters decide which past conversations truly help and which hurt, then use only the helpful ones when deciding what to suggest next.

490.p: Recommendation systems must rank items by what users like most, but methods that work well are slow with long histories because they check every pair of past actions.
490.a: Use a faster mathematical method (polynomial-based) that processes the full history once without comparing all pairs, while adding gates to catch sudden interest spikes.

491.p: AI assistants forget previous conversations and lack a way to store and recall facts about you over time, limiting their usefulness in real work.
491.a: Build a memory system where an AI can store experiences as organized thoughts, then retrieve relevant memories by spreading signals through a web of connected ideas.

492.p: Recommendation systems aim to rank top items well, but their designs do not directly optimize for ranking metrics; instead they optimize for generic goals that do not match ranking objectives.
492.a: Build a system whose math directly mirrors how ranking accuracy (precision at K) improves with each step, so training naturally optimizes the metric you actually care about.

493.p: Online ads struggle to predict clicks because historical data overweights popular old categories, and systems miss when people's interests shift or differ from their past behavior.
493.a: Generate fresh interest groups for each person based on immediate context, then use those groups to score ads in a way that balances history with current, fleeting intent.

494.p: Smart cities want to let citizens co-create policies and solve problems together through digital platforms, but AI risks automating too much and eroding trust in the process.
494.a: Design an AI system where humans stay in charge by drawing clear boundaries—AI helps draft ideas and summarize input, but people decide final proposals and policy outcomes.

495.p: AI systems make mistakes when writing code at key moments like the start of each line, where the structure matters most.
495.a: Give the AI simple instructions that guide it to think about structure before writing, without rebuilding the entire system.

496.p: Systems that classify sequences fail when the data source shifts from what they trained on, even if the task is the same.
496.a: Separate the truly predictive features from noise patterns, then test robustness with mixed real and fake data variations.

497.p: AI systems overwhelm themselves trying to grade every part of a homework rubric at once, producing vague or repetitive feedback.
497.a: Have multiple AI agents, each focused on one grading criterion, then combine their specific judgments into one coherent comment.

498.p: Finding where a ground-level photo matches a satellite image is essential for navigation but current methods either work or explain, not both.
498.a: Learn visual appearance and spatial layout together so matches are both accurate and you can see which geographic details mattered.

499.p: Memes carry political messages online but nobody knows whether novel images or emotional words drive more sharing and engagement.
499.a: Measure how fresh each image looks and analyze word emotion, then find which combinations get the most shares and likes.

500.p: AI systems sound confident even when they give completely wrong medical diagnoses, and doctors cannot tell the difference.
500.a: Measure how certain the AI really is, flag predictions it doubts, then ask targeted follow-up questions to verify uncertain diagnoses.

501.p: Testing data deletion usually erases random chunks, but in reality people send written requests in plain English asking for their data gone.
501.a: Build a real dataset of written deletion requests in English, map each to actual data, then test if systems truly forget when asked properly.

502.p: Academic questions need facts linked across author-paper-venue databases, but simple lookups miss the multi-step connections between them.
502.a: Use AI agents that pick different search strategies by question type, expand partial results, and verify answers against actual database facts.

503.p: Finding a photo by showing a picture and saying what to change fails because the AI description focuses on wrong visual details.
503.a: Focus the AI on understanding only the requested changes, then penalize results that keep unwanted parts of the original photo.

504.p: E-commerce sites need accurate delivery time estimates but prediction is hard because packages move through many separate segments.
504.a: Predict each delivery segment separately then sum them up, so predictions stay consistent and learn better what matters at each step.

508.p: Attackers can isolate a blockchain node by monopolizing all its network connections, cutting it off from the real network entirely.
508.a: Poison the node's address book with fakes, hijack the official peer list, and block legitimate connections to trap it.

509.p: When platforms offer paid ad-free plans, users assume less data gets collected, but companies may keep collecting anyway for personalization.
509.a: Export what data platforms actually collect from both ad-free and ad-supported accounts, and survey users about what they expect.

510.p: Finding fraud or strange behavior in financial networks is hard because there are almost no labeled examples to learn from, and actual fraud is extremely rare.
510.a: Instead of looking at all the data equally, pick the most unusual nodes first, then create fake examples that preserve real fraud patterns to teach a detection system.

511.p: When search engines must answer billions of queries fast, they keep a constantly-changing map of similar results, but that map gets out of date as data grows and search habits shift.
511.a: Use a decision-making system that learns which parts of the map to prune as things change, adapting region-by-region rather than using one-size-fits-all rules.

512.p: Predicting how crowded a subway will be requires data from multiple cities spread across different companies, but they can't share raw data due to privacy and organizational barriers.
512.a: Train a prediction system separately on each city's data without moving data anywhere, combining text, numbers, and video feeds together while keeping everything private.

513.p: Real-world facts in organized databases are constantly changing—companies merge, people die, relationships form—but systems that look up facts struggle to update their internal knowledge efficiently.
513.a: Prioritize learning about the most important new facts first, and adjust how closely each fact must match based on how many related facts exist in the database.

514.p: The field of detecting and tracking objects in images is changing rapidly, with hundreds of new techniques emerging that aren't clearly connected to each other or to older approaches.
514.a: Survey 100+ recent papers to map out how detection and tracking are converging into unified systems, and show which benchmark choices guide future research.

515.p: When an AI model makes decisions from online data, it can be biased or change its answers unexpectedly, but companies lack simple tools to measure if a model is trustworthy.
515.a: Build an interactive tool that measures how stable and fair a model's predictions are by testing what happens when you change the data in specific ways.

516.p: New users get poor recommendations because a system knows nothing about them, and borrowing from other sites doesn't work well since users' tastes differ across platforms.
516.a: Instead of adding noise to learn a pattern, gradually smooth out user data using neighborhood relationships between items, then sharpen it back to fill in unknown preferences.

517.p: Social media comments both help and harm people in crisis, but most suicide-risk detection systems treat all feedback the same or ignore it entirely.
517.a: Separate supportive comments from harmful ones and track how they shift someone's mental state over time, while filtering out personal habits that don't predict risk for new users.

518.p: When privacy laws require deleting a person's data from an AI system, simply removing it usually makes the model worse at its job and might still leak information about that person.
518.a: Strip away unused parts of the model first to disconnect it from the training data, then erase dependencies on the deleted person while keeping the model working well.

519.p: Recommendation systems trained on data from many websites often fail when applied to a new site, because domain differences cause the system to transfer knowledge poorly.
519.a: Instead of building a fancy model, generate new training examples from existing data that blend cross-site knowledge into target-site sequences that standard models can learn from.

520.p: Fake videos created by AI are getting so realistic that people can't tell them from real footage, and this threatens trust in video evidence online.
520.a: Detect fakes by analyzing muscle movements in faces together with what's happening around them, catching unnatural patterns that appear only in AI-generated videos.

521.p: Systems that learn from networks (how things connect) often memorize training data and fail when they see new data, especially when the network contains errors.
521.a: Adjust the actual messages flowing through the network based on their local neighborhood, smoothing out noise while sharpening meaningful signals automatically.

522.p: Recommending what users examine or favorite is as important as recommending purchases, but systems trained for one behavior don't learn well for other behaviors simultaneously.
522.a: Learn how different user behaviors influence each other, then let the system pick which cross-behavior signals help or hurt for each specific prediction task.

523.p: Dengue outbreaks spread through cities in patterns nobody fully understands, making it hard to predict where the next outbreak will hit and deploy disease control workers.
523.a: Map which neighborhoods influence each other's outbreaks by studying where cases appear over time, revealing how human movement spreads disease between distant areas.

524.p: AI systems that read documents in sensitive fields hallucinate facts and miss updates, while human annotation of every change is too expensive and slow.
524.a: Auto-generate question-answer examples from raw documents, then train a small search system to pull up relevant pages before answering, cutting down false information.

525.p: An AI system that reads and writes language can think through problems well, but can't reliably say how confident it is about a decision—which matters hugely for stopping fraud or filtering harmful content.
525.a: Train the AI to output its thinking process AND a clear list of confidence scores for each possible answer, using feedback from proven statistical models to reward better confidence.

526.p: Testing new AI training setups on real hardware is extremely slow and expensive, especially when you mix different types of processors and different ways of splitting work across them.
526.a: Build a fast computer simulation that accurately predicts how mixed hardware will perform together, by modeling individual processors and how data flows between them.

527.p: Scammers and disinformation spreaders now use AI to mass-produce fake videos and images; one fake can spawn thousands of near-identical variants, making it hard to spot large deception campaigns.
527.a: Analyzed real fraudulent campaigns to show that scale comes not from creating new lies, but from hiding a small core deception inside a huge volume of similar-looking clones and decoys.

528.p: Hate speech filters catch obvious slurs, but miss subtle discourse that sounds reasonable on the surface while secretly steering people to blame or exclude certain groups.
528.a: Create a test set of hateful opinions rewritten to sound like calm discussions with neutral framing, then measure which content moderation systems fail to catch the same hostile intent.

529.p: When you feed an AI system text plus images plus audio about someone's feelings, the different types of data don't naturally align or work well together, causing the AI to miss emotional nuance.
529.a: Use a geometric structure to rearrange text, images, and audio into a shared space where they align naturally, then feed that unified data to the AI system as special tokens it understands.

530.p: When many companies want to train an AI on their graphs of how things connect, without sharing their raw data, the AI struggles to learn well from each company's small dataset and doesn't work across different tasks.
530.a: Map each company's graph into a special mathematical space using curvature, then combine those maps in a shared space so the AI learns geometry-aware patterns that work across all tasks.

531.p: Shopping recommendation systems look at text and images, but ignore the rich web of who-bought-what and who-clicked-what, leaving money on the table by missing important signals.
531.a: Merge visual, textual, and behavior-graph data into one unified space using attention mechanisms, then feed that combined signal to an AI system so it recommends better items.

532.p: When you show an AI system thousands of almost-identical items—like near-duplicate search results or a huge product catalog—it gets overwhelmed, misses subtle differences, and makes poor decisions.
532.a: Instead of listing each item separately, encode them once as a single learned token that captures what makes them similar yet preserves which ones are genuinely different.

533.p: Finding hidden root causes in data is hard because most methods assume you've observed everything, but in reality some key factors are invisible, and we don't know what to call the ones we do find.
533.a: Have multiple AI systems collaborate using incomplete information to guess what hidden factors exist, checking their reasoning against multiple real-world data sources to verify they're plausible.

534.p: Time-series data—stock prices, sensor readings, traffic—changes in two different ways: old patterns repeat, and completely new patterns appear. Most models treat these the same.
534.a: Build a system with separate expert models for old patterns (look them up from history) and new patterns (start fresh), then switch between them depending on how much uncertainty you see right now.

535.p: Generating fake time-series data (for privacy or because you don't have enough real data) is hard because data has repeating weekly patterns AND slow long-term trends that are hard to create together.
535.a: Encode the data at multiple time scales separately, then generate coarse-to-fine the way humans sketch: rough shape first, fine details second, using repeating patterns as guides.

536.p: Finding and answering questions on the web requires knowing not just if information is relevant, but whether it's still true right now—and this matters more as the web changes faster.
536.a: Survey the evolution of methods for handling time in search and question-answering, from old rule-based approaches to modern AI systems that check current facts before answering.

537.p: Blockchain systems need to detect when miners cheat by censoring transactions or reordering them, but the monitoring method that people actually use can wrongly accuse innocent miners.
537.a: Analyze real blockchain data to measure how often monitoring fails, and find the conditions where it reliably works—mainly when transactions are far apart in time.

538.p: Knowledge bases usually store facts as pairs (A relates to B), but real facts often involve three or more things at once, forcing facts to break apart and making reasoning longer and worse.
538.a: Use hypergraphs that hold entire multi-part facts intact, with an AI system that reasons over these whole facts at once without breaking them into pairs and losing their meaning.

539.p: Detecting news and events on social media is hard because posts are short, messy, and tagged by no one; existing unsupervised methods rely on connection graphs that shift as new posts arrive.
539.a: Use an AI system to auto-label posts as a starting point, filter out its mistakes by checking whether labels make sense within the graph of who-posted-what, then cluster into events.

540.p: Recommendation systems struggle to suggest products for brand-new users and fail to transfer knowledge across different websites, wasting learning from one site on another.
540.a: Combine visual pictures and text descriptions together, and let one system learn from many different websites at once so it grows smarter as it sees more data.

541.p: Predicting Middle East conflicts is hard because each expert thinks differently about politics, history, and culture, but current AI systems use only one viewpoint.
541.a: Create a system where multiple AI experts debate and argue with each other, each focusing on different aspects of geopolitics, to cover more ground than one alone.

542.p: When AI systems look up facts in a document to answer questions, they break long documents into chunks badly, so they lose important context and miss key information.
542.a: Treat breaking text into chunks as a puzzle: ask questions first to decide where to cut, check if cuts make logical sense, and fill in missing links between pieces.

543.p: Small AI models on phones and embedded devices gradually forget how to learn new tasks over time, and shrinking them to fit devices makes this even worse.
543.a: Expand the model slightly at each new task to learn it, then shrink it back down while keeping mechanisms that preserve the ability to learn new things.

544.p: When PR crises hit, public opinion swings wildly because people feel emotions now but hold deeper beliefs that change slowly, yet AI can't model both at once.
544.a: Simulate how people think and feel separately, then combine those two forces to predict how opinions shift during a crisis.

545.p: Short video apps are designed to hook people, and we need to understand which users get addicted and how to help them before damage happens.
545.a: Use economic addiction models with real behavior data, then build a simulator that learns each person's unique addiction pattern so we can test safer design changes.

546.p: Automated systems find disaster locations in crisis texts but ignore poor regions, so aid gets focused on already-visible places and misses people who need it most.
546.a: Use AI systems that read context carefully to find locations correctly, and test them fairly across rich and poor areas to catch and fix bias.

547.p: Code that runs on the web works differently than the same code on computers, and these differences cause real problems but we don't know why.
547.a: Build a tool that runs identical code on both platforms, finds cases where outputs differ, and traces the root cause of each mismatch.

548.p: When an AI system answers complex questions by pulling facts from a huge web of connected information, it uses too many tokens and can't explain its reasoning clearly.
548.a: Pick the shortest paths through the fact web, score them by meaning, and feed only the best ones to the AI so it answers faster and shows its work.

549.p: As AI systems get more power to make decisions alone, we don't know if they can police themselves or if humans must always watch over them.
549.a: Check whether AI can truly monitor and correct its own behavior, or whether it needs humans to set the rules and hold it accountable.

550.p: Sticker apps struggle when users ask for emotions or styles they've never seen before, so they return wrong or offensively mismatched stickers.
550.a: Understand what users really want to express and match it to stickers by capturing the shared intent beneath different words and pictures.

551.p: AI systems that try to satisfy many conflicting human values at once either get expensive to train or end up bad at all of them.
551.a: Filter out preference examples that fight across different values, train separate models, then blend them by combining weights to balance all values.

552.p: Predicting whether two people will connect in a social network is hard because relationships change at many different speeds and scales.
552.a: Use wavelets to break apart time patterns at different scales, then merge those patterns with a system that reads both time and frequency information.

553.p: Social media users behave very differently from each other, and blanket content rules harm some groups more than others without platform designers knowing it.
553.a: Track what people actually do day-to-day, find distinct user types, and see how each type sees different news and gets affected by policy changes differently.

554.p: When users block each other on social media, nobody knows at scale whether blocking actually stops bad behavior or just hides it from sight.
554.a: Examine millions of public blocking records to see which users get blocked, what they did wrong, and whether blocking actually changed their activity.

555.p: People spread false information online, but predicting who will engage with it requires understanding how social pressure and emotional appeal work together across different platforms.
555.a: Model how each person's decision to share or like misinformation evolves over time, treating it as a give-and-take between personal effort and social rewards shaped by each platform's rules.

556.p: When a website must learn from constantly arriving user data, it wastes training time on redundant clicks and forgets old patterns, making predictions worse over long periods.
556.a: Use compact digital fingerprints to score which new user actions are worth learning from and which old patterns to remember, avoiding costly calculations.

557.p: Fraud detection systems trained on past data fail when bad patterns change, and existing methods either adapt to one domain poorly or require lots of human labeling.
557.a: Train one powerful model on normal patterns, create fake fraud examples to test against, then reuse that knowledge to spot new fraud types without labeling.

558.p: Automated ad bidding often makes inexplicable choices because it's trained as a black box, and it fails when market conditions shift or rare scenarios arise.
558.a: Use an AI system that reads and writes language to think through the economics first, then make specific bid decisions, bringing human reasoning to automated auctions.

559.p: Predicting future events from news requires blending images, text, and dates, but existing systems treat each source separately and don't capture how knowledge shifts over time.
559.a: Process text and images through different geometric lenses to discover deep relationships, then learn which modality matters more for each new prediction.

560.p: Predicting traffic flow tomorrow requires understanding both nearby roads and time patterns, but AI systems built for language struggle to handle the non-linear spatial layout.
560.a: Borrow an AI system that reads and writes language but add direct awareness of which roads connect to which, so it reasons about space and time together.

561.p: Real-world graphs have both known and unknown shifts in patterns, making models fail on new data, and fixing one problem often breaks the other solution.
561.a: Learn stable relationships that don't shift, generate subgraphs without labels, then use a method that learns patterns repeating across changes to handle both problems at once.

562.p: Once AI image generators are released, makers lose control over bad outputs, and currently nobody can stop unsafe results without blocking all usage.
562.a: Add digital signatures and control layers that a third party can use to monitor and halt unsafe content during both training adjustments and image creation.

563.p: Proving something happened without revealing how is crucial for secure online transactions, but existing proof systems trade off speed, size, and trustworthiness in incompatible ways.
563.a: Compare two proof methods side-by-side on real hardware, measuring how fast they work and how big the proofs are, revealing which fits each use case.

564.p: Mental health treatment is scarce, and people need support beyond office hours, but AI systems built for general chat miss the subtle ways therapists build trust.
564.a: Train a smaller AI system on therapy conversations, teach it to look up clinical facts before answering, and give it the ability to reason through each case carefully.

565.p: Criminals hide fraudulent money transfers by mimicking normal behavior, and detection systems trained on incomplete transaction records miss rare but real fraud patterns.
565.a: Watch for subtle mismatches across different views of the same transaction, inspired by how the brain spots unexpected situations, to catch disguised fraud.

566.p: Recommending videos or articles should predict where a person's taste is heading, but treating interest as fixed snapshots misses how curiosity naturally evolves.
566.a: Model each person's interest as a continuous journey through content space over time, updating as they click and watch, to stay ahead of shifts in taste.

567.p: Fake news with doctored images spreads quickly online, but detecting it requires understanding both how the image was faked and what the text actually says.
567.a: Extract local tampering clues and big-picture oddities from images, then blend them with text meanings to catch coordinated image-and-word forgery.

568.p: Recommendation systems rank millions of items in seconds but waste computation on obvious choices while underfitting hard cases, slowing learning and serving.
568.a: Separate easy and hard items, use lightweight ranking for obvious ones, and deploy stronger methods only where choices truly matter, balancing speed and accuracy.

569.p: New products buried in recommendation algorithms stay unknown, but pushing unknown items to everyone wastes exposure, so systems must find the rare people who want novelty.
569.a: Predict which users would organically discover and share each new item in the future, then target those specific people first to jumpstart organic growth.

570.p: Companies using AI on your personal data need a way to prove they're protecting your privacy, but you can't verify this happens without seeing their systems.
570.a: Create a mathematical proof system—like a receipt from a bank—that shows privacy protections were actually applied, without revealing the company's private methods.

571.p: City council meetings produce long, dense documents that ordinary people can't navigate, but nobody has built tools to make them readable.
571.a: Built a collection of Portuguese meeting summaries and tested AI systems that could auto-summarize long government discussions into short, clear versions.

572.p: Security camera footage can now be faked with AI, so courts and police can't trust video evidence as they once did.
572.a: Use blockchain—a tamper-proof ledger—to record when footage was captured and unchanged, making fake-detection possible without trusting one authority.

573.p: When you click 'view' then 'add to cart' then 'buy,' the site tries to guess what you want next, but can't explain why.
573.a: Track causal reasons behind your clicks using symbolic logic rules, so the system can explain its recommendations like a human would.

574.p: AI systems struggle to understand smaller languages with less training data, and scaling them to work worldwide is very slow.
574.a: Inject grammar rules into the AI's training, then use live error signals to automatically adjust learning, building stronger language models for rare languages.

575.p: AI systems answering questions with facts from hundreds of documents are too slow because they must read everything to find what matters.
575.a: Use a fast prediction to guess which facts are important, then fetch only those few before the main system starts reading, like a librarian finding relevant books first.

576.p: Travel planning sites overwhelm you with choices, but they never notice when you're confused and don't adjust their help.
576.a: Watch your facial expressions and eyes to detect confusion in real time, then have AI assistants slow down, simplify, or give different kinds of help.

577.p: People buy and sell others' private information—addresses, phone numbers—on underground markets, turning privacy violation into a business.
577.a: Studied the Chinese underground where these illegal data markets operate, exposing how they organize, advertise, and pay to understand the threat.

578.p: Safety filters on AI chatbots block bad requests, but the AI system itself can still understand those requests if you rephrase them slightly.
578.a: Use typos and unusual phrasings to slip past filters while the AI still understands you, showing a mismatch between filter security and AI resilience.

579.p: AI systems could help design drugs that bind to disease proteins, but they don't understand protein structures well enough to find good molecules.
579.a: Use an optimization technique to explore the AI's learned molecular space beyond its training, finding valid drug candidates it wouldn't generate on its own.

580.p: Delivery drones in a city must coordinate where to go without one central control, but simple rules lead to inefficiency and crashes.
580.a: Use thermodynamics—modeling drones like gas molecules in physics—to describe how local decisions create city-scale patterns of good service balance.

581.p: Fact-checkers often guess wrong or can't decide on technical claims, and manually searching the web for every fact is too slow.
581.a: Break claims into atomic pieces, check each locally with calibrated confidence, and only search the web if the answer is genuinely uncertain.

582.p: Crypto trading bots exploit price differences between centralized and decentralized exchanges, but patterns of these opportunities are unpredictable.
582.a: Model cryptocurrency price movements as a probabilistic system using financial math, then fit it to real blockchain data to predict profitable moments.

583.p: Hateful memes hide meaning in combinations of text and image that look harmless separately, and AI systems miss the poisonous interaction.
583.a: Train AI to reason step-by-step through image-text interactions using rewards that improve both detection accuracy and explainability of its reasoning.

584.p: AI systems that take independent actions are new, but decades-old web standards already solved similar problems for automated services.
584.a: Show how Semantic Web techniques for describing services and reasoning about them directly apply to modern autonomous AI systems.

585.p: Managing big networks—like delivery systems—requires deciding what to make and ship constantly, but current methods either break the rules or can't handle truly large networks.
585.a: Add a rule-checker layer after an AI system predicts actions, then train it by copying from expert decisions so it learns both faster and bigger.

586.p: Predicting cloud server load, traffic, or energy consumption days ahead is hard because thousands of signals interact across time in ways that slow down computers.
586.a: Use a speedy math technique called autocorrelation across all time points and variables at once, then streamline it for deep learning to drop computing time from quadratic to linear.

587.p: When an AI needs to look up facts to answer questions, it must balance searching everywhere for all relevant info versus searching just locally to stay fast—but doing both at once wastes time.
587.a: Search a hierarchy of fact groups from big to small, filter aggressively at each level, and train the system to pick the right level of detail for each question.

588.p: Finding a person in a crowd by written description is hard because the same person looks different in photos and the same description fits many different people.
588.a: Clean up irrelevant photo details using the text description, then match image regions to individual words to spot subtle differences.

589.p: Finding fraud on financial networks fails because fraudsters act different from honest users, but normal graph tools assume everyone plays by the same rules.
589.a: Check for unusual local changes in person features plus suspicious tight clusters, combining both angles to catch cheaters hiding in groups.

590.p: Time-series data—sensor readings, air quality, electricity demand—often has gaps missing, but filling them is slow and requires lots of training or messes up time order.
590.a: Convert time-series into images, use an AI trained on real photos to fill in missing pixels, then convert back to recover the missing measurements.

591.p: Building machine learning workflows by hand is tedious; most AI helpers struggle because they focus on writing code rather than understanding what the user actually wants.
591.a: Parse the task description first to understand intent, then pick the right tools from a big catalog and assemble them into a no-code workflow automatically.

592.p: Understanding emotion from video requires reading text, audio, and visuals together, but each stream is sometimes broken or unreliable and current methods treat them as equally trustworthy.
592.a: Assign each stream a confidence score, let confident streams override noisy ones when predicting emotion, and report the uncertainty in the final answer.

593.p: Finding relevant tables from search queries is hard because text and table structure are totally different beasts, and sampling a few table rows misses key patterns.
593.a: Group similar rows together, pick representative rows from each group, generate varied search phrases per group, and weight parts fairly to make tables searchable.

594.p: Teaching an AI agent to browse the web and click on things fails because it can't see where the cursor is, misreads instructions, and falsely assumes clicks worked.
594.a: Train it to first check if the cursor is already on target before moving, then execute one move or click at a time and verify the result before proceeding.

595.p: Answering questions by repeatedly looking up facts and reasoning is expensive and slow because each cycle needs to run an AI system multiple times across thousands of words.
595.a: Convert all facts into mini question-answer pairs offline, then answer user questions only by retrieving relevant pairs and synthesizing—AI runs just twice total.

596.p: AI doctors can diagnosis images well but doctors can't trust them because they work like a black box; showing the result isn't enough without showing the reasoning.
596.a: Extract human-readable concepts from images, draw how concepts influence each other, trace causal chains from concepts to diagnosis, then let doctors see the whole path.

597.p: Watermarking AI-generated images to catch fakes makes the image quality worse; methods focus on watermark strength but ignore that people want nice-looking pictures too.
597.a: Let different parts of an image get different watermark strengths based on importance, and use multiple specialists to boost quality while keeping watermarks strong.

598.p: Finding the smallest subgraph connecting scattered groups of nodes (like tags in a knowledge base) is slow when there are thousands of groups instead of just a few.
598.a: Create new algorithms that work fast whether there are many nodes or many groups, not just one, by rethinking the problem structure.

599.p: As AI agents replace humans on the web, old measures of who's important (like PageRank) fail because agents optimize for information usefulness differently than people do.
599.a: Measure importance by how well information travels through an agent network as details decay, rewarding agents who preserve semantic meaning, not just volume.

600.p: Shopping recommendations tend to repeat the same items over and over as they're built, making suggestions boring and less useful by the time they finish.
600.a: Read user history in layers, from rough to detailed, and reason through each step, so bias doesn't pile up and kill variety in the final list.

601.p: Detecting hate videos requires looking at images, sound, and text together, but systems that judge videos rarely show their reasoning or admit when they're unsure.
601.a: Treat each type of evidence separately, label what came from where, and show exactly which words or images led to the final decision.

602.p: Phone-automation agents get stuck when they encounter unfamiliar apps or screens because they don't have enough background knowledge about how things work.
602.a: When an agent feels uncertain, pull in documentation and past examples about that app, then let the agent consider them before deciding what to do next.

603.p: Predicting world events from news articles fails because AI systems miss hidden connections between historical events and make up false details they seem confident about.
603.a: Look at how events unfolded over time and what was happening at the same moment, then spot and fix the system's own mistakes as it reasons.

604.p: Robot arms and self-driving cars controlled by AI can be hijacked by enemies who subtly alter photos to fool the AI, making robots do the wrong thing.
604.a: Inject careful, hard-to-spot changes into images that break how the AI links vision to instructions, while keeping the tampering invisible to humans.

605.p: Self-driving cars need to spot attacks and failures in real time via satellite, but satellite delays are too long to send data to the cloud and get answers back safely.
605.a: Run the threat-detection system on a computer inside the vehicle, fuse data from engine sensors, road messages, and cameras, and check if threats match real physics.

606.p: Finding bugs in websites by sending random inputs is slow because there's no way to know if you're making real progress or just wasting time testing the same paths.
606.a: Watch how the website responds to each test input and use clues from those responses to decide what to try next, balancing exploring new pages with finding vulnerabilities.

607.p: E-commerce apps with full-screen swiping face a tricky problem: showing products that drive sales, views, and swipes down all at once creates conflicting goals.
607.a: Balance what to show in each slot and across a series of swipes so that all three goals work together instead of fighting each other.

608.p: Apps that learn without gathering everyone's data in one place struggle to share useful information across users because each class of item is treated as one fixed thing.
608.a: Break down each class into reusable building blocks that can be mixed and matched across users and classes, guided by language descriptions of what they mean.

609.p: When websites change over time, AI systems that learn from connections between things tend to forget old skills while learning new ones, and old methods are too slow.
609.a: Evolve the AI's inner state over time by watching the current data, then generate specialized tweaks that adapt to what's new without erasing what worked before.

610.p: Figuring out where someone lives from their social media posts is hard when few posts have location tags and the clues come from scattered places and platforms.
610.a: Pull together clues from profiles and posts using an AI trained on text, then teach it to connect those clues to places using location-specific words and hints.

611.p: Recommendation systems that explain their picks often produce generic or wrong reasons because they ignore what was actually said about past items users saw.
611.a: Mix detailed opinions from item reviews into how the system learns items, fusing text with click history at the right moment, to build better and more personal explanations.

612.p: Large AI systems that recommend products struggle with huge user history and make up fake preferences that contradict what users really want and have actually done.
612.a: Split long histories into chunks, infer preferences chunk by chunk, and use future clicks as a signal to reward right predictions and penalize wrong ones.

613.p: Knowledge databases grow constantly with new facts, but updating the mathematical summaries without forgetting what was learned before is slow and uses old, limited methods.
613.a: Extend a popular software library to add new facts with smart starting values, measure both progress and forgetting, and let people track how summaries change over time.

614.p: Knowing whether a student understands programming is harder than traditional topics because test scores are messy and success depends on logic, not just memorized facts.
614.a: Use an AI trained on text to break down what went wrong in code, assign meaningful error labels, and track what knowledge a student has across multiple skill levels.

615.p: When predicting future values in messy real-world data (weather, traffic, sensor readings), AI models often spiral into errors or freeze up, making them unreliable for actual use.
615.a: Use a smarter search method that explores many directions instead of getting stuck, paired with a lighter AI model that combines time patterns and image analysis in one system.

616.p: Systems that track changing facts about the world miss crucial details: what kind of thing just happened (was it political or financial?), and how events connect to each other beyond just sequence and structure.
616.a: Add descriptive labels to facts using an AI system that reads text, then build a double system—one tracks how relations change, and feeds that into another that tracks how items change, together.

617.p: When a search engine generates document IDs instead of links, adding new documents breaks it—retraining wastes huge computing power and the model forgets old knowledge, making it impractical to keep current.
617.a: Identify the specific neural pathways that map to document IDs, and surgically edit just those connections without retraining the whole system, using a label strategy that prevents confusion.

618.p: Project README files on GitHub contain gold-mine information (dataset names, tool versions, code functions) but are messy text, so researchers can't automatically extract and index these building blocks.
618.a: Manually label examples of what's important in READMEs (ten types of things, over 10,000 examples), then train an AI to spot and extract these entity types automatically.

619.p: Traffic prediction today sees only which roads are next to which—but traffic actually depends on complex patterns across space and time, like rush hour cascades, that simple neighbor-to-neighbor models miss.
619.a: Build a graph of roads where connections include higher-order groups and daily cycles, then blend a recurrent neural unit with a multi-layer perceptron to capture both local and global time patterns.

620.p: Surveillance cameras try to re-identify the same vehicle seen from different angles or blocked by trees, but features get mixed up—an angle view looks totally different from a side view.
620.a: Split the features into meaningful vehicle parts using multi-head attention, then use region-aware channels and symmetry awareness to highlight the parts that actually matter.

621.p: AI systems now review contracts and job applications, but they're tricked by false or misleading information, leading to bad decisions about hiring or legal obligations with no way to explain why they failed.
621.a: Build a map of fraud tactics and suspicious keywords, then feed this organized knowledge to the AI so it sees the warning signs and explains which red flags triggered its decision.

622.p: Companies deploy independent AI agents that act on their own with stored memory and authority—but "insider threat" was defined for humans, leaving security teams blind to AI agents who drift or get exploited.
622.a: Expand the definition of insider threat to cover autonomous systems, then outline what companies need to watch (agent behavior, memory isolation, audit trails) to catch when an AI goes rogue.

623.p: Graph learning systems can be poisoned: an attacker sneaks bad data into a graph so the AI learns to classify certain nodes wrong, and existing defenses can't detect clever poisoning that blends in.
623.a: Find the specific AI neurons that respond to the poison, learn which triggers activate them, then systematically erase that learned pattern from those neurons while keeping the rest intact.

624.p: Most users interact with very few products, most products rarely sell—recommendation systems work great for bestsellers but fail for long-tail items, and forcing tail accuracy usually tanks bestseller accuracy.
624.a: Use AI-generated item descriptions to let rare products borrow patterns from similar popular ones, and align similar users with sparse histories so they share each other's knowledge.

625.p: Graph AI systems trained on one data distribution fail on new data that looks similar but different (like April traffic vs December traffic), because hidden conditions in training don't match test conditions.
625.a: Create a mixture of expert AI units, each handling a different hidden condition, and train them all to output the same prediction so the model generalizes across invisible shifts.

626.p: Systems that catch hacked computers or malicious processes by tracking program actions can be fooled if an attacker slightly rewrites the action sequence to look normal while staying hidden.
626.a: Generate valid alternative versions of action sequences that preserve meaning, then teach the system to recognize threats even when the sequence looks different, while staying blind to harmless changes.

627.p: Decentralized identity systems let users own their identity without a central authority, but they can only work within one community—users switching between DeFi, gaming, and DAOs leak their identity across each.
627.a: Split the system into independent domain committees, add a secret protocol that proves you belong to trusted communities without naming them, and make it faster to trace abusers.

628.p: Detecting events in social media (a protest, a meme trend, a disaster) treats messages as independent items, but real information spreads like waves—bouncing, reinforcing, interfering, then bouncing again.
628.a: Build a graph where connections model wave-like propagation and physical attraction-repulsion between messages in the same event versus different events, using oscillating math from physics.

629.p: Reviewing millions of documents to find the ones you need (legal discovery, research papers, web content) is now multilingual and mixed with AI-generated content—current systems lack transparency and fairness.
629.a: This is a workshop gathering researchers to share methods for human-guided search systems that are explainable, fair, and work across many languages with AI assistance.

630.p: Organizations store vast, interconnected facts about people, places, and ideas, but these collections change over time and become messy—nobody has tools to track how they degrade or evolve in ways that matter.
630.a: Built a web tool that measures hundreds of health signals for these fact collections—like how tightly connected they are and how their structure changes—so teams can spot problems and watch quality over time.

631.p: Cloud datacenters hold data in separate memory pools to save money, but when multiple tenants use the same network at once, they step on each other's toes and everything slows down.
631.a: Designed a system that watches which network paths are clogged in real time and automatically routes urgent memory requests around the traffic jams, while fairly sharing resources.

632.p: Cameras and AI models on phones work poorly in new places because they were trained in different lighting and backgrounds, and downloading new training data to the cloud every time is slow and wasteful.
632.a: Use one photo of the new place plus cloud computing power to tweak the phone's camera AI in seconds, so it adapts to that specific room without moving lots of data around.

633.p: People rely on search and recommendations online to discover music, products, and ideas, but these systems are becoming more complex and placing AI at their core in ways we don't fully understand.
633.a: Discussed how Spotify evolved search and recommendations from static matching into conversational experiences where users explore together with AI, and the system challenges that creates at massive scale.

634.p: Simulations of society using AI agents often fail because they trap agents in fixed thinking patterns—either everyone agrees (groupthink) or they deadlock—rather than mimicking how real people fluidly shift between cooperation and skepticism.
634.a: Agents track changing beliefs about each other's skills and automatically switch between teamwork and critical challenge, using game theory to make choices that don't lead to stuck conversations.

635.p: When AI answers questions about a document with text, tables, and pictures, it treats them as isolated scraps instead of recognizing how humans naturally read them as a connected whole with sections, captions, and cross-references.
635.a: Built a map of the document showing how all parts relate—text beside figures, sections grouped together—then had AI reason through this structure like a human would, rather than hunting randomly.

636.p: Email marketers want to pick which messages to send to billions of people while respecting budget and other rules, and balancing learning about what works with actually deciding what to send at huge scale.
636.a: Combined a learning method that samples outcomes with a massive optimization solver that instantly picks millions of emails to send while respecting all constraints, tested live at LinkedIn.

637.p: AI systems predict and generate content but don't truly grasp the human world—how time flows, why people act, what matters emotionally—so they fail at reasoning about meaning and consequence.
637.a: AI needs to build and maintain two models at once: one of physical reality (space, time, cause-and-effect) and one of the mind (goals, emotions, beliefs, social rules), so it can actually reason like a thinking being.

638.p: Systems that forecast website traffic or transportation demand use methods that treat each time point separately, missing the hidden rhythms and patterns that repeat at different time intervals, causing poor predictions.
638.a: Redesigned how to slice up time-series data into multi-scale chunks that capture those hidden repeating patterns, then combined it with a modern architecture to predict much more accurately.

639.p: E-commerce sites must recommend new products with no purchase history, but copying suggestions from 'similar users' often suggests wrong items because not all past actions are equally telling of real preference.
639.a: Find users who actually share the target customer's deeper taste, then pick their most meaningful purchases to recommend new products, using images and text to understand new items without wait for sales data.

640.p: Systems that predict missing facts in historical event logs often see only immediate connections between events, missing how sets of facts interact together or getting distracted by irrelevant old information.
640.a: Use two calculation methods in tandem—one capturing tight local event clusters and another capturing broader multi-hop relationships—while filtering to focus only on truly relevant historical facts.

641.p: Mimicking the brain's efficient spiking neurons for graph problems lets systems run faster, but binary spiking is too weak to express nuance, so existing work adds expensive operations that kill the efficiency gain.
641.a: Keep the efficiency edge by blending spiking neurons with precision numbers only where needed, and dynamically adjusting how long computation runs based on how complex each graph is.

642.p: Recommender systems use offline tests to compare whether one recommendation strategy beats another before rolling it live, but those tests are fragile—tiny changes in the test setup flip which strategy wins.
642.a: Analyzed why offline tests give unstable answers and found that logging behavior, seed values, and dataset size all shift rankings unpredictably, so teams need more robust evaluation practices.

643.p: Recommending videos or products using images and text together is hard because fusion methods treat all users as if they weight modalities the same way, missing that one person might trust images while another trusts text.
643.a: Decomposed text-and-image signals into what's unique to each type and what's shared, then weighted them per user—so the same system learns different fusion rules for different people.

644.p: Search (where you type a query) and recommendations (where the site guesses what you want) are treated separately, losing the chance to build one coherent profile of what you're truly looking for across both channels.
644.a: Unified search queries and past browsing into a single interest model, then assigned AI modules strategically to search and recommendations based on that shared understanding, so each channel helps the other.

645.p: AI systems trained on human preferences often learn from mislabeled feedback, causing them to adopt wrong behaviors instead of improving.
645.a: Automatically detect and downweight unreliable preference judgments by scoring each one on how confident and consistent it is, rather than treating all feedback equally.

646.p: Finding odd nodes in networks is hard when some parts of the network are tightly clustered while others are spread out, and processing huge networks is slow.
646.a: Use layered filtering to capture both tight and loose network patterns, then weigh information differently for each node based on its local neighborhood structure.

647.p: When AI systems translate English questions into database commands, they often produce broken queries that can't run or return wrong answers.
647.a: Build a specialized error-spotter trained on synthetic mistakes, then teach it to identify and label what went wrong so problems can be fixed automatically.

648.p: Hiding secret marks in graph-shaped data fails because the mark gets tangled into the data itself, making it fragile or undetectable.
648.a: Separate the mark from the data structure using neural networks that learn them independently, then embed and recover the mark without corrupting the original.

649.p: When people share personal information over time on websites, companies can gradually piece together a detailed profile, and defenses treat each share as isolated.
649.a: Model privacy as a multi-round game where users learn their true risk and adapt, using AI to find the best strategy for disclosing information over time.

650.p: Networks with weighted connections are hard to cluster well: adding weights costs memory and noise in the weights corrupts the results.
650.a: Shrink the network to keep only important nodes, then use attention to identify and downweight noisy connections during clustering.

651.p: Mapping services like Baidu Maps need new API connectors as user questions diversify, but finding and integrating them manually is expensive and slow.
651.a: Automatically extract what users are actually asking for, then discover and design matching APIs, plus generate training examples with minimal human input.

652.p: Doctors reviewing thousands of medical studies to summarize them for comparisons is slow, and current AI often misses details or hallucinates facts.
652.a: Use AI with logical reasoning to extract key details from medical papers, with a voting system to filter out false summaries before humans review them.

653.p: Creating fake financial data that is both realistic and private is hard, especially when the real data has many rare cases and mixed attribute types.
653.a: Test several AI generation methods on financial tables, with new privacy protections, measuring whether the fake data is realistic and actually protects individuals.

654.p: Large AI models that work on graphs must fit all knowledge into their parameters, wasting space and making it hard to adapt to new graph types.
654.a: Store graph knowledge separately in a retrieval system and pull it in at prediction time, letting the model focus on learning patterns instead of memorizing facts.

655.p: Understanding sentiment in videos with text and audio requires catching both overall mood and subtle emotional hints from local details across both types of data.
655.a: Align sentiment clues separately at the big-picture and detail level across audio and text, then fuse them using attention while filtering redundant information.

656.p: Measuring whether a search engine ranked results well requires metrics, and choosing the right metric shape determines how fairly we judge quality.
656.a: Use a mathematical model of how people browse results to assign weights: pages near the top matter more, and the weights follow a well-understood pattern.

657.p: Knowledge bases mixing images and text are hard to search because most systems treat the two separately and fail to line up what images actually show.
657.a: Use vision-language AI models that naturally merge images and text into shared meanings, then apply that alignment to build better searchable knowledge bases.

658.p: Chatbots with long-term memory either summarize everything (losing details) or use fixed retrieval (missing context), wasting computation and hurting quality.
658.a: Break conversation history into segments by detecting when topic or people change, then retrieve relevant parts by type, adapting how much memory to use per query.

659.p: Events in real-world streams (medical alerts, trades) are hard to predict because they depend on each other in complex ways, and current methods are too slow.
659.a: Use a fast neural model that processes events one at a time, remembers long histories efficiently, and learns different time scales for different event types.

660.p: Amazon's 'Buy Box' (the main purchase button) disappears on some products, instantly tanking seller visibility and sales. Nobody understands when or why this happens, or how it shapes fair competition online.
660.a: Tracked 17,754 real Amazon products hourly for 8 weeks, compared them to competitor prices across 59,000 sellers, and measured what actually changed when the Buy Box vanished.

661.p: Criminals trick AI systems into saying harmful things by phrasing requests in sneaky ways; current safety guards stop most tricks but the cleverest attackers still get through.
661.a: They found that spreading harmful instructions across many separate pieces bypasses AI safety checks 95% of the time, and built a new defense to spot this trick.

662.p: Self-driving cars need to see the road from many angles at once, but sharing video from every car to a central hub wastes network bandwidth and slows decisions down.
662.a: Roadside boxes analyze camera feeds locally and share only the important insights with passing cars, cutting network traffic by over 5000 times while keeping perception sharp.

663.p: Billions of documents online—papers, business files, social posts—sit as raw text but contain valuable facts no computer can easily extract or organize for reasoning.
663.a: Tutorial on methods to turn messy documents into structured networks of connected facts, combining classical extraction with new AI systems.

664.p: Online shopping recommendations use negative examples to train, but naive methods pick bad examples too early or from too narrow a pool, causing training to fail.
664.a: Start training with simple random examples, then gradually shift to harder examples from the entire catalog, adjusting difficulty based on learner readiness.

665.p: When matching entities across knowledge bases with images, text, and structured data, combining everything naively loses important traits unique to each modality.
665.a: Score alignment both within single types and across types separately, treating each score as a vote, then combine them for final decisions.

666.p: Checking if an AI system is fair takes weeks of training full models, wasting time and compute on systems that will fail fairness tests anyway.
666.a: Fairness patterns emerge early in training; stopping unfair models at the 25% mark cuts total training cost by 74% while keeping fair ones running.

667.p: Customer service bots today either need constant manual routing between agents or are too rigid to handle real variety in customer issues without breaking.
667.a: Extract flowcharts automatically from real service conversations, then train smaller AI locally on those flowcharts without gathering sensitive customer data centrally.

668.p: Workshop description: False claims, bias, and echo chambers spread on social media; understanding debates and lies online requires mixing computer science with social science.
668.a: Forum bringing together researchers in NLP, journalism, social science, and computer science to analyze online discourse, arguments, and disinformation.

669.p: Social media bots hide by mimicking humans in obvious ways, but traditional bot-detection systems only look at who talks to whom, missing group behavior patterns.
669.a: Detect coordinated bot teams by analyzing how groups move and interact together, weighing each relationship type by how important it is to each individual.

670.p: A company's credit risk and power usage feed back on each other: bad credit kills investment in energy, low power use hints at failing operations. Most systems ignore this loop.
670.a: Jointly forecast power and credit using one system that explicitly models how credit decisions ripple into energy plans and vice versa.

671.p: Students use AI to look up facts from databases, but if they cannot see which fact came from where, they cannot learn to judge sources or think critically.
671.a: System shows students exactly which document was searched, which part answered them, and why—making transparency part of the design from the start, not an afterthought.

672.p: Online stores organize products into hierarchies, but expanding these by hand is slow; existing systems fail to capture the fact that one item can fit multiple categories.
672.a: Use box-shaped regions in mathematical space where covariance models uncertainty, allowing one product to partly belong to many categories instead of just one.

673.p: Spotting the main claim in a long document for fact-checking is hard and needs expertise; asking an AI to do it without examples often misses what human fact-checkers care about.
673.a: Ask AI to extract claims that match expert values (importance, specificity, factuality) described in prompts, then auto-score results against those same values.

674.p: Both crowd-written and professional fact-checks aim to counter false claims, but we do not know if they persuade differently or if crowds reward manipulation.
674.a: Analyzed thousands of fact-checks from crowdsourced and professional sources, finding no evidence crowds abuse persuasion more, though they do communicate differently.

675.p: When blockchain systems move user accounts between servers to speed things up, they have to shut down temporarily, causing people to lose service—and this gets worse as the system handles more data.
675.a: Move accounts in batches that naturally work well together, and keep the system running by handling transactions for unchanged accounts in a separate queue during the migration.

676.p: When websites send video, audio, and text together, noise and missing pieces wreck the meaning—right now systems just copy the raw signals, so small corruption destroys understanding.
676.a: Extract the core meaning first, strip away unimportant details, and send only essential facts in a shared code that video, audio, and text can all understand the same way.

677.p: Phishing attacks happen on dark web forums where criminals trade stolen tools and passwords, but most research only studies attacks after they've already hurt people.
677.a: Gather and analyze twelve years of dark web forum posts to see what tools criminals use, what targets they pick, and how attacks are built before they're launched.

678.p: Traffic prediction systems need custom-built designs for each city or use-case, so they don't work well when you move them to a new place or problem.
678.a: Use an AI system that reads instructions to pick and connect building blocks of proven designs, then automatically writes working code for the traffic problem at hand.

679.p: When you grab a pre-trained model from a library to use on a new dataset, you don't know if it will work well—you have to try fine-tuning it to find out, which is expensive.
679.a: Calculate one number from the model and the new dataset that predicts whether the model will transfer well, without actually spending time training it.

680.p: Graph systems that learn from unlabeled data struggle to understand complex patterns that span multiple steps, because they throw away edges and can't tell apart false negatives.
680.a: Use subgraph patterns to preserve important connections and create richer descriptions of how pieces fit together, then fix the loss function to distinguish good examples from bad ones.

681.p: Short-video recommendations based on user-item connections fail when the graph is noisy and when video, sound, and text representations say redundant things.
681.a: Learn cleaner graph structures from the different modalities, then squeeze each one to keep only the information that helps recommend videos, discarding overlap.

682.p: When you have several similar networks and want to figure out their hidden structure, each network has too little data to solve the puzzle alone.
682.a: Solve all networks at once by using each one's solution to improve the others' guesses, cycling until all improve together without more data needed.

683.p: Web-browsing AI agents trained with trial-and-reward often collapse because they explore too many uncertain tool choices, wasting compute and losing focus.
683.a: Balance exploration by pre-checking uncertainty before each step and penalizing too many risky tool calls in a row, while updating the policy to learn from high-risk moments.

684.p: Recommendation systems are judged by clicks and time spent, but real people care about trust, honesty, and whether they feel in control—two goals that often clash.
684.a: Build a framework to measure what people actually value: do they trust the system, do they understand why it recommended something, and do they feel agency?

685.p: Training giant AI systems on shared data across companies means huge costs and privacy risks, and nobody trusts that rewards are divided fairly among the players.
685.a: Use math from game theory and a public ledger to assign each participant a fair share of credit for improving the final system, then automate reward payouts.

686.p: Testing systems that pick and mix AI services needs realistic data about how services behave in the real world, but there's no good way to generate enough of it.
686.a: Build a tool that simulates thousands of AI service instances with realistic performance numbers and interaction patterns, creating a dataset for testing service selection.

687.p: Wireless sensor networks lose data when sensors break or power down, and current fixes require sending all raw data to one server, which violates privacy.
687.a: Learn a recovery model where each sensor sends only changed numbers, not raw measurements, and the model learns patterns across space and time without centralizing data.

688.p: Online stories need ads, but putting them in tense moments ruins the drama, while slow moments feel like empty space—finding the right spots is hard.
688.a: Use an AI system that reads each paragraph and rates how tense it is, so ads go in places where readers won't mind the interruption.

689.p: Predicting rare real-world events from a flood of information is nearly impossible because the events are so scarce and because earlier events show warning signs that existing methods miss.
689.a: Identify key earlier events that often lead to rare events, then build a system that links those precursors to the main event through learned pathways.

690.p: Social science research using online data is hard to verify because there's no shared checklist for how to do it right, so bad studies spread.
690.a: Build a platform with templates, checklists, and guidelines so researchers can publish their methods openly and others can copy and verify the same work.

691.p: When companies train AI models across many users who want different privacy levels, some users get better results than others, which feels unfair.
691.a: Give more influence to people who protect their privacy less, rewarding them for helping the shared model improve while letting everyone choose their own privacy level.

692.p: Shopping sites track many behaviors (clicks, favorites, purchases) to guess what you'll buy, but analyzing all that data is too slow for real-time suggestions.
692.a: Use a smart system that learns which type switches matter most, cutting unnecessary analysis in half so recommendations are both accurate and instant.

693.p: E-commerce sites must obey strict rules (show items from many sellers, promote new products) while still recommending what you'll actually buy.
693.a: Use an AI that splits the job into two parts: one optimizes accuracy within the rules, another explores new options, with the AI deciding how much focus each deserves.

694.p: Harmful chemicals (PFAS) hide in water and food, and scientists need an organized, searchable database to track them and share what's known.
694.a: Build a structured catalog of these chemicals with their properties, names in multiple languages, and links to safety data so anyone can search and compare.

695.p: Quantum computers could one day break the encryption that protects your passwords and bank accounts on the web.
695.a: Show exactly how a quantum computer would do this using a step-by-step simulation anyone can follow to understand the real risk.

696.p: Researchers use AI to simulate survey answers from fake people with specific backgrounds, but it's unclear if that AI actually captures their real opinions.
696.a: Test this AI against actual survey data and find that adding background details often makes answers worse, especially for minorities and specific questions.

697.p: Cities have lots of data about traffic and crime, but those predictions don't get acted on fast enough to actually fix problems before they happen.
697.a: Connect predictions directly to decision-makers and track how well actions work, then feed that back to improve next time's forecasts.

698.p: Recommenders struggle to suggest unpopular items because few people have tried them, leaving new sellers and rare products invisible.
698.a: Combine what actual users did (pure data) with word meanings from an AI system, aligning them so rare items get fair recommendations too.

699.p: Fake news spreads when a photo is paired with a lie, but spotting this mismatch usually requires checking outside sources, which is slow.
699.a: Extract what's in the photo and what it says, have an AI check if they match, all without looking anything up, fast enough for real news checking.

700.p: Social networks often hide people's sensitive details (race, gender, age) to protect privacy, but that makes it hard to spot unfair treatment in recommendations.
700.a: Use math to encode fairness into the network structure itself without guessing or reconstructing missing details, keeping people private.

701.p: Most plant databases are in English and global, but Vietnam has medicinal plants with local names that are nowhere online for Vietnamese speakers to find.
701.a: Gather thousands of photos of Vietnamese medicinal plants, label them in Vietnamese, and link them to global plant databases so locals can search in their language.

702.p: Finding hidden patterns in new data is hard because you don't know what you're looking for yet, and even AI suggestions are rough and inconsistent.
702.a: Zoom out first to see where patterns cluster in the data, then zoom in to verify each one is real, repeating until you have a solid taxonomy.

703.p: When AI predicts whether two people online will be friends or enemies, it's a black box, so you can't trust or explain its decisions.
703.a: Find the core chain of connections the AI used for its guess and show it in a way humans can understand and verify.

704.p: Recommender systems pick which features (price, brand, reviews) matter most, but their importance scores sometimes use only part of the data.
704.a: Balance the importance scores across all layers and data points, using a stable reference point, so the most useful features are truly identified.

705.p: Platforms must predict fraud and recommend items from billions of user actions, but current systems ignore how all users connect to each other.
705.a: Use a map of which users bought what together to improve fraud detection and recommendations alongside the timing of their actions.
