706.p: AI can now write convincing answers on Q&A sites, so platforms must figure out which answers are human-written versus AI-generated to maintain trust.
706.a: Built multiple detectors that spot patterns unique to AI writing (length, punctuation, word variety), then combined them to accurately flag AI answers.

707.p: Weather forecasting systems predict rain incorrectly because most days have zero rain, leading to false alarms and missed storms.
707.a: Added a lightweight fix to adjust predictions without retraining the system, handling the mismatch between forecasts and the reality of sparse rain.

708.p: Real-world data keeps changing—new categories appear, feature styles shift—and systems forget what they learned before.
708.a: Separate what matters for classification from surface-level style, then use a teacher-student approach to remember both old and new knowledge together.

709.p: Web advertising is shifting toward privacy-first methods and AI-driven personalization, requiring experts to share insights on balancing innovation with ethics.
709.a: Hosted a workshop for researchers and industry experts to discuss emerging ad technologies, privacy standards, and responsible innovation in digital marketing.

710.p: Searching for niche videos returns clickbait and shallow content because few people watch them, making ranking systems unreliable for unpopular topics.
710.a: Use AI's world knowledge to judge video quality without needing user clicks, then rerank results to surface high-quality videos even if nobody's watched them yet.

711.p: Medical image segmentation requires pixel-level labels that are expensive to create, but systems need that detail to identify anatomy precisely.
711.a: Use text descriptions of body parts to teach the system which pixels belong to which anatomy, building segmentation masks from image-level labels instead.

713.p: Answering complex questions requires looking up facts step-by-step, but each lookup can introduce errors that compound into wrong answers.
713.a: Build a logical tree of the question's structure first to identify core queries and known facts, then search systematically to prevent error buildup.

714.p: Mobile networks drop packets, freezing video or blurring frames when watching streams live, degrading the viewing experience.
714.a: Send extra copies of video data strategically across multiple frames instead of protecting each frame alone, smoothing out burst packet loss.

715.p: Invisible pixel trackers follow you across websites to spy on your behavior, and current defenses miss cross-site connections that enable the spying.
715.a: Map which websites share trackers, then use a system that learns patterns in these connections to spot hidden tracking that evades filters.

716.p: Small ad campaigns must spend money evenly over time to reach their goals, but unpredictable auctions make this difficult to control.
716.a: Use a simple feedback loop that watches spending in real time and adjusts bids automatically to match the target spend rate.

717.p: Tutoring systems learn what students know in one subject but cannot guess their knowledge in another subject reliably.
717.a: Match skills across subjects using student learning histories and subject descriptions, so knowledge learned in math helps predict performance in physics.

718.p: Recommender systems use relationship maps between users and items but noise in the map and sparse data limit what they can learn.
718.a: Clean the relationship map by gradually adding and removing noise, then use a system that learns connections to identify and refine weak or false relationships.

719.p: People's preferences change between purchases, but recommender systems assume a fixed pattern, missing when interests genuinely shift.
719.a: Learn how to adjust a person's purchase history in meaningful ways that let the system spot real preference changes from just noise.

720.p: When a website's connections form a network, spotting which users or items are odd ones out requires learning from a tiny handful of labeled examples.
720.a: Gradually tweak normal users to look increasingly abnormal—both in their traits and their connections—so the system learns to spot every shade of weirdness.

721.p: News sites want to show you articles you'll love, but your tastes shift hourly as events unfold, and they're trying to guess both your stable habits and your fleeting mood.
721.a: Track your reading in two time windows—a long lens for your usual patterns and a short lens for what you're chasing right now—then blend both to recommend fresher stories.

722.p: When a system that learns from how things connect has no raw data to work with, it can't tell two identical-looking nodes apart, leaving it blind.
722.a: Pick the most central nodes as anchors, measure distance from every node to those anchors, and let the system figure out which anchors and how many it needs.

723.p: Online shops want to predict how much money a customer will spend after clicking an ad, but orders arrive late and people buy multiple times, making labels unreliable.
723.a: Build two separate prediction paths—one for one-time buyers and one for repeat buyers—and dynamically recalibrate targets as late data trickles in.

724.p: Subtle hate speech hides in word choice and tone, but AI often fixates on surface patterns and misses the real poison buried in metaphors and innuendo.
724.a: First hunt for the actual toxic ideas hiding in the text, then carefully reason about each piece before deciding whether something is hateful.

725.p: When you have a new time series with no name, picking the right prediction method takes weeks of trial and error across dozens of algorithms.
725.a: Extract patterns from the time series and match it against 41 known datasets to quickly recommend which algorithm will work best for this specific problem.

726.p: AI systems trained on images and text can leak private details about real people, and erasing that knowledge without breaking everything else is nearly impossible.
726.a: Give the system different forgetting instructions for different types of tasks—making it refuse to recognize faces, answer questions, or complete sentences about protected people.

727.p: Websites and IoT devices pump out torrents of high-dimensional data every second, and spotting the broken sensors or unusual spikes requires extreme speed.
727.a: Build a fast nearest-neighbor index and score each observation by how unlike its neighbors it is, updating the index as new patterns emerge.

728.p: Scammers hide fraud and hate speech under symbols, emojis, and misspellings to slip past filters, and fixing obfuscated text in real time is slow.
728.a: Use a lightweight character-level model with bidirectional alignment to quickly unscramble encoded text without needing a huge AI system.

729.p: Weather stations and IoT sensors sit scattered across a city, leaving huge gaps in coverage, and guessing values at blank spots from sparse data is hard.
729.a: Learn which sensors actually matter to predict at each location by paying attention to similarities in their readings, then progressively refine guesses using those key sensors.

730.p: Graph systems that look at all pairwise relationships become impossibly slow on huge networks, and rigid attention rules fail when the data distribution shifts.
730.a: Compress the graph into discrete code blocks and do attention on those codes instead, cutting computation while improving predictions on unfamiliar data.

731.p: Knowledge bases that map facts about products contain noise and irrelevant links that confuse recommendation engines and hide true customer patterns.
731.a: Scrub the knowledge base to remove garbage while keeping meaningful connections, focusing on facts that help pick better products for each user.

732.p: Fraud detectors that watch for lies in facial expressions, voice tone, and speech fail when crooks learn to fake emotions in ways that fool multiple signals at once.
732.a: Train the detector on fake attacks combining face, voice, and text tricks so it learns to spot coordinated deception across all channels simultaneously.

733.p: Graph prediction systems make overconfident guesses when faced with data unlike anything they trained on, breaking trust in high-stakes applications like healthcare.
733.a: Run the graph through iterative error correction that exposes where predictions become unreliable, showing both uncertainty and why.

734.p: People with low vision, clogged minds, or full hands can't easily access the web, but if smart glasses could understand the world around you and help in real time, the web becomes a wearable layer.
734.a: Chain AI reasoning over video from the glasses to answer long questions, turning speech and eye gaze into web commands, all running on the device or in the cloud.

735.p: Websites must predict which people will connect or interact, but current AI systems either miss big-picture patterns or get too slow with millions of people.
735.a: Combine a fast pattern-detection method that looks at how people naturally cluster together with a smarter way to guess connections while keeping the system explainable.

736.p: When people comment on photos online, their feedback can either discourage or encourage someone to share private pictures of others—but sometimes feedback backfires.
736.a: Test how different types of comments (supporting, opposing, or mixed) actually change behavior, and discover when and why certain people ignore warnings.

737.p: Security teams track logged events with multiple pieces of information (time, addresses, data sizes), but current systems can't properly handle a mix of words and numbers together.
737.a: Treat each type of information according to its true nature, then spot unusual patterns in how these grouped behaviors change over time.

738.p: Scientists want to share working code and research methods online so others can run them, but actually getting that working requires specific setup steps.
738.a: Show researchers step-by-step how to package code with its dependencies so one click runs it, and provide templates and checklists to avoid common mistakes.

739.p: Phishing scams hide on decentralized storage networks where content lives forever even after attackers disappear, defeating traditional detection systems.
739.a: Monitor the decentralized network across multiple sources of data to find and map phishing campaigns, then identify which public gateways amplify attacks.

740.p: AI systems that recommend products inherit unfair biases from their training data, but retraining them is too expensive and slow.
740.a: Identify which training examples teach the AI its biases, then surgically remove only their influence without rebuilding the entire system.

741.p: AI struggles to guess what emotion a sentence expresses because different datasets label emotions differently and systems miss subtle word clues.
741.a: Extract specific language patterns that always signal emotion, then feed those patterns directly into the AI alongside its usual numerical analysis.

742.p: Detecting malicious websites is hard because so few examples exist of actual attacks, and normal sites have weird structures that fool the detector.
742.a: Generate fake variations of known attacks to teach the AI about unseen threats, and isolate only the parts of a site structure that truly matter.

743.p: Very fast AI chips need to compute Hadamard transforms and multiply numbers in radically efficient ways, but both require different circuits.
743.a: Design one circuit that performs both tasks by reusing the same components, reducing the wiring overhead.

744.p: When shoppers search e-commerce sites, their words don't match product listings, so search has to guess what they meant—but AI rewrites queries wrong.
744.a: Teach the AI how humans actually think when fixing vague queries, combining worker feedback with search-system signals to match human expectations.

745.p: Finding the right table in a database is hard because structured data confuses search systems, and regular numeric fingerprints models designed for text fail.
745.a: Pick important parts of tables using a smart grouping method, then have AI write natural-language descriptions of those parts to improve matching.

746.p: Traffic prediction systems only look at past traffic numbers, but real traffic depends on road layout, satellite images, and unexpected events.
746.a: Extract patterns directly from aerial photos to understand road context and combine them with traffic flow models to make better predictions.

747.p: Detecting abnormal people in social networks usually requires training a separate system per network, wasting effort when patterns should transfer.
747.a: Convert graph structure into a data table format that pretrained AI systems already handle well, letting one model work across different networks.

748.p: AI that flags hateful comments produces unfair results for certain groups because it misses coded language and subtle attacks.
748.a: Detect cases where the AI is likely to be biased and apply extra judgment only then, improving fairness without changing the core system.

749.p: Security cameras catch threats like robberies, but systems only spot them—they don't explain what caused them or how dangerous they are.
749.a: Analyze human behavior, object interactions, and background details from video to both find threats and explain what led to them.

750.p: When you search for images using text, the system struggles to match them accurately because important details hide in just small parts of the picture, and similar-looking results confuse the ranking.
750.a: Use an AI system that reads and writes language to add detailed descriptions of images, then analyze the picture in two ways at once: zooming out for the big picture and zooming in for fine details, while forcing the system to rank results more carefully.

751.p: Videos in social media often use sarcasm, where people say the opposite of what they mean, making it nearly impossible to understand the real feeling they're expressing.
751.a: Separate what the words, sounds, and pictures each say about feeling, then use them independently to decode sarcasm instead of mixing them all together where the signals cancel out.

752.p: When grouping data that naturally forms clusters, systems learn to categorize items but have no direct way to know if clustering is their actual goal, so they learn useless patterns.
752.a: Build clustering directly into the learning process: measure how well individual points and their neighborhood connections group together while simultaneously organizing them into clusters.

753.p: When you want an AI system to forget something (like private data or false information), some facts get erased quickly while others stubbornly persist, leaving gaps and inconsistencies.
753.a: Identify which facts are hardest to forget, then focus the erasing process on those stubborn pieces so everything leaves at an even pace without accidentally breaking other knowledge.

754.p: AI systems power search and recommendations across the web, but they can be biased, confusing, and break in unexpected ways when real-world data changes.
754.a: This workshop brings researchers together to figure out how cause-and-effect thinking can make these systems fairer, more transparent, and more stable.

755.p: Online ads compete for space on your screen, and one ad's success depends on where nearby ads sit, but current systems ignore how ads interfere with each other.
755.a: Model ads as dots in space where each ad's value drops based on how close or crowded other ads are, then use math to find the best arrangement that keeps sales honest.

756.p: Creating random versions of large graphs for statistical testing requires multiple passes through the data, making it slow and memory-heavy for real-world datasets.
756.a: Scan the data just once by treating the random shuffling as a sampling problem and using statistical bounds to avoid calculating exact counts upfront.

757.p: Tables on the web have complex layouts and need multi-step reasoning to answer questions, but AI systems rated on simple tests don't show which structural challenges actually trip them up.
757.a: Create a test set that separates layout difficulty from reasoning difficulty, so you can see exactly which kinds of table structure and logic each AI struggles with.

758.p: Predicting radio signal strength everywhere is hard because signals vary smoothly over distance but also bounce chaotically off buildings in unpredictable ways.
758.a: Break radio maps into coarse and fine layers, then predict from rough to detailed by tokenizing layers in a way that skips the artificial limits of discrete symbols.

759.p: Recommendation systems show popular items constantly while burying lesser-known ones, but fixing this fairness problem usually hides how the system actually works.
759.a: Find and tweak the specific neurons in a trained model that encode popularity bias, using test users to identify which signals steer toward or away from popular items.

760.p: False information spreads on social media when people cluster into polarized groups and dismiss opposing views, but systems can't spot these danger signs early enough.
760.a: Track topics in real-time as they emerge and measure how much feeling splits along topic lines, then use that polarization pattern to predict which stories will spread as false.

761.p: News and documents contain facts tied to places and times, but turning that messy text into organized searchable data requires expensive manual setup for each domain.
761.a: Let users define what dimensions they care about, then use an AI system that reads and writes language to extract and locate events automatically, with built-in error-checking.

762.p: Designing new medicines requires generating molecules that fit multiple requirements at once, but current systems don't accurately follow the combined goals during generation.
762.a: Break molecule-making into steps where the structure gradually shifts to satisfy all conditions together, using a two-stage training method to teach each step correctly.

763.p: People write instructions to AI systems, but the exact wording hugely changes how well it works, forcing users into tedious trial-and-error guessing.
763.a: This workshop shares proven techniques, lessons, and new ideas about how to write better instructions and use AI systems reliably at scale.

764.p: When evaluating AI systems that solve research problems through many reasoning steps, a single success score hides whether the reasoning was sound or just lucky.
764.a: Measure the entire path the AI took: how efficient it was, whether it backed up claims with evidence, and how robust it stays when given hints or harder versions.

765.p: When data flows through AI systems with many steps, nobody can prove which data went where or whether it was tampered with—creating impossible-to-verify black boxes.
765.a: Create a detailed record of every piece of data's journey through the system, locked with cryptography so it can't be forged, without slowing down the AI.

766.p: AI systems now have thousands of different models available, but picking which one to use costs money and nobody knows how to choose wisely for each question.
766.a: Automatically route each question to the cheapest or fastest model that can still do good work, adjusting the choice as your budget runs out.

767.p: Short videos spread lies fast and in many ways—some are manipulated, some are deepfakes, some are old clips used wrong—but current tools only catch one type.
767.a: Build a system that looks at the video's content and fact-checks against real sources to spot which specific kind of manipulation is being used.

768.p: AI systems look up facts from documents to answer questions, but they treat each fact separately and miss the bigger picture that comes from combining them.
768.a: Organize facts in layers so the AI can understand both individual pieces and how they relate, then look up answers at whichever level works best.

769.p: When AI systems learn on phones without sharing data, they still leak it through the math equations they send back, and there's no good way to both remove data and keep the system working.
769.a: Carefully split privacy protection across training and recovery steps so the system can forget someone's data without breaking down.

770.p: Clickbait headlines trick AI systems into thinking false stories are true because AI tends to go along with what people believe, not what's actually real.
770.a: Use AI to argue both for and against a headline, then train a smaller AI to spot when the arguments disagree with what's actually verified.

771.p: YouTube lets you tell it to stop recommending videos, but testing shows these buttons barely work—most unwanted videos still come back anyway.
771.a: Run a massive real test with 22,000 people using each button type and measure whether the bad recommendations actually stop.

772.p: AI systems that make choices for many people at once can't do it fairly without revealing who gets what, so there's no private way to handle multiple users.
772.a: Use a method that picks the best choice for each person while keeping their identity hidden throughout the whole process.

773.p: AI deepfake voices sound real now, but spotting them requires looking at how layers of learned sound patterns work together—and current tools ignore that layering.
773.a: Treat the layers as connected layers of clues and look at how they relate to each other, like reading a story where each line makes the next make sense.

774.p: When you ask AI to do important things for you on websites—like make a payment—websites have no good way to let the AI do critical tasks while staying safe.
774.a: Add a permissions system to websites so an AI agent can do what you asked without being able to do anything else harmful.

775.p: Millions of AI agents will soon need to find each other and work together across the internet, but we have no agreed-on rules or infrastructure for that yet.
775.a: Design the foundation protocols and systems now—like DNS for the web—so agents can discover, trust, and cooperate with each other safely.

776.p: People can trick AI systems into saying harmful things using sneaky prompts that look innocent, and current defenses are slow and easy to get around.
776.a: Add a safety prefix to the prompt and watch where the AI's attention changes shape—if it changes a lot, the prompt is probably an attack.

777.p: AI doesn't know when it's confused, when it's making things up, or when the question is out of its depth—so people can't tell when to trust it.
777.a: Give AI systems a way to track their own confidence and uncertainty, then automatically switch to slower, more careful thinking for hard questions.

778.p: Search engines find things similar to what you typed, but sometimes you want things similar to several different search terms at once, not just one.
778.a: Extend search to handle multiple reference points—find things that match all of them, or things that match any of them.

779.p: Lies on social media are hard to spot because they hide among massive amounts of true information, and when multiple AI agents discuss it, they often focus on the wrong clues.
779.a: Have different agents look at different parts of the evidence to catch the weak misleading signals, then combine their findings smartly.

780.p: Websites need to predict traffic spikes and demand patterns weeks in advance, but directly forcing AI systems to learn these patterns requires expensive retraining for each task.
780.a: Feed the AI system example patterns from past data without retraining, using a small learned adapter that injects compressed context about what to expect into the system's core.

781.p: Voice-cloning services hosted online raise privacy fears because companies store and might misuse your biometric data, yet local alternatives run slowly or require lots of your computing power.
781.a: Build a modular voice-synthesis system that runs entirely on your own computer, accepting just a few seconds of your voice to clone your speech or hours of custom audio to refine quality.

782.p: Fact-checkers must verify false news quickly but often look for evidence in the wrong places because the news text itself doesn't directly say what they should search for.
782.a: Use a small AI to rewrite the news claim into better search queries, then improve those queries based on what evidence it finds, feeding the refined evidence back to verify the claim.

783.p: Online platforms rank people's importance using network measures, but bad actors can hide their true influence by creating fake accounts spread across different groups.
783.a: Show how attackers can use fake accounts to distort importance measures and design practical methods to detect when networks have been manipulated this way.

784.p: Large web services log millions of events daily, but finding the rare errors that matter requires auditable explanations and must run on cheap machines without killing your infrastructure.
784.a: Stage one retrieves suspicious logs, then stage two refines these into readable pattern rules that explain exactly what went wrong, enabling fast matching without expensive computation.

785.p: New types of bad content emerge on video platforms faster than human reviewers can notice and write rules to block, causing delay in protecting users.
785.a: Deploy AI agents that scan for recurring new content problems, group them by issue type, and auto-generate updated moderation policies to catch these emerging patterns immediately.

786.p: Creating realistic 3D textures for web objects from photos is hard because text descriptions are vague and standard textures lock in lighting, breaking when lights change.
786.a: Combine photo hints plus text description plus shape geometry to generate separate maps for base color, shininess, and roughness, enabling the texture to work under any lighting.

787.p: Payment fraud detection systems forget old fraud patterns when adapting to new tricks, but storing years of fraud cases strains storage and privacy concerns.
787.a: Generate synthetic replay fraud cases using a image-generating model that preserves the structure of old patterns, allowing the system to remember without storing real private transactions.

788.p: Meme moderation systems trained mostly on Western content misread cultural references in jokes from other regions, making safety rules fail across languages.
788.a: Test image-understanding AI across multiple languages and cultures, finding that prompting in native language and showing one example works far better than translating and detecting.

789.p: Emotion detection in dialogue needs text, audio, and video but noisy data from one channel can ruin the combined prediction, and feelings shift throughout a conversation.
789.a: Dynamically pick which text-audio-video pairs to combine based on quality, use information overlap to align meaning across channels, and track how emotions change turn by turn.

790.p: Cross-platform recommendation systems that learn from your behavior on multiple sites without privacy concerns risk being poisoned by bad actors or ignoring real differences between domains.
790.a: Separate what users like in common across platforms from what's unique to each platform, then audit each person's contribution to detect when someone sends misleading updates.

791.p: On social media, some groups have outsized influence on collective opinion due to network position, yet fairness tools to balance this haven't been formally studied.
791.a: Adjust how stubborn each person is about their own views versus listening to others, using precise formulas to ensure groups end up with equal say in shaping collective opinion.

792.p: Satellite internet services bringing connectivity to remote zones face radiation damage that drains batteries and breaks sessions, but standard fixes waste energy and still fail.
792.a: Reroute traffic during radiation storms while carefully managing power to avoid battery collapse, balancing energy use against keeping sessions alive and stable.

793.p: Recommendation systems implement fairness rules at training time, but different users and companies want different fairness rules at different times, forcing expensive retraining.
793.a: Train once with special adapter layers that can dial fairness up or down after training, guaranteeing improvements at each level without retraining for each fairness choice.

794.p: Vaccine misinformation spreads as images and memes combining pictures and text, but image-based fact-checking is hard because it's unclear which visual cues matter.
794.a: Use image-understanding AI to extract named visual concepts supporting stance, then let classical models trained on these concepts predict and explain why each image is misleading.

795.p: AI agents running independently across the internet need ways to prove who they are and whether they can be trusted, but nobody has built the infrastructure for that yet.
795.a: Create a control system inspired by how the internet manages domain names and certificates—so agents can get certified, be found, and work together safely across networks.

796.p: Tor users think their web visits are hidden, but someone watching the encrypted traffic patterns can often guess which websites they visited, eroding their privacy.
796.a: Build a smarter pattern-matching system trained on real Tor data that accounts for irregular bursts and varying lengths, catching more site visits while staying practical.

797.p: Predicting how network performance or power usage will change weeks ahead is hard because the patterns happen at different time scales and real data is noisy.
797.a: Use a lightweight mix-and-process model that randomly samples different time windows and blends patterns across scales, handling noise better than older methods.

798.p: Scientific knowledge databases built by many people have duplicate entries, confusing names, and unclear meanings, making it hard for AI systems to use the data correctly.
798.a: Use an AI system to read and write language combined with human experts to clean up duplicates, standardize naming, and rebuild the database for machines to understand.

799.p: Science unfairly recognizes men more than women, and famous institutions get cited much more than equally good work elsewhere—perpetuating unfair advantage.
799.a: Build a model showing how homophily, prestige bias, and underrepresentation compound each other; prove that adding more women alone won't fix it without reducing bias too.

800.p: Searching knowledge databases for paths between facts is either slow or returns useless detours, forcing systems to choose between accuracy and speed.
800.a: Pre-build and index a smart subset of paths that covers all the important facts, turning slow searches into quick lookups while keeping results clean.

801.p: When you need to delete sensitive or wrong data from a trained system that learns from how things connect, existing deletion methods either don't work well or lose too much utility.
801.a: Understand what the system actually remembers about each piece of data, then adaptively decide how hard to push deletion based on what's harder to forget.

802.p: Live-streaming platforms need to suggest the right streams to watch, but everything changes constantly—streamers switch topics, users change interests, and the platform itself evolves fast.
802.a: Model real-time interactions within each live room—tracking how streamers and viewers collaborate—and update the suggestions using two time-varying connection maps.

803.p: Predicting future connections in real-world networks fails when edges rarely repeat and events happen fast, because old methods get confused by noise and sudden changes.
803.a: Focus on when each node interacts, not just who, and use frequency analysis to amplify important local patterns while dampening noise from chaotic sequences.

804.p: Existing forecasting methods struggle to predict far into the future, often missing the biases and complex errors that pile up over time.
804.a: Generate predictions for how far off the system will be, using a compressed error model, then combine that with a backbone predictor to correct long-term drift.

805.p: A system that learns from how things connect fails when connected items are dissimilar, especially when it can't tell the difference between important and noisy neighbors.
805.a: Look at local neighborhoods and fairness constraints to understand meaningful patterns, then selectively blend homophily and dissimilarity based on context.

806.p: Fitting new items into an organized hierarchy of categories is hard because some places in the hierarchy have many more examples than others, biasing the training.
806.a: Train two separate lightweight AI systems—one focused on leaf positions, one on balance—and combine them with a learning method that emphasizes the overall structure.

807.p: When a broker sits between a buyer and seller, each willing only once, the broker may suppress deal quality to keep profit—unless you use the single samples wisely.
807.a: Prove that simple, sample-only mechanisms achieve solid deals and profit for the broker, with only modest losses compared to a world without middlemen.

808.p: Fast image search across different websites fails when the source website's training data is mislabeled or crowdsourced carelessly, dragging down search quality.
808.a: Separate noisy labels from clean ones using uncertainty estimates, then gradually align the search system across domains by prioritizing well-matched images first.

809.p: Spotting unusual graphs in a dataset is hard when you have no labeled examples and no baseline for what 'normal' looks like in graph-structured data.
809.a: Learn hidden patterns using both explicit graph structure rules and a system that learns from connection patterns, then flag graphs that deviate from learned norms.

810.p: Hackers hide their attacks across many connected computer systems over weeks, making them nearly impossible to spot with traditional tools that only look at pairs of events.
810.a: They built a detection system that treats attacks as webs of interconnected events rather than simple pairs, allowing it to see how multiple actions coordinate and how attacks spread across the whole network.

811.p: AI systems used in web apps can be tricked by carefully modified text designed on a simpler AI model and then used to fool the real system without permission.
811.a: They created a method to craft more reliable tricks by testing multiple AI models together, scoring which words matter most, and keeping only the tricks that actually transfer to the real system.

812.p: Recommendation websites must retrain their models constantly as tastes change, but training on millions of user interactions is expensive and wastes time on messy, unreliable data.
812.a: They pick a small, smart subset of clean training examples that captures the important patterns, filtering out wrong labels and unreliable signals to train faster without losing quality.

813.p: Open source projects on GitHub are hard to measure fairly because current metrics only track quick responses and star counts, missing how communities actually collaborate and influence each other.
813.a: They built a flexible data collection tool and dashboard that computes network-based metrics showing how developers actually work together and influence the health of open source projects.

814.p: AI systems used to rank search results work too slowly because they generate one item at a time, which wastes time and computing power when you need to show ten results at once.
814.a: They speed it up by predicting multiple possible rankings in a single pass, using a smart grouping trick to reduce the impossible number of combinations to something workable.

815.p: Phone identity systems in many countries keep your personal data in one company's servers, creating huge privacy risks and single points of failure that hackers can exploit.
815.a: They created a decentralized system where your identity lives on your device, not company servers, using mathematical proofs so companies can verify you without seeing your private information.

816.p: Social media posts often leak private information that isn't directly written down but can be guessed from surrounding context, and it's hard to automatically catch these sneaky leaks.
816.a: They built a tool that maps the relationships between words in text to find both obvious secrets and hidden clues that together could reveal private information about a person.

817.p: Video streaming apps need to predict what you'll watch next, but time gaps between your clicks matter as much as the clicks themselves, and most systems ignore this information.
817.a: They improved prediction by having the AI track the pattern of time gaps between your actions, not just the gaps themselves, so it better understands your interests and mood.

818.p: Building AI systems that know about specific fields like medicine requires expensive experts to fix mistakes, and the system doesn't know how to choose between its own knowledge and expert answers.
818.a: They created a system where the AI catches its own made-up answers and uses that to decide when to trust expert corrections, gradually improving without needing experts for everything.

819.p: When companies train AI models together while keeping their data private, a malicious participant can sneak poisoned data into the system that breaks the final model.
819.a: They detect and remove the poisoned pieces by finding small differences between clean and broken data and voting out the suspicious ones before they affect the trained model.

820.p: As billions of AI agents work together across the web, there's no standard way for them to discover each other, communicate, or build trust and reputation with users.
820.a: This workshop brings together researchers to design open standards for how AI agents should act on the web, from technical protocols to solving problems of trust and accountability.

821.p: Finding which people will spread a message the most requires knowing how everyone's connected, but in real life that network is often secret, incomplete, or constantly changing.
821.a: They built a system that learns how people influence each other directly from their past behavior without needing the connection map, then picks the best spreaders using trial-and-reward learning.

822.p: When you search and find something different than you expected, it throws you off, and websites can't currently tell when this happens so they can't help you recover.
822.a: They used eye-tracking to spot when search results surprise you, discovering that the time you keep staring at something matters more than how quickly you first look at it.

823.p: Video apps like Douyin need to remember what you watched weeks ago to make good recommendations, but storing and processing 10,000 hours of history would be impossibly expensive.
823.a: They cut the computational cost in half by redesigning how the AI attends to history and reusing computations for multiple videos you'd watch, training on short clips but working on long histories.

824.p: Digital maps built from car GPS trails often get road connections wrong in busy cities because treating the trails as pictures misses how roads actually connect to each other.
824.a: They map roads in two ways at once—as pictures and as movement paths—so the system understands both the visual look and which roads actually connect, fixing mistakes in congested areas.

825.p: We need to measure whether a conversation is actually going well, but there's no perfect definition and humans disagree on what makes one engaging.
825.a: Use math about how likely an AI would generate each response given what was said before—if responses are surprising, the conversation flowed naturally.

826.p: Text messages increasingly carry harmful pictures, and current filtering tools are too slow and inaccurate for the massive volume companies must check daily.
826.a: Built a visual classifier trained on a taxonomy of eight image categories, using a type of system trained on billions of text-image pairs and adapted to this specific task.

827.p: Online gaming and video calls freeze when network delays become erratic and unpredictable—detecting these patterns at line-speed in massive traffic is nearly impossible.
827.a: Use a compact algorithm that flags jittery internet flows by filtering out stable ones first, so we catch only the problematic traffic fast.

828.p: AI systems now write convincing fake news headlines that fool people; we need to detect AI-written stories before they spread.
828.a: Compare writing style of AI-made and real headlines—AI tends to be more toxic, negative, and relies heavily on authority claims—then spot fakes with targeted analysis.

829.p: Large AI models are too big to run on phones because they require more memory than the device has, even though most phones have plenty of computing power.
829.a: Use a smaller draft model to answer easy questions fast, then verify answers with the full model only when needed, reusing memory smartly.

830.p: Library systems that only store book titles fail readers because vocabulary differs, and people lack expertise to judge whether results actually fit their need.
830.a: Deploy three AI agents that talk to each other: one clarifies what you want, one searches by keywords, one evaluates matches with domain expertise.

831.p: When predicting with multiple data sources, some are noisier than others, but current systems treat all sources the same way and over-penalize ambiguous categories.
831.a: Adjust constraints for each data source individually: relax strict penalties for naturally confusing categories and suppress noise from unreliable sources.

832.p: AI systems that learn from text and network structure together are vulnerable to attacks, and no one knows how to test these safely across different model types.
832.a: Use AI's own understanding of how graphs work to design universal attacks that change both text and connections, testing defenses across different backends.

833.p: AI systems use enormous energy because they apply deep reasoning to every question, even simple ones that need only a quick factual lookup.
833.a: Route each question based on difficulty: skip reasoning for simple factoid queries, reserve heavy computation for complex logic, cutting energy by 40 percent.

834.p: Fact-checking claims with pictures is harder than text alone because pictures add evidence but systems ignore or misuse visual information.
834.a: Retrieve similar pictures, enrich understanding of images in context, improve textual evidence with facts, and teach AI to reason through all pieces.

835.p: Fake news uses both social networks and writing tricks to spread, but single detectors fail because they only catch one type of camouflage.
835.a: Use two independent detectors—one for network patterns, one for language—that cross-check each other and agree on whether news is fake.

836.p: Predicting outcomes from databases is hard because finding useful new columns requires reasoning about complex schemas and trying countless combinations.
836.a: Have AI agents identify relevant tables, generate diverse candidate columns, filter useful ones through testing, and repeat until predictions improve.

837.p: Recommendation systems that train on phones fail for users with few purchases and items with few ratings because there's not enough local data.
837.a: Share knowledge across phones: enrich data for sparse users by borrowing from similar people, and for sparse items by prioritizing phones with diverse ratings.

838.p: Finding key people or genes in networks is hard because most methods ignore rich attributes and only look at connections.
838.a: Use a graph learning system's own explanations to find which groups of people matter most, considering both structure and attributes together.

839.p: AI recommendation systems tend to repeat what you already like instead of broadening your horizons, trapping you in a filter bubble.
839.a: Make AI think through multiple viewpoints by analyzing sentiment in reviews and simulating social influence, so it suggests diverse items instead of just agreeing with your past.

840.p: When people delete their account, the system must forget them—but removing them exposes protected info and can unfairly hurt some groups while helping others.
840.a: Build the deletion process to actively shield sensitive attributes, ensuring fair treatment for all groups even as the person vanishes from the network.

841.p: Network protocols break because code doesn't truly understand what the spec means—automated testing can't catch hidden violations that crash systems.
841.a: Use an AI system to extract the real rules from official protocol documents, then deliberately violate them to spot bugs before they reach the real world.

842.p: When weather sensors fail or data is private, forecasts train on complete data but must predict with missing pieces—shifting patterns make this even harder.
842.a: Rebuild missing data by spotting which parts stay stable over time and which parts wobble, then handle both separately to stay accurate across seasons.

843.p: Predicting someone's opinion on a brand they've never seen requires learning from known targets but guessing for novel ones—old methods fail when targets change.
843.a: Expand training data with AI-written variety, mix different feature types, and update mental prototypes of opinion patterns in real time as new targets arrive.

844.p: Live streamers spend hours writing descriptions and answering repetitive questions, slowing sales and boring viewers with copy-paste answers.
844.a: One tool extracts product details automatically before streaming, another answers viewer questions in real time by looking up the stored product info.

845.p: Recommending based on many actions (view, click, buy) confuses models because users have habits and items behave differently—mixing them in naively hurts prediction.
845.a: Model why users act in ways they do, then carefully blend each action type by watching which mix works best, weighing bias along the way.

846.p: Psychologists use drawings to spot mental health issues in kids, but automating this with an AI risks missing real problems or seeing ones that aren't there.
846.a: Test whether AI can reliably interpret kid drawings on specific mental health dimensions, using clinician-grounded metrics that match real screening workflows.

847.p: Fairness audits of platforms disagree wildly—different tests give different answers, leaving regulators confused about whether the platform is actually fair.
847.a: Pool many audits into a single honest statement about fairness with clear uncertainty bands, showing what policy risk each range truly carries.

848.p: Long sequences of user clicks overwhelm models with noise—old interests resurface, making it hard to know what the person actually wants right now.
848.a: Group sequences into themed chunks, route similar themes together, and ignore noise from old interests that don't apply to today's prediction.

849.p: AI reasoning fails at strict logic puzzles because small typos break formal notation—AI avoids brittleness but loses step-by-step rigor and error fixing.
849.a: Organize reasoning as a matrix of steps with explicit links, verify the whole plan at once, and automatically fix broken steps rather than restarting.

850.p: Criminals run fake versions of security report buttons so real complaints never reach the platform, letting malware hide in plain sight.
850.a: Hunt for fake report buttons that impersonate official ones, build a dataset of malware using them, and expose the obfuscation tricks they hide behind.

851.p: People are using AI for health advice and personal matters but don't know whether the tool treats them as a tool or a friend—roles keep shifting.
851.a: Analyze real ChatGPT chats to track how conversations change, how users open up more, and when people follow the AI's suggestions instead of asking their own.

852.p: AI agents lack a clear moral foundation—they optimize for goals without understanding fairness, honesty, or why people cooperate at all.
852.a: Ground AI ethics in the Golden Rule: teach agents to reason about how their choices affect others, then show this produces fair and honest behavior.

853.p: Telegram moderators can't predict toxic comments before they flood a post, so bad threads spiral out of control.
853.a: Extract clues from the post itself—tone, word choice, emotion—to forecast what kind of comments will follow and what risks the post carries.

854.p: Most items almost nobody buys, while a handful dominate—models learn the popular ones well but ignore tail items, so users with niche taste get bad suggestions.
854.a: Carefully add fake interactions for rare items that relate to popular ones, boosting tail learning while keeping the system good at popular picks.

855.p: Annual financial reports are stuffed with repeated boilerplate, making it hard to spot what actually changed and what that means for investors.
855.a: Compare sentence-by-sentence between two years to flag what was deleted, added, or kept; measure sentiment shift from the new versus removed content.

856.p: AI systems that read and write language can't explain their answers or verify facts, risking misinformation when they manage real data on the web.
856.a: Connect AI language systems to organized webs of facts so answers are grounded, transparent, and can be checked against known relationships.

857.p: When an AI system reads facts before answering, shorter summaries create dense information but lose detail, degrading accuracy below the original method.
857.a: Instead of shrinking all information equally, choose what's relevant to each question first, then compress, keeping task-critical facts intact.

858.p: Spam and fake-news detectors only flag whole documents, leaving readers unable to pinpoint which specific phrases or claims are problematic.
858.a: Build a system that identifies anomalies at the sentence and word level, showing exactly which parts of a text are suspicious.

859.p: Learning systems shared across many users remain vulnerable to hidden sabotage that quietly degrades one competitor's accuracy without raising alarms.
859.a: Introduce a stealthy attack that manipulates ranking signals to poison a rival's model while evading detection via normal-looking learning progress.

860.p: Medical AI models need huge memory tables to represent medical terms and concepts, and can't explain how they organized that knowledge from medical hierarchies.
860.a: Compress medical concepts into small, efficient codes that align with official medical hierarchies, linking discrete choices to clinical structure.

861.p: Shopping sites struggle to recommend relevant items from massive catalogs using simple math that treats all user behaviors the same.
861.a: Build a two-step system that first expands the candidate pool smartly, then ranks with rich interaction models tuned to each person.

862.p: As AI systems absorb text, images, audio, and video together, explaining decisions and building trust becomes harder without new visualization tools.
862.a: Combine AI with web-based interactive visualizations so people can see and interact with how the system processes multiple types of information.

863.p: Critical infrastructure like power grids must detect rare equipment failures from mixed data types while keeping private information secret from learning systems.
863.a: Use shared facts looked up before answering, plus frequency-domain signal alignment and game-theory privacy shields, without centralizing sensitive data.

864.p: The web evolves constantly, but tools to study how pages, content, and topics change over time remain fragmented across different research communities.
864.a: Create a research hub connecting methods for time-aware data mining, web archiving, and large-scale analysis to study how the web shifts.

865.p: Manual feature engineering for data tables is tedious, and AI systems that auto-generate features produce black-box changes that experts can't understand or verify.
865.a: Use a domain-specific language to represent feature transformations as logical trees, letting AI search for interpretable, well-structured features via small edits.

866.p: Dense search models are fast but opaque—they can't explain which document parts matter or defend against attacks that artificially boost irrelevant results.
866.a: Teach search models to be sensitive to changes in relevant passages while ignoring irrelevant ones, using game theory to improve robustness and explainability.

867.p: Most cause-and-effect tools assume flat, complete data, but real knowledge bases contain gaps, mixed entity types, and logical constraints that break those assumptions.
867.a: Extend causal reasoning frameworks to work directly with organized fact webs, respecting their structure, incompleteness, and semantic rules.

868.p: Academic peer review quality varies widely, and reviewers sometimes make claims that the paper doesn't actually support, undermining research integrity.
868.a: Deploy AI systems to audit review comments for quality and factual grounding, combining AI scoring with retrievable evidence from the paper.

869.p: Cause-and-effect discovery from time series struggles because raw data lacks context and semantic meaning, leading to overfitting and poor real-world results.
869.a: Combine time series with semantic context from language models, using a shared attention mechanism to find causal patterns across both types of information.

870.p: E-commerce sites have huge product catalogs with errors and incomplete information that stop shoppers from finding what they need.
870.a: Use brand reference data and an AI system to automatically fix and match product information at the same time instead of separately.

871.p: Recommendation systems push popular items and ignore lesser-known products that might actually be better for what each person wants.
871.a: Identify which unpopular items matter to each user, then use two specialized models plus a learned selector to recommend better choices.

872.p: Verifying complex claims requires checking many connected parts, but current systems check each part alone and miss how they relate.
872.a: Map how claim pieces connect to each other, then verify them as an interdependent group instead of checking each one in isolation.

873.p: Recommendation systems can't personalize travel suggestions because they don't know how places actually feel and sound to real people.
873.a: Collect photos and sensory descriptions from actual visitors, then visualize this lived experience on maps to enable better recommendations.

874.p: When people ask questions across multiple turns, systems must find the right entity from a vast database while remembering conversation history.
874.a: Gather related facts around each possible answer, then use a neural system that combines multiple relevance signals to rank the best match.

875.p: Misinformation spreads because people believe false claims that exploit how brains process conflicting emotional signals in text.
875.a: Measure how real people judge credibility in actual posts, then detect lies by spotting linguistic conflicts like mixed emotions or contradictions.

876.p: Ad click prediction systems share the same feature data across models, making them noisy and unable to capture distinct patterns separately.
876.a: Give each model its own customized features and filter noise layer-by-layer, letting them capture different signals without interfering.

877.p: AI systems show political bias, but no one has carefully measured whether this bias comes from the raw internet text they learned from.
877.a: Analyze massive web text for bias across topics, then test whether measured bias in the data actually transfers into AI system outputs.

878.p: When people search, the system needs to understand what they really mean, but it only has a few words to work with.
878.a: Use three AI agents to turn a search into questions, generate multiple interpretations, then filter to keep only the most helpful context.

879.p: Building helpful AI assistants requires rethinking how to combine image, video, and sound understanding with logical reasoning ability.
879.a: Shift toward one AI system that handles text, images and video together, reasons through problems, and learns what each person needs.

880.p: Academic citation networks have incomplete author and venue data that limits how well researchers can find related work and collaborators.
880.a: Use an AI system to fill in missing keywords and descriptions from metadata, then encode this richer information into the network structure.

881.p: When people ask multi-turn questions about databases, systems must find the right entity while tracking what was said in earlier turns.
881.a: Model how entities connect within the database structure using neural systems that understand conversation flow to rank the best answers.

882.p: Biased language in news articles misleads recommendation systems into making poor predictions about what readers will enjoy.
882.a: Train a text-only AI to extract factual, unbiased information from articles using image data as a guide, then use clean facts for recommendations.

883.p: Workshop announcement about combining generative AI models with recommendation and search systems.
883.a: Bring together researchers and industry practitioners to discuss how new AI models are changing how systems recommend and search.

884.p: Real-world web systems predict numbers like prices on skewed data, and the data patterns change constantly after the system launches.
884.a: Train specialized models for different data groups and dynamically reweight them at prediction time to adapt without expensive retraining.

885.p: Cities flood dangerously because rain prediction models can't handle unpredictable storms or terrain that channels water differently.
885.a: Combine rainfall data with geography maps to track how water flows and pools, using a system trained on rainfall and terrain patterns together.

886.p: Emergency call takers need practice handling diverse situations, but role-play training is limited and expensive because instructors are scarce.
886.a: Create a web system that simulates emergency calls with AI, gives immediate feedback to trainees, and tracks their decision-making to help them improve.

887.p: Predicting house prices or other numbers from data fails when features interact in complex ways that simple binary rules can't capture.
887.a: Build decision paths that branch in multiple directions instead of just two, guided by an AI system that suggests meaningful conditions at each step.

888.p: Food-sharing groups hidden across cities are invisible to researchers and policymakers, making it hard to understand or support them.
888.a: Search the web for food-sharing groups automatically, verify them by hand, and show them on an interactive map that anyone can explore.

889.p: AI language systems often hide how they make decisions, and common explanation methods give misleading or false reasons for their outputs.
889.a: Focus on explaining AI in ways humans actually need, using concepts they understand rather than trying to decode every internal calculation.

890.p: Teaching a language model to work well in low-resource languages causes it to smash semantic differences between languages, breaking its accuracy.
890.a: Keep different languages' meanings separate by pushing apart clustered units and preventing bias when adding more training data.

891.p: Companies using AI chatbots need them to follow brand voice and legal rules, not just repeat facts from the internet.
891.a: Combine targeted training with company data and real-time fact-fetching to make the AI act like a trained employee who knows the business inside out.

892.p: Traffic forecasts break down during accidents or unusual events, because models are trained only on normal-day patterns.
892.a: Detect unusual traffic events first, then predict flow separately for normal days using only clean historical data.

893.p: When people ask to delete their photos from an AI image system under privacy law, models often erase their faces but ruin the whole picture.
893.a: Use semantic graphs to remove just the requested object from an image while keeping everything else intact and sensible.

894.p: Companies that sell AI models need to prove they built them if someone copies and resells them without permission.
894.a: Embed a hidden fingerprint in the model so multiple users can independently verify ownership without sharing one secret key.

895.p: City planners guess traffic layouts from experience, but they often pick suboptimal designs because the search space is too huge to explore by hand.
895.a: Use a simulation-based system that generates and tests road layouts automatically, learning patterns from thousands of possibilities.

896.p: Short video platforms can't catch creators hiding agendas in videos or stealing viral content with tiny tweaks.
896.a: Divide video analysis into specialized agents: one detects subtle signs of manipulation, one fetches similar videos, one judges originality.

897.p: App stores struggle to recommend apps to brand-new users because user data and browsing history pull recommendations in opposite directions.
897.a: Learn from user profile and browsing history separately, then combine them selectively to avoid conflicting signals.

898.p: AI language systems can use item IDs from click history and text descriptions, but fusing them introduces noise and misalignment.
898.a: Train two separate processes on a shared AI system—one for each type of information—then blend them at inference time with text taking the lead.

899.p: Search engines work well in English but don't retrieve documents across languages, blocking users who speak other languages.
899.a: Build a test set where English queries must find relevant documents in any language to measure multilingual search quality.

900.p: Shopping sites struggle to recommend items to brand-new users who haven't bought anything yet, and must update those recommendations as users reveal new preferences over weeks.
900.a: Learn which features of users change and which stay the same, then keep the stable part as you adapt to each person's new tastes.

901.p: AI systems that pick tools to solve tasks fail because real training data has too few examples of rare tools and includes mistakes.
901.a: Teach the system step-by-step, starting with easy, common tool choices, then advance to harder cases with fewer examples.

902.p: Spotting breaking news on social media by analyzing photos and text together requires having labeled examples, but real-world events keep changing unpredictably.
902.a: Build stronger photo-text pairs from raw social media by describing what the photos show and what events they depict, then learn without labels.

903.p: During Black Friday sales, user behavior changes so much that ads models trained on normal days fail to predict if someone will buy.
903.a: Build a model with stable parts and promotion-sensitive parts that adjust separately, then learn which parts to use for each sale period.

904.p: Large shopping sites use multiple systems to pick which items to show, but they often show overlapping results, wasting space on duplicates.
904.a: Train a new system to find items the existing systems missed, focusing on picking things truly new to recommend.

905.p: Recommending across different shopping domains fails because information that looks shared, like 'durable', means different things in clothing versus tools.
905.a: Automatically sort item descriptions into three buckets: words unique to one domain, shared words, and universal words; transfer knowledge only where safe.

906.p: Finding the most influential people in massive social networks is too slow to calculate exactly, even with fast computers.
906.a: Use random walks to quickly estimate who matters most, which can run in parallel on many computers.

907.p: E-commerce search pages now show grids, not lists, but ranking systems only optimize one thing at a time and ignore long-term customer satisfaction.
907.a: Use causal statistics to measure two-week revenue instead of just same-day sales, then optimize how items and images fit the entire page layout.

908.p: AI systems that generate recommendations by reading long customer history are too slow for real-time shopping, even though longer history helps them.
908.a: Compress old purchases by grouping them into product categories, keeping key patterns while cutting processing time by six times.

909.p: When customers are connected by a network, measuring whether an ad caused a sale is hard because showing it to one person influences their friends.
909.a: Learn separate hidden patterns for confusing effects, instruments, and adjustments, then use network structure to untangle what actually causes sales.

910.p: Machines struggle to catch anomalies in sensor data because they try to predict many measurements at once, spreading their focus too thin.
910.a: Pick one key measurement to predict and include only similar measurements as input, letting the model focus its learning effort.

911.p: AI systems trained on extracting people names and dates from one company's documents fail on another company's documents with different label styles.
911.a: Split the work: AI finds entity names and assigns meaning, while simple models map that meaning to each company's unique labeling scheme.

912.p: Teaching machines to find person names in text using limited examples fails because the machine makes mistakes that reinforce themselves.
912.a: Use an AI system with world knowledge to judge which guesses are likely right, combining its confidence with smoothed probability scores.

913.p: AI systems that look facts up before answering struggle when knowledge is organized as tables, trees, or social graphs instead of flat text.
913.a: Tutorial covering how to adapt fact-lookup systems to handle different data structures safely and effectively in real applications.

914.p: Simplifying matrices by peeling off layers mathematically requires choosing when to stop, but humans disagree on the right stopping point.
914.a: Use AI agents: one generates layer-by-layer simplifications, another visually judges and decides when to stop without fixed thresholds.

915.p: Harmful memes on social media spread divisive stories, but it's hard to tell if a meme's real meaning matches what it literally shows because deceptive look-alikes distract from the truth.
915.a: Train an AI system by showing it both images and text together, plus real fact-checked sources, so it learns to ignore fake-similar distractors and ground answers in actual evidence.

916.p: Scientists use AI to predict how materials will behave in experiments, but these predictions are only tested once on old data, not checked as they run continuously or when ingredients change.
916.a: Test AI predictions over time as a simulation runs and across different material mixtures to catch when accuracy breaks down or drifts, not just on a snapshot.

917.p: Complex questions need answers hidden across many documents, but breaking them into sub-questions before searching makes both worse: bad clues create wrong sub-questions, which pull back wrong evidence.
917.a: Go back and forth: ask a sub-question, search for evidence, read the answer, then ask the next sub-question based on what you found, letting each step fix the last.

918.p: Knowledge bases grow unevenly and never stop—some facts appear constantly, others rarely, and old info gets buried—but AI systems trained once assume a steady, stable world.
918.a: Use a system that watches how knowledge base topology changes over time, replays important old examples, and shifts how much it values new facts versus keeping old ones alive.

919.p: Knowledge bases store both facts (who is connected to whom) and descriptions (words about each person), but AI systems usually ignore one or the other, missing insights.
919.a: Align fact-based and text-based knowledge, then use the question context to weight which candidate entities matter most before making a prediction.

920.p: AI must make decisions that affect people's lives, but it can't predict outcomes accurately if it ignores how humans talk, look, think, and connect across cultures.
920.a: Expand AI data across language, images, behavior, and how people link together in networks, then test whether the AI reasons consistently across different cultures and professions.

921.p: E-commerce sites measure if you click and buy after, but they only train on clicked items—so at checkout they guess conversions on items you never clicked, a hidden mismatch.
921.a: Teach the AI to distinguish between items you actually rejected versus items you never saw, so it learns from the full picture without favoring misleading signals.

922.p: Investment advisors must balance your return goals and your willingness to tolerate risk, but popular recommendations chase returns alone and miss your real comfort zone.
922.a: Adjust ranked investment picks to maximize utility for your risk tolerance and likelihood you'll actually follow the advice, while keeping the list diverse and trustworthy.

923.p: AI systems that learn from graph connections like social networks or product catalogs make decisions we can't see inside, so we can't tell if they're wrong or biased.
923.a: Build tools that explain not just final decisions but show step-by-step how information flows through the AI and where errors come from, in ways both experts and regular people understand.

924.p: A new website can't recommend items to a returning user from another site without learning their tastes there first, so new customers see poor suggestions.
924.a: Borrow hints about what you liked on site A to guess what you'll like on site B by finding similar users and comparing how they rate things across both platforms.

925.p: Recommendation engines only see what you clicked and browsed, missing why you looked—what search terms brought you there tell the real story of what you wanted.
925.a: Predict your real intent by studying your past searches and clicks together, so the recommender knows you want fishing gear when you click a reel, not just any reel.

926.p: Recommendation systems must grab the right item fast from millions of choices, but capturing what users want right now (short-term trends) usually costs too much compute.
926.a: Add a lightweight memory layer that spotlights which items went together recently, so the system catches fleeting fads without slowing down or using extra storage.

927.p: AI systems that learn how things connect (like how people form groups) are accurate but slow; simpler systems are fast but worse, and shrinking one to match the other loses knowledge.
927.a: Teach the fast AI to learn from the slow one's outputs and its own hidden insights at the same time, then use a smart decision-maker to balance multiple improvement goals.

928.p: Hiring and loan systems trained on history inherit decades of bias, so they hurt minority groups even with no one trying to discriminate.
928.a: Build a fair training dataset by matching how a fresh AI learns on synthetic data with how it learns on real data, while ensuring equal outcomes across groups.

929.p: Classifying articles or products from just text descriptions fails without labels to learn from, because the AI doesn't know the categories without examples.
929.a: Generate fake samples for each category using a joint model of text and graph structure, so the AI can guess labels for brand-new unseen items.

930.p: Online stores use one-size-fits-all math to guess if shoppers will buy, but different shoppers need different logic.
930.a: Automatically split features into two groups: some help predict who buys, others help customize the math separately per shopper type.

931.p: Making fake training data by labeling what you want first leads AI systems to learn poorly, but nobody tests if the order matters.
931.a: Generate diverse examples first, label afterward—matching how real data happens—and compare it against the backwards labeling approach.

932.p: When AI fact-checkers use web facts to verify claims, they sometimes trust their own old knowledge more than the new evidence, leading to wrong answers.
932.a: Figure out what the AI system actually knows versus guesses, use new evidence only when helpful, and remove the AI's self-bias during reasoning.

933.p: Finding cause-and-effect relationships in organized webs of facts is hard when data is incomplete and entities influence each other indirectly.
933.a: Use a system that learns from connection patterns to fill missing pieces and measure effects while accounting for how entities ripple through the network.

934.p: Phishing websites fool millions of people every year by looking like real banks or services, costing victims time and money.
934.a: Train AI systems on both today's phishing sites and real banks to spot fakes, then explain the red flags to help people learn.

935.p: Recommending bundles of items together is hard when new bundles are created constantly and the system knows nothing about them.
935.a: Learn patterns from how items and people relate to popular bundles, then use both old and new bundle info to guess preferences for unfamiliar combos.

936.p: Hundreds of new causal learning methods exist but researchers have no unified way to test and compare them fairly across problems.
936.a: Create a shared testing ground with standard datasets, metrics, and tasks so the community can measure which causal methods work best where.

937.p: Researchers need to search millions of academic papers for citations and find peers to review submissions, but tools often ignore how papers connect.
937.a: Build a flexible search system that combines four different ways of measuring paper similarity—from reading text to analyzing citation networks.

938.p: AI systems can unknowingly memorize which celebrities are in training photos, creating privacy risks even after being asked to forget.
938.a: Build a test dataset with famous faces and varied captions to measure whether unlearning actually removes a person's influence from image descriptions.

939.p: The web, social networks, and knowledge bases are vast webs of connections, but AI systems struggle to reason about them fairly and explain decisions.
939.a: Bring together experts to discuss how to build graph systems that reason reliably, catch false info, track origins, and partner with humans transparently.

940.p: Recommending groups of items together is hard when new groups are constantly created and only popular items have history.
940.a: Mine how items relate to each other and learn popular bundle patterns, then use both information sources to predict what new bundles fit each user.

941.p: Organizing new words into hierarchical dictionaries by hand is slow, and automated methods rely on weak negative examples.
941.a: Generate strategically harder negative examples by gradually transforming random examples, forcing the system to learn finer distinctions for placement.

942.p: Predicting what users will click next is hard when past behavior is noisy and the system wants to be confident in messy sequences.
942.a: Add stable geometry constraints to the noise-removal process and use guided attention to make predictions that adapt to noisy real behavior.

943.p: Online discussions spread feelings between people—anger, fear, joy—and those emotions drive polarization, misinformation spread, and group divides.
943.a: Track discrete emotions in social media posts to show how feelings amplify within groups, create us-versus-them thinking, and reshape entire communities.

944.p: Hospital patient records are messy and incomplete, making AI predictions of health outcomes unreliable without smarter ways to prepare the data.
944.a: Train an AI system to rewrite messy records into cleaner versions, aligned with what doctors care about, using generated examples to guide the rewriting.

945.p: When many people write different opinions on one topic, creating a summary that captures all viewpoints fairly and explains why they disagree is extremely difficult.
945.a: First build a summary of the most common view, then find specific passages that prove disagreements exist, and expand the summary to include those opposing views.

946.p: Time-series data like stock prices or sensor readings often contain unusual spikes or drops that signal problems, but spotting them automatically across many different types of data is unsolved.
946.a: Survey decades of algorithms for finding unusual patterns, introduce tools to measure which methods work best, and show how to pick the right method without manual tweaking.

947.p: AI systems answer questions by pulling facts from Wikipedia-like databases, but they waste time fetching irrelevant facts and struggle to explain their reasoning step by step.
947.a: Plan exactly which facts to look up before searching, follow that plan strictly, and pause if you hit a dead end to re-plan, so you waste zero effort.

948.p: Systems that learn from how things connect (e.g., friends-of-friends networks) lose important information when they combine each person's data with their neighbors' data.
948.a: Before combining, diversify each person's features so they don't blend into mush, then save structural details afterward so neighborhood relationships stay visible.

949.p: AI chatbots struggle to recommend products or explain choices when they lack facts about product features, and they grab too much irrelevant information when they try to look things up.
949.a: First pick which product to suggest, then pick which features to explain using step-by-step reasoning, so each suggestion is backed by only the most relevant facts.

950.p: Spreading labels across millions of people in a network (e.g., predicting who likes what) requires impossible amounts of computer memory and time with today's methods.
950.a: Instead of storing direct connections, work purely with compressed numerical summaries, shrinking memory from billions to millions of numbers and running on graphics processors.

951.p: For decades, recommendations have simply predicted what people will do next, but powerful new AI systems could discover surprising insights and guide people toward breakthroughs.
951.a: Trace how AI personalization evolved from data helper to self-improving chatbot to thoughtful agent, and explore what's needed to make super-intelligent guidance real.

952.p: Recommendation systems that use images and videos alongside text often fail when a picture is missing or video won't load, and reconstructing them adds pointless complexity.
952.a: Build unified summaries from whatever images or videos are available, skip the missing ones entirely, and feed that blend into a social-network-style recommendation engine.

953.p: Finding bugs in C code requires understanding both the code's exact structure and its hidden logical relationships, but scanning tools only catch surface patterns.
953.a: Map code to a network of structure and logic, learn what patterns hide bugs by mining that network unsupervised, then teach a language model to understand context.
