954.p: Recommendation engines perform well for loyal customers but fail for brand-new users, because there's almost nothing to learn about someone on their first visit.
954.a: Route loyal users to a high-accuracy model and new users to a semantic search engine that finds similar items, sacrificing precision for discovering novelty new users love.

955.p: Distinguishing real news from AI-generated lies is hard because AI fakes are fluent and believable, and different types of fakes need different fact-checking strategies.
955.a: Train a system with multiple fact-checking experts that independently decides whether to search for facts and how much evidence to gather for each post.

956.p: Machine learning models are valuable intellectual property, but an attacker can copy a model by sending questions and observing answers without knowing how it was trained.
956.a: Generate fake training data using patterns of the target system, query it to learn its behavior, then build a copycat model that mimics the original.

957.p: Search engines show different results based on your location, trapping people in regional filter bubbles where they only see locally-biased news on controversial topics.
957.a: Search from different countries on the same topics, use AI to analyze results from multiple viewpoints, and measure how regional differences and time create distinct bubbles.

958.p: Traders struggle to turn mountains of financial news, filings, and social posts into winning trading strategies without hiring armies of experts to read and interpret.
958.a: Automatically extract facts from web data, build a knowledge network, generate trading ideas, and backtest them historically to find strategies that truly make money.

959.p: Choosing which AI system to ask for advice is hard when different models give different answers and each is better at different things.
959.a: Show responses from many AI models side by side, let real users vote on which they prefer, and rank models by performance across many real-world tasks.

960.p: Scientists struggle to find and predict repeating patterns in large, messy datasets where timing can shift between occurrences.
960.a: Break down time data into a steady trend and repeating wave parts using mathematical sine and cosine waves instead of complex neural models.

961.p: Ad platforms can't accurately predict if a click leads to a purchase when the sale happens days later, causing underbids and lost revenue.
961.a: Use historical wait-time patterns to predict which clicks will eventually convert, fixing cost calculations before bids are placed.

962.p: Shopping sites build recommendations one piece at a time, missing how product connections shape what users want across their whole journey.
962.a: Weave a system that learns product connections during data prep, uses them when training, and adapts on-the-fly while serving results.

963.p: Facebook's social network is too enormous for traditional methods to suggest new friends fast enough without overwhelming the servers.
963.a: Use an AI system trained on language to learn both nearby friend groups and what they have in common, making suggestions efficient at scale.

964.p: Recommendation systems only show what they think you'll click, forgetting you have diverse interests and narrowing your options over time.
964.a: Adjust recommendations to match the actual mix of your interests and refresh them as your tastes shift month by month.

965.p: Real networks change constantly, but systems that learn from yesterday's connections forget old facts when new ones appear.
965.a: Save knowledge from before by keeping old and new connection patterns similar, so the system grows without losing what it knew.

966.p: Shopping forecasts miss why people add random items to hit free-shipping thresholds and can't separate normal repeat buys from exploring.
966.a: Model purchases as a two-stage learning process that captures unplanned additions and separates habit from exploration naturally.

967.p: Chatbots give answers that contradict their personality indirectly—saying one thing about movies, then behavior that clashes with that identity.
967.a: Build a common-sense web of personality rules, then catch and rewrite contradictory answers before they reach the user.

968.p: Recommenders use a popular math trick to fix bias, but it actually works by accident and sometimes fails in unexpected ways.
968.a: Prove the trick helps by forcing systems to learn varied patterns, then use multi-task training instead of bias correction alone.

969.p: When people search online, the system doesn't know whether "blue shoes" means sneakers or heels, and products change every day.
969.a: Train an AI system using real search clicks to suggest related search terms that stay true to actual products and match what people want.

970.p: AI systems that recommend well are too big and slow to run on phones without internet, breaking privacy and real-time use.
970.a: Shrink the AI model using math that removes redundant weights, simplify text reading, and refine it layer-by-layer so phones run it fast.

971.p: Network models fail at nodes connecting opposite groups because neighborhoods disagree too much, but existing methods ignore this.
971.a: Spot these critical nodes, then treat them specially by mixing information differently so contradictory neighborhoods don't wash each other out.

972.p: Recommenders can't help brand-new users or products because there's no history to learn from and no second chances to improve.
972.a: Combine what text descriptions say about new products with how existing products connect, so new items get good matches immediately.

973.p: Sequential recommendations fail for new users because learning their behavior pattern needs old data, but new users have none.
973.a: Filter a new user's first actions to find true preferences, then use cause-and-effect logic to generate likely behavior patterns automatically.

974.p: The gap between streaming companies' real needs and academic research on AI keeps them from working together effectively.
974.a: Create a workshop bringing practitioners and researchers together to share ideas and align on what matters in AI for streaming.

975.p: When Spotify launches ads or promotions for new podcasts, the system doesn't know what people want because there's almost no data yet about who listens to what.
975.a: Use what the system learned from millions of past ads to instantly help new ads find the right listeners, even with zero history.

976.p: Real-world networks like power grids or disease spread are constantly changing, but we often don't know the exact connections or rules—so predictions fail when reality surprises us.
976.a: Measure exactly how much our uncertainty about missing or wrong network data affects our predictions, so we can plan for those surprises.

977.p: Learning systems that work with networks of connected things process so much data that it's expensive and slow, and they store lots of noise that doesn't help.
977.a: Compress networks by replacing many nodes with a few clean symbol codes, keeping only the important connection patterns and throwing out noise.

978.p: Network-based AI systems are vulnerable to sneaky attacks where bad actors inject fake nodes, but existing attack methods don't work well against defended systems.
978.a: Teach an attacker to gradually learn which fake nodes work best by trial and error, while hiding in plain sight by copying real user behavior.

979.p: When searching facts in structured databases (like finding papers through authors), we need to guess what paths the answer follows, but people rarely write down those hidden rules.
979.a: Automatically discover the common search paths by learning from what users actually need, then use those patterns to find answers faster.

980.p: Recommendation systems work poorly for unpopular items because there's too little data on them, and random noise messes up how the system learns.
980.a: Use a process that adds and removes noise carefully to create clean, similar versions of what people interact with, boosting unpopular items with global patterns.

981.p: Recommendation systems need a single unified code representing each item, but items have many different kinds of information that don't easily mix together.
981.a: Learn to align all kinds of item features—images, text, creator info—into one shared code by teaching them to speak the same language.

982.p: Fake-news detectors look at article text and user comments, but attackers can fool them by adding strategically written fake comments that are hard to spot.
982.a: Use a technique that shows which words tip the detector toward 'fake,' then have an AI write human-sounding comments using exactly those suspicious words.

983.p: Tiny, believable edits to news stories can shift whether people trust them, but nobody has measured how precise attackers can be with these subtle changes.
983.a: Use AI to make minimal tweaks—removing qualifying phrases, swapping evidence—that are invisible to readers but quietly flip credibility signals.

984.p: AI coding models are tested only on whether code runs correctly, missing whether they can actually reason through hard problems like skilled programmers do.
984.a: Break coding problems into four stages—understanding examples, picking algorithms, describing the solution, writing code—and score each step separately.

985.p: When AI systems label whether search results are relevant, they get biased by their previous answers, making later judgments unreliable.
985.a: Give the AI a personality prompt before labeling—some personalities are naturally more independent and ignore their previous answers.

986.p: YouTube's recommendation algorithm is impossible to study at scale because you can't run thousands of fake accounts without breaking realism or rules.
986.a: Automate fake accounts with AI, use databases to track exactly what each account does, and replay experiments precisely to study recommendation feedback loops.

987.p: Picking the right mix of stocks requires balancing returns against risk, but most AI models either lock you into one solution or complicate training with multi-step guessing.
987.a: Sample many good portfolios on the fly by teaching the system to gradually add clarity to noisy random guesses, adjusting for your exact risk comfort.

988.p: Recommender systems can be sabotaged by fake accounts leaving ratings and reviews, and AI-powered fake profiles are now too realistic to catch.
988.a: Build fake AI accounts that write believable reviews, strategically target which products to praise or attack, and perfectly mimic how humans naturally interact.

989.p: AI recommendation systems predict well but can't explain why they chose something, leaving users confused and distrustful of suggestions.
989.a: Teach the AI to think out loud step-by-step before recommending, show how confident it is in each step, and use that confidence to fix bad reasoning paths.

990.p: Search results often discriminate unfairly when trained on biased data, showing one gender more favorably than another.
990.a: Teach the system step-by-step, starting with easy, unbiased examples first, then gradually harder ones, using only the system's confidence scores to detect bias without needing labels.

991.p: When analyzing time series data like weather or traffic, hidden factors we can't see distort the real cause-and-effect relationships.
991.a: Build different graph views at two levels of detail—zoomed-out for overall patterns, zoomed-in for quick changes—and model invisible confounders separately.

992.p: Knowledge databases used to power recommendations have gaps and wrong facts that destroy the quality of what you're shown.
992.a: Use a image-generating technique to clean and fill in missing facts in the database, treating it like denoising a blurry photo until facts are crystal clear.

993.p: Search engines and chatbots have outsized power over what information people see, concentrating control in a few tech companies' hands.
993.a: Rethink how search systems should be designed and studied to support democracy and human freedom, not manipulation and monopoly.

994.p: Chatbots and AI systems answer questions, but they miss what really matters: tailoring those answers to the person asking and their actual needs.
994.a: Bring back decades of research on writing answers that fit different people and situations—lessons still valid even with today's powerful AI.

995.p: As AI gets smarter at writing, old search methods fail: systems must decide what facts to look up, combine them wisely, and execute multi-step plans.
995.a: Create modular search tools that let large AI models actively search, reason step-by-step, and use many tools together to solve real problems.

996.p: Search engines treat all users the same, but people search differently—age, language, and context change how queries are built and executed.
996.a: Run controlled studies varying age and language to see which search strategies people actually use, then model behavior as deliberate style choices, not just noise.

997.p: Recommenders learn patterns by looking at connected items, but connect similar-sounding things even when they're emotionally opposites.
997.a: Add emotional tone—happiness, sadness, energy—from an AI that reads language, making sure similar items also share how users feel about them.

998.p: Search engines now show AI-generated summaries at the top, but we don't know if people trust them enough to click the real links below.
998.a: Use eye-tracking cameras to watch where users look and what they click when AI summaries replace the old blue links.

999.p: When AI systems recommend using one thinking path, they miss better options and give you the same boring suggestions every time.
999.a: Make the AI explore many different reasoning paths at once, then pick the best ones and combine them into a final recommendation.

1000.p: Building AI recommenders requires two separate steps—creating item codes and training the system—that work at cross-purposes, hurting quality.
1000.a: Optimize both steps together at once, letting the code-creation learn from recommendation feedback so item codes fit better with what the recommender needs.

1001.p: When a student picks the wrong answer, tutoring systems only see right-or-wrong, missing which misconception the student actually has.
1001.a: Use AI to read each multiple-choice option and label what misconception each represents, then blend that with student click patterns to diagnose learning gaps.

1002.p: Ranking systems optimize for order but produce overconfident scores that don't reflect real differences between items, breaking user trust.
1002.a: Prevent the system from inflating scores by limiting how high it can go and reducing fine detail signals that push scores needlessly higher.

1003.p: Searching across millions of documents using multi-part vectors is accurate but crushingly slow and expensive.
1003.a: Split the work between the CPU (which narrows candidates smartly) and GPU (which computes fast in parallel), coordinating their handoff efficiently.

1004.p: Converting natural-language questions into database queries is hard; incomplete logical forms fail to run, leaving questions unanswered.
1004.a: Build answers step-by-step, one piece at a time, checking each piece against the database facts to correct mistakes before moving to the next piece.

1005.p: Search systems need to find relevant documents fast from huge collections, but current speed tricks waste computing power on unnecessary work.
1005.a: Skip entire blocks of irrelevant documents before even looking at them, using a simpler, faster method than before.

1006.p: Systems that understand both images and text together aren't very good at comparing images and text to find similar ones, even when they work great for writing.
1006.a: Force the model to squeeze all the meaning from an image or text into one special token, then learn from that compressed meaning.

1007.p: Recommendation systems trained only from past data struggle to suggest items for people with varied tastes, since averaging different preferences produces useless middle-ground suggestions.
1007.a: Learn what kinds of things a person actually liked, then teach a fast model to suggest only those kinds in one step.

1008.p: Systems that catch fake news by analyzing how it spreads get fooled when bad actors use an AI system to inject fake supporting messages into the conversation.
1008.a: Have an AI system write out the story of how real news typically spreads, then teach the fake-news-catching system to check whether new stories match that pattern.

1009.p: When an AI system looks up facts before answering, giving it too much information slows it down, makes it confused, and sometimes it ignores the good facts.
1009.a: Let the AI system itself decide which looked-up facts actually matter while it's writing, instead of just throwing all of them at it.

1010.p: Recommendation systems using images and text struggle with murky user preferences and end up connecting items that aren't actually similar just because they have similar numbers.
1010.a: Ask an AI system to explain in words why a person would like each item based on their history, then fix the similarity connections between items.

1011.p: Recommendation systems need to learn from contrasts (what a person didn't like), but picking things people didn't like randomly either teaches nothing or wastes time on things they might have liked anyway.
1011.a: Pick things the person probably didn't like by grouping similar items first, then focusing on items near the ones they liked but in different groups.

1012.p: AI agents that use tools (like a calculator or search engine) struggle to decide which tool to use next when solving complex web tasks.
1012.a: Teach the AI agent by learning from examples of good tool chains, then reward it for picking smart sequences of tools.

1013.p: Finding similar images across very different styles or contexts is nearly impossible without labels, since internal guesses about similarity aren't reliable.
1013.a: Use a pre-trained AI model to find truly similar and truly different images across styles as anchors, then learn from those solid examples.

1014.p: Human experts rank search results on multiple dimensions, but current systems treat this only as a way to test ranking quality, not as a way to improve it.
1014.a: Break down relevance into specific qualities, then use those as features to train better ranking.

1015.p: Recommendation systems that generate suggestions must be updated when new items arrive or user tastes shift, but retraining breaks the system's old knowledge while fine-tuning misses the changes.
1015.a: Update the system piece by piece, detecting which old items have changed meaning and keeping everything else exactly the same.

1016.p: Patent examiners and medical researchers must decide when to stop reading through search results, but guessing wrong means either missing crucial documents or wasting hours reading.
1016.a: Use math to calculate the actual cost of stopping now versus finding one more document, then stop when continuing wastes more than it gains.

1017.p: Ranking systems can't tell whether clicks mean a result is good or just happened to show up at the top of the page, so they learn the wrong lesson.
1017.a: Test whether the system can actually figure out which part of a click was about goodness by seeing what happens if you tweak each part slightly.

1018.p: Modern AI models are smart but slow at matching exact words in search, because their word-splitting rules were designed for writing, not for finding things.
1018.a: Switch the model to a simpler set of words that's better for exact matching, while keeping the smart understanding using special transfer tricks.

1019.p: Real recommendation systems need to constantly learn from new user actions (views, likes, purchases), but updating when tastes change causes it to forget what it learned before.
1019.a: Learn from many types of actions at once and update gradually, remembering behaviors from before while adapting to what people do now.

1020.p: Recommendation systems that read through your past purchases ignore the middle part and focus too much on the beginning and end, making worse guesses about what you want.
1020.a: Detect where the system is paying too much attention and rebalance it, then use test scenarios to remove false patterns, so middle items get fair weight.

1021.p: Finding a suspect from a text description (height, jacket color) requires training on huge AI models that break down when the database changes, and costs too much to run.
1021.a: Add a lightweight adapter to an existing AI model instead of retraining the whole thing, plus ignore noisy photo-text pairs that don't match reality.

1022.p: Recommendation systems treat all items the same way, so popular movies drown out indie finds, and the system can't suggest the niche films you actually want.
1022.a: Break user-item patterns into popular and niche versions by analyzing frequency signals, then learn from each separately and combine the results thoughtfully.

1023.p: Searching through thousands of spreadsheets to answer a question fails because layouts destroy meaning and old methods need tons of labeled examples to work.
1023.a: Learn the spreadsheet structure itself instead of query examples, mix dense search, graph walking, and keyword matching to handle implicit questions without labeled training.

1024.p: Finding the right legal case takes precision but using two separate AI systems causes errors to pile up, with the second system missing context from the first.
1024.a: Combine retrieval and ranking in one system that shares knowledge between them, while teaching it to reject truly irrelevant results with high confidence.

1025.p: AI recommendation systems for phones and tablets use too much power because they treat all customer profiles the same way when some matter more than others.
1025.a: Split customer profiles into smart groups and shrink each one separately with lower-precision math, keeping accuracy without wasting battery.

1026.p: Matching a 2D photo to 3D models fails without labels because the two formats are too different and the system can't tell which 3D shapes should logically group together.
1026.a: Fix the decision boundary between photo and model spaces and use a graph to teach the system which 3D shapes go together, all without manual labeling.

1027.p: Spotting depression from Instagram posts is hard because the system treats images and audio separately and misses how mood shows up differently in each.
1027.a: Let images and audio guide each other to form a shared map, then use that map to learn stable features from both and predict mental distress.

1028.p: When recommendation systems use frequency analysis, they either boost noise along with real signals or they can't handle short-term and long-term likes at once.
1028.a: Filter out low-energy noise from each frequency band and route long-term and short-term preferences through separate paths, blending them smartly.

1029.p: Fixing wrong answers in AI systems that see images and text is risky because changes leak to other answers and the system often makes random fixes.
1029.a: Find the exact brain cells that hold wrong knowledge by tracking images and text together, then surgically update just those cells with context examples.

1030.p: Linking mentions in photos and captions to a company database fails because systems treat images, text, and knowledge separately, so they miss how they reinforce each other.
1030.a: Have expert subnetworks each learn one type of link, route experts based on what matters most, and use the graph to connect mentions across levels of detail.

1031.p: Finding answers across databases and websites requires reasoning, but using one AI to both plan the steps and do the work is slow and can't scale.
1031.a: Separate high-level planning from hands-on work—one AI sketches the steps, then specialized agents execute each step with their own tools and knowledge.

1032.p: Table retrieval today picks spreadsheets by topic, but AI agents need results that also follow specific rules like 'exclude this column' or 'only 2019 data'.
1032.a: Build a benchmark that tests whether systems follow both topic hints and detailed rules, and measure if the ranking adjusts when the rules change.

1033.p: Generative recommendation systems trained with one objective end up suggesting the same generic items to everyone because they lack signals to separate individual tastes.
1033.a: Add hidden learning that pulls different users apart before the final score is made, but use the internal features to avoid pushing apart users with truly similar taste.

1034.p: Picking the right software plugin from hundreds to connect an AI agent to a tool is hard because plugin descriptions are messy and tool names are vague.
1034.a: Analyze the plugin code itself to build a clear inventory of what each tool does, then use AI to write crisp descriptions that retrieval systems can actually match.

1035.p: When people have back-and-forth conversations with AI search assistants, there's no good way to fairly grade whether the AI is doing a good job without expensive human reviewers.
1035.a: Break down each conversation into small pieces and score them one by one, then combine those scores to judge overall quality in a way that matches how humans actually evaluate conversations.

1036.p: When long answers need facts from many sources, most search systems rank by relevance to one question but ignore whether they cover all the important angles of the topic.
1036.a: Train a search system to prioritize results that together cover multiple facets of a question, using questions broken into parts to teach it what complete coverage means.

1037.p: Finding the best short phrases that summarize a document is hard because AI systems focus on words that matter globally but miss words that matter to a specific section.
1037.a: Score potential phrases both by how well the document generates them and by checking where they appear locally in the text, recognizing they matter differently in different places.

1038.p: Dense search systems storing word numeric fingerprints for every token in millions of documents use huge amounts of storage, but cutting out low-value tokens hurts search quality.
1038.a: Use geometry to identify which tokens matter most, imagining each token's influence as space it controls, and remove only the truly insignificant ones.

1039.p: AI chatbots can handle long conversations now, but they struggle to organize and reuse what happened in past sessions, causing conversations to repeat or contradict themselves.
1039.a: Organize past conversation chunks like a forest of trees, gluing new conversations onto the right branch based on topic, mimicking how human memory works.

1040.p: When AI systems judge search results, they often say too many things are relevant and disagree with each other, making those judgments unreliable for testing.
1040.a: Give AI systems a full written description of what the person is looking for, not just keywords, which makes their judgments match human experts much better.

1041.p: When recommending items across different stores or categories, systems learn about you in each place separately and miss what they could learn by looking at both together.
1041.a: Build a user model by looking at both your history here and your history elsewhere at the same time, treating your purchases as an unordered collection that order doesn't matter for.

1042.p: When AI systems generate recommendations by reading your history, different ways of describing your behavior lead to contradictory suggestions, even for the same person.
1042.a: Learn which descriptions of your behavior are most reliable, then during recommendations either pick the best one or blend multiple views to stay consistent.

1043.p: Finding exactly the right moment in a long video based on a text search is slow and imprecise because current systems just match words to visual features without truly understanding the meaning.
1043.a: Use an efficient backbone to understand the whole video context, have the AI pretend to write the search request back as a test of understanding, and pinpoint where moments start and stop.

1044.p: When recommending places to visit, systems treat all your visits equally even though some are just nearby options you settled for, not places you actually want to go.
1044.a: Separate your real preferences from forced external choices by looking at your behavior patterns and the distance between where you expected to go versus where you actually went.

1045.p: Recommending many things you like from your history requires capturing your various interests, but averaging them all together blurs the edges and loses what makes each interest distinct.
1045.a: Reconstruct your specific interests by amplifying what appears together in your history, keeping each interest separate rather than blending them into an average.

1046.p: Using AI to understand your interests and recommend items in fast-moving chats is slow and unreliable because there's barely any context, and the AI makes things up.
1046.a: Ask the AI to guess your intent only when uncertain, check if those guesses actually help recommendations, and train a lightweight model to predict intent without AI for every chat.

1047.p: Storing billions of user and item profiles takes massive space, and when systems try to shrink them by hashing, quality and personalization suffer from collisions.
1047.a: Use heat-based image-generating from a small seed set of important users and items to create soft mixing gates that blend compact profiles without hard collisions.

1048.p: Systems that ask humans to label which nodes in a network are important usually assume they know all the categories in advance, but new categories show up in real data.
1048.a: Focus on finding informative regions in the network that either have important unknowns or reveal brand-new categories, then zoom in on the most helpful example within that region.

1049.p: Short video platforms treat each video as one thing to like or skip, but people's feelings change as they watch—they might skip a song but love the dance moves after it.
1049.a: Track the exact timing of what users do (pause, skip, like, comment) and chain those actions together as a sequence to predict whether they'll like a video's specific parts.

1050.p: Online stores waste money giving discounts to the wrong people—they can't tell who actually responds to price cuts versus who will buy anyway.
1050.a: Predict exactly how much discount each type of person needs to buy, then focus the budget on the cheapest way to unlock sales rather than guessing who discounts help.

1051.p: Photos tagged with only an object name stay ambiguous: Is the camera showing part of the table or the whole table, and which bits matter?
1051.a: Spot the individual parts that make up an object (legs, seat, back for a chair), then assemble them to figure out the complete thing, copying how humans see.

1052.p: Online stores can't tell a customer who almost bought something from one who just wasn't interested—both look the same in the data.
1052.a: Use behaviors that led to purchases to guess which shoppers were close to buying, then separate true hesitation from those who gave up because of a better option.

1053.p: Finding a 3D room that matches a text description requires expensive labeled training data, and doesn't work for novel room types or phrasings.
1053.a: Convert both room layouts and text descriptions into the same symbolic structure, then match them without needing paired examples—reusing existing AI models for text.

1054.p: Simple similarity-based recommendation systems are fast but can't capture complicated preference patterns that emerge from multiple related people.
1054.a: Extend similarity to handle groups and multi-step connections, using an efficient approximation algorithm to make the computation feasible.

1055.p: Finding tightly knit groups in social networks requires retraining from scratch each time the network changes—too slow and expensive for new networks.
1055.a: Train once on example networks, then deploy directly to any new network by aligning the learned features and handling unexpected graph patterns automatically.

1056.p: AI chatbots guess at vague user goals but ignore that each person has different mental states and preferences that shift over time.
1056.a: Mirror how human brains track others' thoughts by storing long-term mental states and retrieving relevant ones per query to personalize responses.

1057.p: People use search engines and AI chatbots in fundamentally different ways, but nobody knows if these differences reflect real needs or just habit.
1057.a: Survey actual users about which tool they pick for each task and why, then compare what they say they do versus what they actually do.

1058.p: Big companies run many apps (video, reading, games) but can't share what users learned in one app to recommend better in the others.
1058.a: Extract cross-app interests while honoring that each app has different recommendation scenarios and user behaviors, then align images and IDs for consistent features.

1059.p: Fake accounts hide in the social graph, but spotting them by friends isn't reliable when a user's real behavior differs sharply from their connections.
1059.a: Compare each user's own profile to what their friends look like, and use this mismatch to spot fakes—handling that followers and following may be unbalanced.

1060.p: When an AI answers a complex question by reading multiple documents, users get vague text citations and can't see the actual evidence in pictures.
1060.a: Instead of parsing text, show visual crops from retrieved documents with precise bounding boxes so users see exactly which diagrams or text the AI relied on.

1061.p: Video-search systems break when the query doesn't actually match any moment in the video—they have no way to say 'this video has no answer.'
1061.a: Actively test the model against tricky moments that look right but are wrong, and measure how shaky each prediction is to reject uncertain answers.

1062.p: Graph-based recommenders can't handle noisy data and miss global patterns, even when using self-training to reduce the noise.
1062.a: Use a specialized function decomposer to handle nonlinear patterns and reconstruct a cleaner graph structure, then learn from both views together.

1063.p: Vision-language AI ignores key diagrams in educational videos because other patterns grab attention first, causing wrong answers despite evidence being present.
1063.a: Boost the importance of evidence tokens during decoding by training a lightweight module to pick which evidence to amplify and how much.

1064.p: Picking documents by text similarity hurts when the user's question is biased—the AI then retrieves docs that reinforce the bias instead of correcting it.
1064.a: Simulate user biases during training to teach the system what evidence actually convinces the AI to give the right answer despite biased prompts.

1065.p: When AI systems show their reasoning steps to explain recommendations, they run too slowly and cost too much to deploy on real websites.
1065.a: Train a smaller, faster AI on the thinking steps of a bigger AI, so users get smarter recommendations without the slowdown.

1066.p: Detecting hateful videos is hard, and AI that flags them doesn't explain WHY it thinks a video is hateful—so people can't trust the decision.
1066.a: Build AI that points to the specific video parts and words that triggered the alert, so humans can see the actual reason.

1067.p: Medical AI often confuses similar disease names because it only looks at surface words, missing the actual medical rules that tell diseases apart.
1067.a: Add medical rules into the AI's thinking so it can say 'No, that's the wrong disease' when similar words could match multiple diseases.

1068.p: When running AI on edge computers (like at a store), generic fact databases are too big and slow, wasting storage and making answers lag.
1068.a: Give each edge computer its own specialized facts for its domain, and swap facts between computers so nothing gets duplicated.

1069.p: When ranking products by purchase likelihood, real data contains wrong labels, and these errors compound in ways single-task cleanup can't handle.
1069.a: Use math to undo the noise in click and purchase labels together, accounting for how errors from one step affect the next.

1070.p: Podcast search depends on how you transcribe audio and phrase the query, but nobody knows if these differences actually matter for finding what you want.
1070.a: Test 1.8M search-and-podcast pairs using AI judges and five different AI search engines to see which variations actually break podcast search.

1071.p: When adding new documents to an AI search index, retraining makes it find the new ones but forget how to find the old ones.
1071.a: Keep the old AI frozen and attach a small memory module that corrects errors for new documents without touching the main model.

1072.p: Testing chat search systems with robot users is cheaper than hiring people, but it's unclear if robots should remember earlier parts of the conversation.
1072.a: Compare robot and human conversations in real systems to see whether robot memory helps test results match human-based test results.

1073.p: When explaining a recommendation by changing which items a user liked, it's hard to find tiny, realistic changes that actually flip the result.
1073.a: Use a denoising method to gradually adjust a fake interaction history toward one that changes the recommendation with minimum faking.

1074.p: AI recommendation systems learn from patterns in user clicks, but when given to AI language systems, those learned patterns stay invisible as numbers not words.
1074.a: Convert the pattern-matching into human words so AI language systems can read and understand the exact same signals that traditional systems use.

1075.p: When AI agents do multi-step research, nobody has data on how many steps they take, how fast they work, or whether they reuse old query ideas.
1075.a: Analyze 14 million real research requests to chart how agents actually search, what they repeat, and how they build on earlier results.

1076.p: Real-time search suggestions must be fast and stay current, but generating new suggestions from scratch is slow and stale quickly.
1076.a: Treat suggestions as looking up old queries most similar to the current session, updating the list whenever the search database refreshes.

1077.p: AI systems looking up facts to avoid hallucinating often follow one fixed lookup method, missing chances to ask different fact sources for different needs.
1077.a: Let the AI choose which of several fact-lookup experts to use at each step, based on what it needs to answer the current question.

1078.p: Checking if medical claims are true requires finding evidence online, but smaller AI systems can't do this efficiently without expensive gold-labeled data.
1078.a: Train a small AI on reasoning steps from a bigger AI, mixing web evidence with perfect data, so it fact-checks without huge compute.

1079.p: Verifying complex claims requires searching for several pieces of evidence in order, but no efficient way exists to learn this multi-step search strategy.
1079.a: Use trial-and-reward learning to teach AI to search iteratively and reason through incomplete facts, guided only by true-or-false labels.

1080.p: When people click, save, or ignore items online, these signals tell you what they actually want—but some clicks mean "I love this" while others mean "maybe." Recommendation systems treat all signals equally, leading to bad predictions.
1080.a: Learn which signals are strong hints versus weak ones, then adjust how hard the system pushes to match each signal based on its confidence—so noisy signals don't break what's working.

1081.p: When someone clicks on a search result, you can't tell if they clicked because it was truly relevant or just because it was the first result on the screen. Separating the real signal from the position bias helps you serve better results.
1081.a: Build a system that outputs not just a single guess about relevance and position effects, but a range of possibilities with measures of how uncertain each guess is, so you know when to trust it.

1082.p: Many recommendation sites have only text or only images or only interaction patterns—missing the full picture. Using all three types of signals together is hard because they live in separate mathematical spaces and don't trust each other.
1082.a: Connect items through both direct interactions and their visual-text similarities, then repeatedly clean up broken connections and align all signals into one coherent view so they reinforce each other.

1083.p: Math papers are linked by deep ideas and proof techniques, not by words or citation patterns—so text-based search treats unrelated papers as twins and related ones as strangers. Existing paper-recommendation tools fail completely on math.
1083.a: Ask mathematicians what makes papers related (shared methods, logical flow, generalization), build training datasets by hand and at scale, then use a system that learns from citation chains and author lineage alongside the text.

1084.p: When an AI system tries to recommend items by generating their names, the names become too long and confusing, and it can't use item attributes to understand what each thing really is. Standard methods don't work across different catalogs either.
1084.a: Instead of generating names, use a system that learns from how items connect to each other plus their features, then group them into a short indexed code like an organized book with chapters—much faster and more portable.

1085.p: AI systems often repeat things they memorized during training instead of reading the context you give them. When the context contradicts training data (like a fictional company or updated facts), the AI ignores it and hallucinates wrong answers.
1085.a: Replace the real names of people and places that appear in both the context and the question with generic labels (City-1, Company-2), stripping away the AI's memorized biases while keeping the logical relationships intact.

1086.p: When new products launch, recommendation systems can't rank them because there are no past interactions—this 'cold-start collapse' makes new items invisible. Retraining the model is slow, expensive, and doesn't keep pace with rapid catalog changes.
1086.a: Steal techniques from NLP that inject knowledge into AI systems without retraining, adapted for recommendations by treating the sequence of a user's history as the context that shapes what comes next, then surgically editing in the new items.

1087.p: Search and recommendation are separate, but users search for one thing and expect recommendations in that area—mixing them helps, except many search queries are noise that actually hurt recommendation accuracy when included blindly.
1087.a: Build a system that learns an overall picture of what the user wants, then iteratively picks only the most relevant past searches to reason from, ignoring outdated or off-topic ones that would mislead the recommendation.

1088.p: In online ads, decisions happen every second but you only see full profit data much later, creating sparse, delayed rewards that make learning unstable and risky. The system struggles because it can't align planning speed with feedback speed.
1088.a: Generate sequences of bids and budgets at coarse time scales where feedback is dense, then refine them at finer scales, so the AI learns from clear, timely signals and can make stable long-term plans.

1089.p: When data is missing (like incomplete user profiles), systems smooth it across graph connections—but this creates three problems: fails on disconnected networks, loses unique details, and breaks on new unseen networks.
1089.a: First connect all isolated islands into one network to spread information farther, then learn the natural shape of the data without over-smoothing, and finally correct any remaining bias at test time before using the predictions.

1090.p: Figuring out the time order of events in text is hard—'before,' 'after,' 'overlaps,' and 'identical' between two time periods are easy to mix up, and old datasets oversimplified the problem to make it easier.
1090.a: Instead of jumping straight to interval relations, classify the time order of each pair of endpoints (start and end), then decode those point orderings into interval relations, tackling the easier sub-problem first.

1091.p: Keyword search misses paraphrases; semantic search ranks false positives by topic; you can't tell which is right from a single ranking. Relevant results hide where both methods agree, but single-system confidence is useless.
1091.a: Find documents both search types rank highly, use those as seeds to expand the query with verified terms and context, then filter out off-topic drift with simple geometry, gaining large accuracy jumps with no new parameters.

1092.p: Recommendation systems on TikTok or news sites work differently on different pages (home, live feed, local section), but existing multi-scenario systems force all scenarios to share the same representations, mangling the data across sections.
1092.a: Learn shared knowledge globally and scenario-specific knowledge locally by projecting them separately into their own organized spaces, then transport and align them so each scenario gets exactly the distribution it needs.

1093.p: News readers get stuck reading only their domestic news or only world news, never a balanced mix. Recommendation algorithms push whatever gets clicks without encouraging readers to explore outside their bubble.
1093.a: Nudge the algorithm to suggest balanced domestic and world coverage, and highlight how news connects to what users have already read, which works better at shifting long-term reading habits than generic topic labels.

1094.p: Recommendation systems need massive labeled data and break on new domains, making them slow to deploy and brittle to real-world shifts. A truly general recommender that works with little data would unlock practical deployment.
1094.a: Pretrain an AI on thousands of synthetic user click patterns so it learns the underlying structure, then at runtime it reads just a few real user sequences in one forward pass and predicts without any retraining.

1095.p: People search in different ways based on how their brains work, but search engines treat everyone the same, making search harder for many users.
1095.a: Measure how different thinking styles affect what people click and where they look, then design search pages that match each person's thinking style.

1096.p: Recommendation systems struggle to understand that one person might want totally different things—a song, a book, a coat—all at the same time.
1096.a: Use an AI system that reads and writes language to understand what a person truly wants, then feed that knowledge directly into the recommendation system's core to separate different desires.

1097.p: When you ask a question about a form or bill screenshot, the AI looks at the whole page instead of just the part that answers your question, wasting time and making mistakes.
1097.a: Teach the system to identify which parts of the page matter for your question first, then focus its attention only on those relevant areas.

1098.p: Stores need to know which products are similar enough to suggest as alternatives, but user behavior is messy and many products never get enough data.
1098.a: Combine text and image analysis of items with a noise-filtering method that learns from messy clicks, handling products with almost no sales history.

1099.p: E-commerce sites must recommend lists of items that work well together, but old methods struggle when customer preferences shift rapidly throughout the day.
1099.a: Use a system that learns continuously from live rewards and treats item selection as a math problem that can run backward through its own thinking to improve itself.

1100.p: Doctors need AI suggestions for drug combinations, but existing systems hide their reasoning and use one-size-fits-all safety rules that ignore how risky different patients actually are.
1100.a: Build a system that explains its reasoning by learning from doctor-written examples, then adjusts safety limits based on each patient's individual risk tolerance.

1101.p: Systems that learn from how things connect often make wrong predictions when connected things don't actually share the same category or topic.
1101.a: Use reasoning about cause and effect to identify which connections are real patterns and which are false shortcuts, then ignore the fake patterns.

1102.p: Dense search systems find good documents but searching takes a lot of computing power and time, limiting how fast results can be returned.
1102.a: Refine search queries by adding new words pulled from the best results already found, using a compact method that reuses internal numbers the system already has.

1103.p: Sorting results by relevance is crucial for search, but current math-based methods can predict a soft ranking while actual results need hard yes-no decisions.
1103.a: Use a sorting method that adds random swaps to turn soft predictions into real decisions, plus a loss function that handles tied or uncertain relevance labels.

1104.p: When people talk about their feelings in a conversation, listeners need to know not just what emotions they felt but why they felt them.
1104.a: Model the speaker's personality and memory, then trace emotions through multiple possible causes instead of assuming one simple explanation.

1105.p: When an AI system that reads and writes language searches the web for facts, false or conflicting information can override the company's own trusted knowledge.
1105.a: Automatically find web results that contradict internal documents, then remove those results before they distort the AI system's answers.

1106.p: Predicting what users will do next requires understanding how their tastes change over time, but generative methods treat time as just another input.
1106.a: Build the sense of time directly into the generation process itself, mixing in previous predictions to show how desires evolve step by step.

1107.p: Synthetic data protects privacy but often breaks real-world relationships between fields, like matching products to correct categories or keeping logical rules intact.
1107.a: Generate synthetic records by learning what distributions look like, enforcing connections between related fields, and preventing the system from just copying the same samples over and over.

1108.p: Search systems sometimes rank relevant documents low because the words in the query don't align with how the document's meaning is stored internally.
1108.a: Find phrases in documents that are poorly recognized by the system's internal scoring, then create new queries based on those weak phrases to expose the weakness.

1109.p: AI systems often stop searching for answers after finding one fact, missing cases where a person plays multiple roles or has multiple states at the same time.
1109.a: Test systems with questions where multiple correct answers exist, forcing them to search exhaustively instead of giving up after the first match.

1110.p: When AI systems trained on language learn to describe products, their output takes up enormous storage space and slows down shopping recommendation systems.
1110.a: Compress that data by making the AI learn differently: have it deliberately specialize into separate skills for reading and recommending, not force everything into one final output.

1111.p: When a chatbot asks you about products you want, it doesn't know whether to ask about features first or show you items—or how that changes as it learns what you like.
1111.a: Use a dataset that marks which questions work best at each stage of a conversation, then train a system that picks different questioning strategies as it learns what you prefer.

1112.p: When AI tries to answer hard questions using a database of facts, it wastes compute jumping around and sometimes learns from wrong answers because it rewards any plausible path.
1112.a: Separate the search from the thinking: let the AI explore the fact database efficiently, then penalize paths that don't actually make sense according to the facts.

1113.p: A delivery app won't show restaurants far away—but when predicting if you'll buy, math assumes every restaurant has some chance, creating an unfair learning problem.
1113.a: Identify items that literally can't be recommended, set reasonable limits on their prediction range, and include that fact when training the model.

1114.p: Search results that use AI to expand keywords are precise but create very long lists, wasting space and slowing search speed.
1114.a: Trim results in two ways: a learnable soft cutoff that picks how many words to keep, and per-word thresholds that remove the least useful terms.

1115.p: An AI that watches videos can only see a few minutes at once, but understanding a long movie requires remembering and connecting events from all parts.
1115.a: Build a memory system inspired by how humans recall: let the viewer's question activate all related moments at once, then weave them together into one coherent summary.

1116.p: AI trained to answer easy questions can't handle really long chains of reasoning, and we don't have enough examples of hard questions to train on.
1116.a: Teach the AI to chain short steps into longer ones, and give it explicit training on when to stop—because different questions need different chain lengths.

1117.p: E-commerce search shows mostly similar items on page one, leaving out variety even when shoppers are unsure what they want.
1117.a: Measure what variety shoppers actually want by watching their behavior, then gently adjust rankings to hit that diversity goal without slowing search.

1118.p: Recommending items requires a CPU service for indexing and a GPU service for AI—but running two separate systems wastes money and can't handle complex ranking logic.
1118.a: Combine everything into one GPU system: replace the CPU indexing with a GPU-based index, and fuse the search and ranking into a single unified model.

1119.p: Answering hard questions with facts requires finding multiple pieces of information, but search only grabs top results and misses connections across related items.
1119.a: Use a system that learns connections: model facts at different detail levels, and use the question to activate all matching pieces at once before synthesizing the answer.

1120.p: Predicting what users want next ignores that preferences shift smoothly over time—like velocity and momentum in physics—not as sudden jumps.
1120.a: Model preference change using calculus-like ideas: capture steady long-term taste in one branch, and track the speed and acceleration of preference shifts in another.

1121.p: Single-vector systems for finding related items hit a hard ceiling: they can't learn all possible top-ten combinations no matter how well trained.
1121.a: Replace the fixed comparison math with a learnable one that adapts to data, expanding the space of combinations the system can express.

1122.p: AI trained to rank products works differently at test time than at training time: training ignores that the search algorithm greedy-prunes bad options mid-ranking.
1122.a: During training, enforce that each chosen product's pieces rank high enough to survive the greedy pruning that happens at test time.

1123.p: AI answers questions with hidden bias—reproducing stereotypes from its training data—but we can't edit closed-source AI systems.
1123.a: Reorder the thinking by collecting multiple reasoning paths, cluster them, and weight their conclusions to dial down demographic stereotyping.

1124.p: Finding exact matches of a query pattern inside a huge connected database is slow because current AI methods only find approximate matches.
1124.a: Pre-index small pattern pieces offline, use AI to score candidates, then grow matches incrementally—trading storage for speed.

1125.p: When AI systems look up facts online to answer questions, they inherit political bias from those sources, giving some viewpoints more weight than others.
1125.a: Filter facts by their political angle before feeding them to the AI, and use multiple AI systems to label which viewpoint each fact represents.

1126.p: When AI systems answer questions about images, they grab random relevant text that often misleads or contradicts other sources instead of using organized relationships between facts.
1126.a: Build a structured map of image-and-text facts that shows how concepts connect, then search through that map instead of loose documents.

1127.p: Search systems retrieve outdated or conflicting facts because they treat any passage as equally valid, but real-world facts get superseded or disputed over time.
1127.a: Store small, atomic pieces of fact with expiration dates and conflict markers, filtering out stale information before ranking what to show.

1128.p: Finding a person in photos using a text description fails when there's little labeled training data, since the model can't adapt to real-world differences.
1128.a: Adjust the AI at search time using only unlabeled photos by checking whether images and text descriptions rank highly from both directions.

1129.p: Recommendation systems need to find tight groups in user-interaction networks, but existing methods struggle when you require a strict minimum density inside groups.
1129.a: Rank users by how central they are, then extract and refine clusters to guarantee they meet the density threshold you set.

1130.p: Question-and-answer sites recommend pairs as single items, but questions and answers have independent influence—separating this confusion improves recommendations.
1130.a: Build two separate network models: one tracking which users engage with questions vs. answers, another tracking semantic connections between them.

1131.p: AI systems that generate personalized content can't simultaneously capture your preferences for text and images, and the two often contradict each other.
1131.a: Learn what style you prefer in each medium separately, convert those into discrete tokens the generators understand, then inject both into image and text makers.

1132.p: Matching entities across databases requires extensive labeled examples, but real deployments have almost no labeled data and scenarios shift unpredictably.
1132.a: Extract matching rules from scarce examples, group similar rules into patterns, and look up the most relevant rule for each pair instead of retraining the AI.

1133.p: Matching pictures to database records often produces contradictions—one picture-record pair might match, but be globally inconsistent with nearby matches.
1133.a: Have multiple AI agents examine the evidence, correct each other's errors, and only call the most powerful (but slow) AI for genuinely hard cases.

1134.p: Answering questions using time-based facts is hard because raw facts become tangled with dates and lose their structure, drowning the AI in noise.
1134.a: Parse what time span the question covers, extract a small structured subgraph of only relevant facts with their dates, then feed that cleaner input to the AI.

1135.p: Automated ad-bidding strategies explore aggressively to find better bids but risk huge financial losses, and existing exploratory methods lack safety guardrails.
1135.a: Use a learned AI to explore bidding strategies, track which moves are safe, and fall back to a known-good strategy if exploration goes wrong.

1136.p: AI search agents that think step-by-step are slow because each reasoning step must wait for tool results sequentially, creating bottlenecks.
1136.a: Use a faster AI model designed for parallel generation, train it heavily on agent tasks, and reorder reasoning steps so multiple tools can run together.

1137.p: AI language systems give unfair recommendations based on gender or age because their learned patterns conflate user taste with demographic stereotypes.
1137.a: Use specialized sub-AIs (some focused on taste, some on blocking demographic hints), optimize both recommendation quality and fairness simultaneously with direct feedback.

1138.p: Ad-click prediction ignores the sequence of what users clicked before, missing the dynamic shifts in their interests that context reveals.
1138.a: Combine many specialized prediction models using a image-generating process that learns which sequences of user clicks matter most in each context.

1139.p: Privacy policies are unstructured text, making it nearly impossible to check whether a company collects only the personal data it really needs.
1139.a: Extract what data is collected and why, compare it to patterns in well-written policies, then flag cases where collection seems unnecessarily broad.

1140.p: Image search systems are fast but break when someone slightly changes an image to fool them, creating a security risk for real-world use.
1140.a: Detect which parts of an image matter most for search, then protect only those parts during adversarial training so the system stays both fast and secure.

1141.p: Systems that learn facts from a small number of examples forget old facts when learning new ones, and sometimes old facts actively interfere with new reasoning.
1141.a: Identify facts that conflict with new knowledge and selectively forget them, while keeping older facts that still apply.

1142.p: Question-answering systems retrieve many documents but most are noise, wasting computation and forcing the answer engine to read through useless text.
1142.a: Train the ranking stage by watching whether candidate documents actually lead to correct answers, not by copying human labels that may be wrong.

1143.p: Search and language systems collect personal data about what you ask, and it's unclear whether they truly protect it or whether it leaks into training.
1143.a: Map out where privacy fails in question-answering systems today and propose research directions that protect user privacy throughout the entire process.

1144.p: Systems are tested in isolation, but in reality they compete with each other and users switch between them, making lab tests unreliable predictors of real success.
1144.a: Simulate a marketplace where systems compete, users switch, and preferences change over time, then measure real-world outcomes like retention and market share.

1145.p: Question-answering systems hide their reasoning process, causing people to wrongly assume the system read everything and remembers perfectly.
1145.a: Study how people actually use these systems and show that wrong mental models make users skip verification steps and miss important gaps.

1146.p: Ranking systems use only the question to decide which documents are relevant, ignoring unchanging facts about each document that matter for most questions.
1146.a: Split ranking into two parts: a question-independent part (which facts matter generally) and a question-dependent part (which facts matter for this question).

1147.p: Question-answering systems assume users can write clear questions and remember everything, but this fails when users have dementia or memory loss.
1147.a: Redesign systems for people with cognitive changes by tracking memory over time, enabling caregivers to verify answers, and adapting complexity to comprehension.

1148.p: Systems can remove a document but still answer questions using the same information in a different way, technically complying while breaking the law.
1148.a: Build tests that check whether systems actually stop mentioning a fact at the answer level, not just at the document level.

1149.p: Search tests measure scores that look better, but we never verify whether real users actually prefer those scores or have a better experience.
1149.a: Connect evaluation metrics to real user experience by asking hard questions about whether test improvements truly predict what matters to people.

1150.p: Researchers use a statistical test they believe is safe, but it fails silently in search evaluation, making published results unreliable without anyone noticing.
1150.a: Show mathematically and empirically that this popular test breaks down in search, and recommend better alternatives that actually work.

1151.p: Search, recommendations, and chat systems operate separately for the same user, forcing people to switch tools and losing context about what they're really trying to do.
1151.a: Design one system that learns the user's situation, available content, task, and preferences, then adapts all interactions to help them finish faster.

1152.p: Bundle recommendation systems both assemble packages and rank them, but the two stages are tested separately even though they depend heavily on each other.
1152.a: Test the complete pipeline together and find where it breaks, revealing bottlenecks like swapping items is harder than creating new bundles.

1153.p: AI language systems can rewrite questions in many ways, but running the full system for each rewording is expensive; we need to pick the best one first.
1153.a: Use prediction techniques to estimate which rewritten question will produce the best answer before doing expensive retrieval and answering.

1154.p: Studies claim language models improve search through question rewriting, but each study uses different setups, making it hard to know which gains are real.
1154.a: Implement ten rewriting methods in one framework, test them across four different retrieval approaches, and release public tools so others can verify results.

1155.p: A published method claims to beat existing search techniques, but when scientists tried to rebuild it, the results didn't match and hidden flaws in the data made the original claims unreliable.
1155.a: Carefully re-ran the published method and discovered the authors accidentally leaked information about which documents were actually relevant, letting the system cheat rather than learn real patterns.

1156.p: AI systems that rank search results using modern language models are slow and unpredictable because they need to generate text or scores for every query-document pair.
1156.a: Instead of generating scores, peek directly at the internal signals inside the AI model's thinking process—they found relevant documents get strongest signals in the middle layers, cutting speed by 30-50 percent.

1157.p: Many graph-based recommendation methods that filter out noise claim big wins, but different papers measure success differently, making it impossible to know which technique actually works best.
1157.a: Rebuilt three families of these methods side-by-side with the same tests and data, discovered systematic cheating in some, and proved old simple methods stay harder to beat than papers claimed.

1158.p: A new search method uses a tiny custom neural network per query to rank documents more flexibly, but no one has carefully checked if it really works as advertised across different kinds of problems.
1158.a: Rebuilt the method and tested it on harder, real-world searches, finding it works on some problems but not others, and its speed gains don't always hold depending on what you compare it against.

1159.p: Two popular neural search systems claim to beat traditional methods on benchmark tests, but they may fail on real long queries because their core design has a fundamental weakness.
1159.a: Tested them on long conversational questions and found both systems hit a wall at 20 words—they weight all words equally so they can't distinguish important content from filler.

1160.p: Two open-source search engines use different compression tricks to organize and search huge document lists, but no one knows if speed differences come from the compression methods or other engineering choices.
1160.a: Made their internal formats identical, then measured speed again and discovered which compression method actually wins depends on the hardware—desktop and server chips behave differently.

1161.p: A method teaches AI systems to know when they've looked up enough information to answer a question, but hard details were missing and the system relied on proprietary tools no one else can access.
1161.a: Rebuilt the method and tested it with different ranking strategies, confirmed it works better than basic versions but scored lower than originally reported due to missing code and hidden instructions.

1162.p: Hundreds of studies use the same movie-discussion dataset to test conversational recommendation systems, but each study handles the data slightly differently, making their results impossible to compare.
1162.a: Re-ran seven popular methods under identical conditions and found that half their reported success came from just repeating suggestions users had already seen, and stronger AI models matter more than novel technique design.

1163.p: A method compresses neural search indexes by cutting vectors into pieces and snapping each to the nearest cluster, but no one tested if this trick generalizes to newer and larger models.
1163.a: Reimplemented the method and tested it across different models, finding it works for smaller models but fails on larger ones, though it still lets you pack 32 times more documents into memory.

1164.p: A paper claimed adding random irrelevant documents to search results actually helps AI answer questions better, but the claim might depend on very specific choices about prompt design.
1164.a: Repeated the original experiment and ran it with different AI models and prompt styles, discovering the effect appears or vanishes based on tiny changes to how you ask the question.

1165.p: Three recent methods claim to boost shopping recommendations by treating price as a key signal, but they've never been tested head-to-head on the same data and datasets.
1165.a: Built all three methods and ran them on six public datasets with identical metrics, proving one designs a network that links users, items, and prices together more robustly than graph-based rivals.

1166.p: A method for search planning asks an AI to think ahead about which documents it will rank next, but its decisions may be fragile when questions are slightly reworded or misspelled.
1166.a: Tested the planner with typos, paraphrases, and synonym swaps, finding that small changes can break its prediction of which candidates matter, turning the planning strategy nearly useless.

1167.p: Methods that explain why a recommendation system picked an item typically just show one swap that changes the result, but different papers measure success in conflicting ways, blocking comparison.
1167.a: Rebuilt and re-evaluated eleven explanation methods side-by-side with a single framework that tests both single items and ranked lists, revealing which techniques generalize across different recommendation systems.

1168.p: Learned sparse search models assign extra weight to semantically weird expansion words that seem unrelated to the query, clouding their reputation for interpretability.
1168.a: Systematically analyzed when these odd term weights appear and found they're driven by larger vocabulary size and weaker sparsity penalties, and they actually help with retrieval despite seeming random.

1169.p: learned language systems-based search systems represent queries and documents as multiple vectors and pay a speed penalty for each, so trimming unused vectors saves time but may hurt accuracy.
1169.a: Tested four pruning strategies including prioritizing important tokens by word frequency or learned weights, finding that training matters more than the trimming approach itself for balancing speed and quality.

1170.p: Search engines struggle to answer complicated questions that take multiple sentences to ask, because they were built for short keyword queries.
1170.a: Weight the search terms differently depending on their position in a long question, so the engine can focus on the most important parts of what people are really asking.

1171.p: Building AI assistants that remember your preferences and adjust their answers to fit you personally requires expensive real-world conversations that don't exist yet.
1171.a: Collect a library of real multi-session conversations between people and AI assistants, plus human evaluations of quality, so researchers can study how to personalize chatbot responses.

1172.p: Scientific papers are written for experts, not regular people, so most folks avoid reading them even though they desperately need reliable health and science information.
1172.a: Build a collection of scientific abstracts paired with their plain-language versions so AI systems can learn to translate jargon into everyday explanations anyone can understand.

1173.p: When lawyers need to find past court cases to support their legal arguments, current search tools don't understand how laws and legal reasoning work in countries outside English-speaking jurisdictions.
1173.a: Create a collection of 2,942 Korean court cases with expert judgments about how similar they are, so search tools can learn the specific patterns of legal relevance in that country.

1174.p: Understanding how millions of programmers collaborate worldwide on open-source projects is hard because most data only shows individual projects, not how teams and companies work together.
1174.a: Map the entire ecosystem of 230,000 GitHub organizations with their 2.5 million users and projects, then release this network so researchers can study collaboration patterns.

1175.p: People who speak minority dialects can't find information in their own language online, because AI search systems trained mostly on English and major languages don't bridge the gap to less common dialects.
1175.a: Build a test set using the Ehugbo dialect of Igbo paired with English translations, then measure which AI systems can actually cross that language boundary.

1176.p: When AI systems write answers with source citations, it's hard to know if those answers are actually good because typical human judging is expensive and unreliable judges can easily fool you.
1176.a: Release a standard test set and method for comparing different AI judges against human judgment, so researchers can safely evaluate which judge works best.

1177.p: Search systems suggest refinements to queries, but measuring if those suggestions are good only works if you assume people blindly accept them, which isn't how real people search.
1177.a: Simulate a real user picking and choosing among suggestions based on whether they actually fit the search goal, then use that to fairly evaluate suggestion systems.

1178.p: AI systems trained on languages like Traditional Mongolian perform terribly because nobody has a reliable way to measure and compare how bad the problem actually is.
1178.a: Create a test set of 18,357 tasks in Traditional Mongolian so researchers can systematically measure AI performance and pinpoint where improvements are needed.

1179.p: On Wikipedia, people quietly change articles in ways that shift the historical narrative about who deserves credit for cultural heritage, but these manipulations are hard to spot individually.
1179.a: Collect pairs of Wikipedia edits from the Russia-Ukraine conflict that show how cultural narratives shift, so researchers can detect and study these subtle rewrites.

1180.p: Building conversational chatbots for shared research tasks requires technical infrastructure to connect a participant's system with an AI user simulator in real time, which is complex to set up.
1180.a: Release a middleware tool that exposes the user simulator through simple web endpoints so researchers can easily test their chatbots without managing complicated back-and-forth plumbing.

1181.p: Real-estate search engines need to understand location, market trends, and what affects property value, but this requires private data that most researchers can't access for privacy reasons.
1181.a: Release a dataset of 456,000 clusters of apartment listings with privacy-protected prices, locations, and transit accessibility so researchers can study how to rank and price properties fairly.

1182.p: Banks can't share real transaction data with researchers because of regulations and privacy, so people studying how to catch financial fraud can't build and test their systems properly.
1182.a: Create an open web tool that generates realistic synthetic fraud scenarios and fake transaction data so researchers can safely practice building fraud detection systems.

1183.p: Tests for search systems that help find things you can't quite remember what to call are mostly in English, so researchers can't build better systems for people who speak other languages.
1183.a: Generate test datasets for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and English using AI to simulate real queries, then validate that the tests actually match how people really search.

1184.p: Building a working conversational search system requires connecting many different pieces of code, but researchers have no shared framework to build and share these components with the community.
1184.a: Release an open platform with 45 ready-made modules for understanding questions, ranking results, and generating answers, so researchers can quickly assemble and test full systems.

1185.p: Finding calming music for autistic children requires testing which songs actually help, but there's no standard collection to evaluate music recommendation systems fairly.
1185.a: Built 432 versions of songs with different musical layers, had people rate which ones help kids with autism most, then tested AI systems that pick calming music using these ratings.

1186.p: Search engines sometimes return better results for people of certain genders and worse results for others, reinforcing unfair stereotypes baked into training data.
1186.a: Created a dataset of search queries reworded to both find better answers AND reduce gender bias, then trained models to learn both goals at once.

1187.p: Most business data lives in tables and spreadsheets, but AI systems struggle to understand and reason about this structured data compared to plain text.
1187.a: Built a large test collection covering 26 kinds of table tasks, from simple lookups to complex reasoning, to measure how well AI systems handle real-world spreadsheet work.

1188.p: Voice search doesn't work well when there's background noise like traffic or crowds, but most tests use quiet conditions that don't reflect real usage.
1188.a: Created a test collection mixing real office, street, and construction noise at different volumes with queries in English and Chinese to measure how systems handle messy real-world sound.

1189.p: Most code AI focuses on fixing bugs, but users usually want to call library functions in the right order to build new applications without modifying the library itself.
1189.a: Built a test set of real Python libraries with instructions showing what end result users want, then created a multi-step AI system that retrieves the right functions and assembles them into working code.

1190.p: Finding the right group of experts to solve a hard problem is tricky when you also need to make sure the recommendations don't favor famous or male experts unfairly.
1190.a: Designed a system that models how experts collaborate and skills connect, and added fairness checks to the ranking to catch and reduce biases against certain groups.
