1191.p: Email searches return sensitive personal information people never wanted found, but we need to build search systems that balance usefulness with privacy.
1191.a: Took a real email collection with manually marked sensitive content, crowdsourced test queries, and created a benchmark to measure how well systems find helpful information while hiding private details.

1192.p: Search engines now show many more things than just links—ads, maps, news—but there's no standard way to talk about or study these interface pieces across different search engines.
1192.a: Examined Google, Bing, Yandex, and others to find all the different things they display, gave them consistent names, and organized them into a shared catalog for researchers.

1193.p: Tribal languages in India have almost no text on the web or in training data, so search systems can't find names and places people care about in those languages.
1193.a: Manually annotated 166,000 words in seven tribal languages to mark names and places, then tested how well multilingual AI systems could learn from this small dataset with special techniques.

1194.p: Testing whether AI agents can shop online requires building multiple realistic stores with real product data, which most benchmarks don't have.
1194.a: Created a sandbox with four simulated online shops filled with real product data, then asked AI agents to do complex tasks like comparing prices across stores and finding substitute items.

1195.p: Most recommendation datasets are static snapshots, but live streaming platforms have constantly changing content and viewers interacting in real-time.
1195.a: Collected 21 days of real interaction logs from a major Chinese streaming platform with click, comment, and gift data, capturing how streamers and viewers come and go.

1196.p: Recruiting patients for medical trials is slow and manual, and there are few datasets to test AI systems that match patients to trials across different languages.
1196.a: Translated patient recruitment materials and trial criteria into seven languages, then tested how well AI systems could match patients to appropriate trials in languages beyond English.

1197.p: Detecting AI-written peer reviews assumes someone either wrote it or an AI did, missing the messy reality where people and AI work together on the same review.
1197.a: Created a benchmark with human reviews, fully AI-generated reviews, and mixed reviews where ideas came from humans but writing from AI, to see if detectors conflate authorship with actual contribution.

1198.p: Finding useful datasets is hard because search only looks at file names and descriptions, ignoring the actual data inside and how datasets relate to each other.
1198.a: Built a system that automatically pulls connections from both metadata and the actual contents of different data files, then ranks datasets by these enriched relationships.

1199.p: Writing survey papers by hand takes months, and testing whether an AI agent can do it automatically requires a fair way to grade the surveys it produces.
1199.a: Created a benchmark with over one million research papers and expert-written surveys, then designed a multi-part grading system combining automatic metrics and AI judges to measure quality fairly.

1200.p: Testing tools for Japanese financial writing are scarce; we need to know if AI systems actually understand this specialized language.
1200.a: Built a collection of real Japanese financial texts with retrieval and classification tasks to measure how well different AI systems perform.

1201.p: Modern search engines must find four types of things at once—papers, datasets, tools, variables—but we lack proper test sets for this unified search.
1201.a: Created a test set from real searches on a social science platform, covering all four item types, using AI to speed up labeling.

1202.p: AI can spot single events in text, but struggles when real-world events chain across many documents in complex ways.
1202.a: Built a test set with four event tasks ranging from spotting single events to predicting future ones, using AI pipelines for scalable labeling.

1203.p: Training AI to do real multi-step web research requires examples of reasoning and searching, but creating these is slow and expensive.
1203.a: Built a dataset of 9,000 research questions with search paths and answers, plus an open-source training system using trial-and-reward learning.

1204.p: As AI assistants talk with you over months, they forget what you care about, so they can't give truly personal advice.
1204.a: Created a test set from real month-long conversations tracking what users want, measuring if systems extract, update, and recall memories accurately.

1205.p: Online sellers hide policy violations using tricks like splitting words or cropping images; moderation AI must catch these evasions.
1205.a: Built a Chinese marketplace test set showing 2,800+ text tricks and 14,000+ image manipulations, measuring if AI sees through obfuscation.

1206.p: Climate researchers need to learn how communities coped with extreme weather by reading old newspapers, but OCR errors and archaic language block this.
1206.a: Built a test set measuring if AI can find relevant 100-year-old weather articles and extract stories of how people survived disasters.

1207.p: Training AI agents requires step-by-step thinking examples, but current data shows only final answers, not the searching and fact-checking.
1207.a: Built a tool that auto-generates detailed reasoning traces where agents explore documents, plus a 100,000+ verified step corpus.

1208.p: Simulating user behavior is valuable for testing search engines cheaply, but it requires heavy coding, blocking most researchers from using it.
1208.a: Built a web interface where you design and run user simulations visually, without writing code, storing experiments as reusable templates.

1209.p: User simulators can look human-like but give wrong answers about whether one search system actually ranks better than another.
1209.a: Built standard tests showing that looking human-like has almost no connection to valid system rankings, pinpointing better realism measures.

1210.p: Arabic search systems lack evaluation resources; we need to know if AI can reliably rate Arabic search results like it does English.
1210.a: Tested whether three AI systems agree on Arabic search result quality and whether their ratings match real system rankings across languages.

1211.p: Some retrieval methods are smart but slow; search services need fast scoring without losing accuracy.
1211.a: Modified a retrieval method to run at multiple speed-accuracy points, achieving 7x fewer computations without major quality loss.

1212.p: People search for experts both by name and by skill area, switching modes as they learn; we don't know how to support this well.
1212.a: Analyzed half a million real expert search queries, finding that people switch modes when they find something, reshaping search design.

1213.p: Ad systems fail when they can't measure results for weeks and miss seasonal patterns; they need to bid better under uncertainty.
1213.a: Combined AI reading ad text and trends for daily budget plans with a real-time control system adjusting bids minute-by-minute.

1214.p: Retrieval systems that code items based on click patterns go stale as trends shift; full rebuilds waste computation.
1214.a: Update old item codes to match new click patterns by aligning them to existing codes, then retrain lightly instead of starting over.

1215.p: Millions of people describe their mental health struggles online, but doctors can't manually read all of it. Systems need to spot depression symptoms buried in posts to help overworked clinics.
1215.a: Instead of guessing what counts as depression evidence, feed an AI system real labeled examples to learn brief rules about each symptom, then use those rules to flag relevant posts.

1216.p: Online networks constantly change—Bitcoin trades, messages flow, new patterns emerge—but catching hidden bad actors is hard because unusual behavior might be normal elsewhere in the network.
1216.a: Learn what normal nodes look like over time, find similar healthy examples from the past, and spot anything that strays far from those patterns.

1217.p: Teaching apps struggle to guess what students know when they barely click anything yet. Systems must figure out learning from sparse activity to give good next lessons.
1217.a: Notice that students with similar skills often follow similar learning paths, so use patterns from other learners to make smarter guesses about newcomers.

1218.p: When AI reranks product lists, the order you show items matters—a different order can flip which item gets picked, making ranking unreliable and dependent on accident, not true preference.
1218.a: Redesign how the AI looks at items so order becomes irrelevant; score all items together in a way that ignores position and produces the same ranking no matter how you sort the input.

1219.p: Search engines must balance speed and accuracy: exact search works best but is slow under load. When busy, they must cut corners without losing users' results.
1219.a: Shrink the search data when traffic spikes and grow it back when quiet, automatically picking the right size to hit response deadlines.

1220.p: Libraries with millions of books need to group similar ones together to search fast, but the standard grouping method gets too slow as the library grows.
1220.a: Use a faster splitting strategy that groups books almost as well as before but runs hundreds of times quicker, even on the largest libraries.

1221.p: Every search engine starts with the same text cleaning steps, but no two types of text (news vs. medicine vs. Twitter) need the same cleaning. Wrong cleaning hurts results.
1221.a: Automatically try hundreds of different cleaning and chunking combinations and learn which one works best for each dataset, without manual guessing.

1222.p: When you accidentally click a product or buy something you hate, that click is treated like a real preference signal. Noise in the data breaks personalization and makes recommendations worse.
1222.a: Treat each noisy click as a set of possible explanations (real interest or accident), then use math to figure out which clicks were likely mistakes and downweight them.

1223.p: Teaching an AI to rank results in a medical database costs huge effort to build training data. Adapting a general-purpose AI to specialized fields stays hard and expensive.
1223.a: Extract knowledge from pretraining, tune how much of that knowledge helps ranking in each domain, and keep everything stable across different field types without retraining.

1224.p: Recommendation models learn to pick items from millions of choices, but when an item becomes popular, the model only shows the same items to everyone, killing diversity.
1224.a: Fix trained recommendation data by realigning user and item relationships, keeping the original taste preferences but restoring lost variety.

1225.p: Booking apps see user clicks hours late due to system delays, but they predict demand from stale data, so forecasts are often wrong when patterns have already shifted.
1225.a: Model how long data takes to arrive, then learn connections across different time lags so predictions work even when the recorded history is out of sync with real actions.

1226.p: Wikipedia and online guides must link photos and words to the right people, places, or things. Current tools either are slow, use too much memory, or get the match wrong.
1226.a: Squeeze both text and image information into compact vectors that match the accuracy of complex systems but run 1000 times faster and use 10 times less storage.

1227.p: Evaluating a fact-retrieval system requires hundreds of specific questions to catch subtle differences between good and bad answers. More questions mean higher cost and slower evaluation.
1227.a: Learn key differences from pairs of answers, building a small, sharp set of questions that still catch meaningful gaps between strong systems.

1228.p: When someone asks a conversational question, the system ranks results for topicality but misses what that person actually wants—negatives, formats, style preferences stay hidden.
1228.a: Route simple questions to fast ranking, and for complex ones, automatically generate personalized rules from the conversation history to guide a smarter ranker.

1229.p: Hotel booking sites show many rooms in one hotel, and when one room's price drops, people switch to it, but models ignore this substitution and predict total demand wrong.
1229.a: Break booking into two steps (click hotel, then pick room) and learn how price changes for one room shift people to alternatives, so predictions and pricing decisions are accurate.

1230.p: When analyzing data for unusual patterns, companies face hundreds of tools to pick from but can't practically try them all on new data.
1230.a: Train a system on past dataset problems and which tools worked well, then use it to predict which tool will work best for a new dataset without running them.

1231.p: When building tests to measure how well an AI system answers questions pulled from external sources, builders don't know whether to split test cases finely or broadly.
1231.a: Create 5,872 test questions at three different levels of detail and measure which granularity best separates good systems from bad.

1232.p: Medical reviews search thousands of papers to answer a specific question, but reviewers read far more documents than needed if the answer has already emerged clearly.
1232.a: Stop screening documents once evidence is strong enough to make a confident decision, rather than reading everything available.

1233.p: As search databases grow larger, the quality of existing speed-estimation methods breaks down, making it impossible to predict if a query will work well.
1233.a: Adapt existing speed-estimation methods to account for growing databases and test whether they predict performance loss as databases expand.

1234.p: Evaluating whether an AI correctly sources its facts requires judging answer quality, but the field doesn't know if AI-written judgments match human judgment.
1234.a: Compare how humans and AI systems grade the same answers, then test which automatic grading methods humans actually agree with.

1235.p: When asking large AI systems to rank search results best-first, their rankings vary wildly depending on how the question is phrased, making them unreliable in production.
1235.a: Test whether ranking quality stays consistent when changing the instruction from 'put best first' to 'put best last' to understand brittleness.

1236.p: Bitcoin transactions involve complex networks where money flows between accounts with hidden timing clues, making fraud extremely hard to spot.
1236.a: Build a system that learns patterns from how accounts interact over time, treating each interaction as part of a larger web of connections.

1237.p: When generating radiology reports, AI systems retrieving similar past reports sometimes pull ones clinically wrong for the patient, then copy their mistakes.
1237.a: First match medical facts like 'tumor present, left side' exactly, then within that safe set find reports with similar descriptions.

1238.p: Documents with both text and images are hard to organize by topic because existing models work poorly on directional image data.
1238.a: Model topics on a sphere where normalized image directions fit naturally, then refine topics using an AI system to pick better names.

1239.p: Large AI systems catch some of their own false claims, but often rely on surface words instead of actually understanding source material.
1239.a: Test AI's fact-checking with 1,032 annotated examples and remove unreliable detections by watching which key phrases it trusts too much.

1240.p: Building chatbots that recognize human emotion in conversation usually requires expensive manual labeling, so researchers use AI systems to label instead.
1240.a: Compare AI-labeled emotion against human judgment to measure how much AI labeling bias quietly enters the training and testing pipelines.

1241.p: Matching sentences in an article to specific moments in a video is hard because models focus only on the overall message and miss fine details.
1241.a: Model the article as layers (words, sentences, paragraphs) and video as clips that cooperate and compete to find the best match at each level.

1242.p: Modern AI search has three breakpoints—finding docs, generating answers, and judging quality—but it's unclear if the same queries fail at all three.
1242.a: Analyze four years of benchmark data to see where difficulty comes from in each stage and test if fixing one stage alone helps.

1243.p: Re-ranking search results costs money and time, but systems default to checking the same number of candidates for every query regardless of need.
1243.a: Learn from past queries which ones need deeper checking, then predict depth per query to cut costs while keeping quality.

1244.p: When pulling documents for an AI system to read before answering, using a fixed number wastes time with irrelevant pages or misses important facts.
1244.a: Classify each question to predict how many documents will actually help, then retrieve that specific amount instead.

1245.p: Search engines struggle to find exactly what you want because they either guess poorly from your words alone or they need expensive AI to rephrase your query better.
1245.a: Combine an old, fast search method with a new AI trick: the AI writes fake documents that could answer you, then the fast method learns which terms matter most in those fake answers.

1246.p: Shopping sites that ask an AI to make suggestions ignore a crucial signal: people's ratings range from hate to love, but current systems treat all ratings as equally good or bad.
1246.a: Tell the AI to treat ratings as a scale (one star versus five stars means very different things), then align those gradations so the AI understands strength of preference.

1247.p: When a database searches for buildings in a certain neighborhood, it wastes time checking points outside the area, slowing down the answer.
1247.a: Use a smarter way to divide the search area into chunks so fewer irrelevant points are checked, speeding up the query by roughly 3.6 times.

1248.p: Finding two nearly identical documents in a massive collection takes forever because existing systems waste effort checking documents that are clearly too different.
1248.a: Use tighter limits (checking length first) to skip non-matching documents much faster, shrinking the work load by up to 58 times.

1249.p: Recommendation systems that predict what you'll click on need huge lookup tables to store information about every item, but these tables take so much memory they slow down predictions.
1249.a: Store less-popular items with fewer numbers and popular items with more numbers (like Huffman coding for text), shrinking the table while keeping accuracy.

1250.p: Suggestion systems struggle when users have sparse histories (few past purchases or clicks), so they pad the history with dummy data that repeats the same items over and over.
1250.a: Instead of repeating the same item, extract multiple hidden angles from each real item and use those varied angles to fill the gaps.

1251.p: When you ask a search engine a follow-up question in a conversation, it must re-train on conversation data or lose its skill at finding answers to single, standalone questions.
1251.a: Blend two trained versions of the model (one for chat, one for single queries) without retraining, so it works well for both without forgetting either.

1252.p: Grouping similar documents into topics works better when you know what people, companies, or ideas appear in them, but most methods ignore that extra information.
1252.a: Extract the people and organizations mentioned, build connections between documents based on shared names, then smooth the document fingerprints using those connections.

1253.p: Systems that answer questions by first looking up facts work best when they pick the right fact-lookup method for each question, but they use only one method for all questions.
1253.a: Teach a system to rank fact-lookup methods by how well they'll help answer each specific question, then pick the best one automatically.

1254.p: Recommendation systems that use item categories or genres don't always actually rely on that information, so it's unclear when adding categories helps and when it doesn't.
1254.a: Shuffle the category labels on items and measure how much the recommendation breaks, revealing whether the system truly uses categories or ignores them.

1255.p: Systems that use multiple AI agents debating to filter out harmful chat messages run slowly and expensively because they debate every single message in real time.
1255.a: Store past debate outcomes and reasons in a memory bank, then reuse them to instantly answer similar new messages without re-debating.

1256.p: Recommendation systems attend to past purchases with weights learned during training, but it's unclear whether those learned weights actually matter or if equal weight works just as well.
1256.a: Replace learned attention weights with uniform weights and measure performance: when performance stays the same, the learning was unnecessary.

1257.p: News recommendation systems that learn from data are expensive to run and slow down news delivery, but simplicity and speed are crucial for real-world news sites.
1257.a: Build a fast, no-training system using just user and article statistics, delivering recommendations 600 times faster with quality nearly as good.

1258.p: Tests that measure how well a search system finds nearby items penalize it for missing items that aren't actually relevant, even though it found the right ones.
1258.a: Measure only whether the system finds the items that truly matter semantically, ignoring false penalties for missing irrelevant neighbors.

1259.p: Guessing the GPS location of a photo fails when the place isn't in the reference database, because the system can only reason about places it has seen before.
1259.a: Search the entire web for similar images to get coordinates from real places, then use those web results to help the AI make a location guess.

1260.p: Small AI systems run on your phone, but each one works better for different tasks—none is best for everyone. Picking the right one means wasting time trying many options.
1260.a: Build a profile of what a user likes, then match them to the one small AI system that fits best, and explain why in plain language.

1261.p: Search engines show polished summaries from AI that look reliable and cite sources, but readers can't tell if those summaries are actually wrong or if the sources really support the claims.
1261.a: Check what search engines actually say and trace whether their cited sources back them up, to measure how often the summaries mislead even when good information exists.

1262.p: Search engines store huge lists of numbers to represent each page, but shrinking those lists to fit in memory breaks search quality unless you know exactly how much to shrink.
1262.a: Automatically find the right shrinking amount by analyzing the data itself, without needing labeled examples or trial-and-error tuning.

1263.p: Search systems try to guess what results you want by tweaking your question automatically, but this guess helps some people and hurts others, and nobody knows which.
1263.a: Watch real people search with different tweaked versions to see which actually make their lives easier, then avoid the harmful ones.

1264.p: Organizing short chat messages by topic is hard because a message might fit several topics at once, but old methods force each message into just one bucket.
1264.a: Give each message multiple topic labels, find what those labels have in common, and group messages by how much they share labels.

1265.p: AI search agents look up information step-by-step to answer questions, but they often fetch the same facts over and over and think too long, wasting computing power.
1265.a: Measure where the waste happens as the AI thinks, then give it feedback rewards to make it skip the useless steps.

1266.p: Real descriptions of pictures range from vague ("a dog") to detailed ("a golden retriever on a couch"), but search systems treat these as equal, missing how humans group them by specificity.
1266.a: Use curved geometry instead of flat geometry to make search systems understand and respect these natural levels of detail without retraining from scratch.

1267.p: Brain signals from listening differ from brain signals from watching, but scientists didn't test them fairly because the experiments were different, leaving it unclear which is truly better for search.
1267.a: Run the same setup for both listening and watching, so the brain data can be compared honestly and show what each one is actually better at.

1268.p: Recommending new products is hard because the system only has product descriptions, not user history, and descriptions miss subtleties that matter to real people.
1268.a: Train only on product descriptions to find which products are similar, using a method that focuses on the most telling comparisons and ignores noisy ones.

1269.p: Improving search by using user-chosen results usually works, but some results actually make search worse, and this gets more unpredictable with newer search methods.
1269.a: Test which results hurt or help, and find that bad results alone stay bad, but sometimes pairing them together actually fixes the problem.

1270.p: Tools that compare two rankings need to decide how much to care about early results versus later ones, but one fixed setting doesn't fit all experiments.
1270.a: Add a second dial so ranking comparison tools can tune both the steepness and shape of importance, fitting more different scientific goals.

1271.p: AI systems excel at looking up facts but struggle when questions need detective work—combining hints from multiple sources into a new insight.
1271.a: Select passages where each sentence narrows down wrong answers, and AI systems that read these concentrated clues answer detective questions much better.

1272.p: AI systems favor famous people and things, but it's unclear whether they learned this from seeing more mentions during training, or whether they genuinely know real-world fame.
1272.a: Count exactly how often each famous person appears in the AI's training data, then check whether the AI's sense of fame matches that exposure.

1273.p: AI systems that look up facts before answering get tangled on multi-step questions because they rank facts by how closely they sound related, not by how they fit together.
1273.a: Rerank facts by checking how well they form a connected chain, using curved geometry to measure structural closeness alongside word similarity.

1274.p: Personalizing a big AI system to each user means teaching it both what people do (their history) and what that says about them (their taste), but these two views often conflict.
1274.a: Tweak the AI's weights separately for each person to generate both their behavior and their taste, then blend both views into one final recommendation.

1275.p: When search companies upgrade their AI models, they must rebuild their entire index from scratch—a costly ordeal for massive production systems.
1275.a: Test whether systems based on matching specific words can keep working with old indexes when you upgrade just the query part.

1276.p: Online shops show products to searchers, but sometimes showing hurts the customer—the top result may be wrong or already listed twice.
1276.a: Use causal reasoning to measure whether hiding a product actually helps customers, accounting for uncertainty in these predictions.

1277.p: Small AI systems used for question-answering often answer anyway, even when told the documents don't support an answer, and get confused by distractor documents.
1277.a: Train them with reward signals to think step-by-step and refuse to answer when evidence is too thin.

1278.p: Ranking systems must adapt as preferences shift over time, but they cannot track individual users or build profiles without raising privacy concerns.
1278.a: Detect genuine preference shifts in item ratings using time-weighted signals and anomaly detection, without assigning scores to users.

1279.p: When AI systems trained on general images and text try recommending products, the gap between general and recommendation-specific data breaks alignment and causes training conflicts.
1279.a: Use specialized adapters for each type of data (images versus text) to separate and reduce conflicts during training.

1280.p: Adversaries can inject fake documents into retrieval systems to make AI output dangerous misinformation with high confidence, fooling uncertainty checks.
1280.a: Detect attacks by monitoring internal attention patterns—poisoned documents cause attention to collapse in a telltale way.

1281.p: When PDF question-answering systems use abstract vectors, they lose concrete details like exact numbers, specific entity names, and which document each fact came from.
1281.a: Replace vectors with searchable text transcribed from PDFs, then apply iterative search that digs deeper only when needed.

1282.p: Users judge AI-generated information they created themselves more favorably than identical information from others, but the reason for this selective bias remains unclear.
1282.a: Run experiments where users evaluate their own AI output versus identical output framed as someone else's to measure the bias.

1283.p: Retrieval systems often fetch facts that contradict what the AI already knows internally, but detecting these conflicts is expensive and introduces delay.
1283.a: Predict conflicts training-free by comparing internal confidence scores against semantic alignment with retrieved text.

1284.p: AI ranking systems use simplified training tricks because the true success metric—quality ranking—cannot be mathematically differentiated for learning.
1284.a: Learn the training method jointly with the ranker, adapting it to each dataset's relevance patterns while keeping it differentiable.

1285.p: Knowing if users are satisfied with generated answers is hard without user feedback; current methods ignore how much effort users spent interacting.
1285.a: Estimate satisfaction as a trade-off between answer quality and interaction effort, using signals like dwell time and click counts.

1286.p: Linking biomedical terms like disease names to official databases is slow and resource-heavy with current AI systems, blocking real-world deployment.
1286.a: Retrain smaller open-source models to quickly rank and pick the right candidate from a shortlist instead of searching from scratch.

1287.p: Retrieval systems invent numbers that aren't in documents, and standard detection methods fail to catch these fabrications.
1287.a: Build a number-aware check that catches all fabricated numbers and outperforms AI judges on finding numerical errors.

1288.p: AI shopping agents interact with users in different ways, but it's unclear which style helps people think critically or feel socially comfortable.
1288.a: Test two interaction personas against a neutral agent and measure their effects on critical thinking and social comfort.

1289.p: Before sales promotions, customers browse and add items to carts but don't buy; most conversions happen during the promotion itself, making pre-promotion prediction hard.
1289.a: Use multi-task learning to model both direct and delayed conversions, accounting for the shifted patterns that occur before promotions.

1290.p: Recommendation systems can't tell whether you genuinely want something or just follow the crowd, so they give you the same generic suggestions as everyone else.
1290.a: Split the recommendation into separate mental models—one for your true taste, one for social pressure—then weight them based on what an AI system thinks matters most.

1291.p: Software engineers use AI agents to find and fix code bugs, but half the AI's work time goes to exploring the codebase, not solving the actual problem.
1291.a: Train a smaller, cheaper AI just to search and explore, then have it hand useful clues to a bigger, stronger AI that fixes the bugs.

1292.p: Ads predict whether you'll click, but tech companies worry that sharing click patterns with cloud servers exposes private information about millions of users.
1292.a: Use mathematical encryption so predictions happen on secret encrypted data, with no one able to read the user information—keeping both accuracy and privacy.

1293.p: To comfort someone upset, you need to understand why they feel that way—but AI systems today treat spotting emotions, understanding causes, and offering support as separate jobs.
1293.a: Use a network that learns how speakers and images relate to each other, then chain three tasks together so each step builds on what came before.

1294.p: People ask search engines long, detailed questions now, but testing how well AI systems answer these requires thousands of human-written examples.
1294.a: Group simple search queries together to build realistic long-form questions automatically, then verify that people can't tell them apart from genuine ones.

1295.p: Search engines in other languages don't have good ways to expand a query when users say it poorly, especially if the system can't access raw word details.
1295.a: Test different clustering methods to group similar results, then pick the most helpful groups as additions to the original search query.

1296.p: Describing an image by looking at tiny objects in it requires checking what's really there, but most image systems only look at the whole image at once.
1296.a: Split the image into small pieces, find similar pieces in a search database to get object names, then blend those names with the full image to write better captions.

1297.p: AI agents in languages like Vietnamese and Thai refuse to call unavailable tools poorly, hallucinating fake answers instead of simply saying they can't help.
1297.a: Teach smaller models to think through their reasoning step-by-step—whether the task makes sense, which tools fit, what could go wrong—rather than just learning examples.

1298.p: Systems that learn new words over time forget old ones, especially rare words, because new examples and old examples compete for the model's attention.
1298.a: Save neurons important for old words and lock them down, while also keeping a memory bank of old word examples to practice alongside new ones.

1299.p: Matching identical people across different databases fails when some information is missing, because guessing the missing info without measuring confidence introduces garbage into the blend.
1299.a: Estimate how trustworthy each guess is, then use that confidence to weight the guess—ignoring dubious guesses and trusting obvious ones when matching people.

1300.p: Simulating realistic societies with many AI agents costs too much computer power, so you end up with fewer agents or shallower interactions than reality.
1300.a: Automatically pick which agents matter most in each round, so the simulation stays realistic while using far fewer AI calls and less total computing time.

1301.p: Asking questions about complex musical scores—like which parts work together—requires reading and connecting many facts from sheet music, which AI systems struggle with.
1301.a: Give an AI system music-reading tools that extract facts, then have it chain those tools together to answer multi-step questions about compositions.

1302.p: Understanding memes requires grasping jokes and context, but current AI systems process visual and social clues in a fixed line, missing contradictions and confusions.
1302.a: Treat meme interpretation as a puzzle where agents repeatedly spot problems, suggest fixes, and refine understanding until the explanation feels internally consistent.

1303.p: Multi-agent systems accumulate messy memories where facts get updated, retracted, or contradicted—so you can't just combine them; you need to judge what's actually true.
1303.a: Map agent interactions as a timeline showing what changed when, highlight important moments, then suppress old contradicted facts when building the final answer.

1304.p: Recommendation systems that generate item names must choose prefixes one at a time, and a bad early choice locks you into poor recommendations forever.
1304.a: Score all valid item names at once, then use mathematical search on valid names to find the best complete recommendation in a single step.

1305.p: When online stores show you products based on implicit signals like what you browsed, they need to learn from millions of items they know you didn't buy—but picking the wrong non-items to train on confuses the system.
1305.a: Train the system by using both the user and the item you liked as guides when picking which non-items to learn from, using a smooth mathematical method that still allows end-to-end learning.

1306.p: Emotion detection and sentiment analysis each need separate AI systems trained just for that task, so the work doesn't transfer when you move to a new problem.
1306.a: Train one AI system on multiple emotion tasks at once using examples of how similar problems relate, so the system learns skills that work for emotions, sentiment, stance, and sarcasm together.

1307.p: Chatbots that remember who you are must keep notes over weeks of chats, but they have limited space and old facts conflict with new ones.
1307.a: When the bot gets new information, it searches what it already remembers, then decides what facts to keep, change, or delete to stay consistent while using space well.

1308.p: A fast search system called ColBERT works well but needs five to ten times more disk space than the original text, making it expensive to run at scale.
1308.a: Compress the internal representations ColBERT uses by converting them to smaller numerical formats, cutting disk space by half while keeping search quality nearly the same.

1309.p: AI systems that rank documents for relevance are slow and use lots of memory, but people want a small, fast version that's still accurate.
1309.a: Teach a small AI by learning from a large one, but fix how the large one assigns scores on hard cases and make the small one learn from the differences between good and bad documents.

1310.p: Personalized question-answering systems use facts about you, but if those facts come from unrelated fields, the system struggles to give you relevant answers.
1310.a: When the system can't find enough facts about you in the right field, it also looks up public knowledge, combining both sources to give better answers.

1311.p: Identifying cell types from genes is hard because no single gene is decisive—the type emerges only from many genes working together, which existing systems handle poorly.
1311.a: Find the genes that many input genes can reach through biological networks, treating those junction points as the key evidence for what the cell is.

1312.p: People read news but can't verify unfamiliar claims without spending hours researching sources, yet professional fact-checkers do this well through a clear process.
1312.a: Automate the fact-checker's workflow: generate questions about the article, search for evidence, filter what's reliable, and write a report that explains what's trustworthy and why.

1313.p: AI systems that look up facts before writing can be fooled by poisoned documents that secretly push a particular viewpoint, especially when the topic has multiple valid perspectives.
1313.a: When filtering retrieved documents, preserve legitimate disagreements between perspectives while catching sneaky attacks by modeling which facts cluster with which viewpoints.

1314.p: Most AI instruction datasets are in English, so AI systems struggle to understand and follow instructions in other languages and cultures.
1314.a: Pick training examples by scoring how good and diverse they are across 18 languages and cultural contexts, building a balanced dataset that teaches the AI across the world.

1315.p: When you have a pre-trained system that learns from how things connect but only a few examples for a new task, you can't change the core weights without breaking what it learned.
1315.a: Adjust the input connections for each node by scoring which new edges matter most based on patterns from your few examples, keeping the main system frozen.

1316.p: Current systems that add external facts either slow down as context grows or need massive storage, and both approaches may lose important nuances during the translation.
1316.a: Compress documents into compact hidden states and feed them directly into the AI's internal thinking process, letting it blend facts with reasoning at a deeper level.

1317.p: Large AI systems make up false facts, and asking multiple AIs to vote on answers helps, but no method looks at whether different AIs agree on the same answer.
1317.a: When multiple AIs give the same answer, trust it more; when they disagree, trust all of them less, using this agreement signal to pick which answer is actually true.

1318.p: Multi-step question-answering requires understanding the question itself, but you can't understand it without facts, creating a catch-22 before retrieval starts.
1318.a: First explore with many angles to understand the question and find key entities, then do targeted searching to build evidence chains, then check the chain for errors.

1319.p: Teaching a large AI to retrieve facts from a smaller AI teacher works poorly—bigger students barely improve from bigger teachers, unlike systems trained on examples alone.
1319.a: Large student AIs need large teacher AIs to learn from; small teachers create a bottleneck, so matching the teacher size to the student size restores effective learning.

1320.p: Online stores struggle to recommend products when they have little data about a new shopper's tastes.
1320.a: Use an AI language system to better describe what each product is really about, then combine those descriptions with past purchase history to make smarter guesses.

1321.p: Teaching AI agents to search the web for fact-checking requires complex training data that doesn't exist yet.
1321.a: Start with organized web facts, find evidence to build realistic questions, then train the AI agent by first showing examples and later rewarding good intermediate steps.

1322.p: Recommendation systems that mix text and images often let one type of information drown out the other.
1322.a: Check that both text and images pull in the same direction before combining them, and use special markers to keep the system working smoothly.

1323.p: Search engines rank documents quickly, but sometimes miss subtle reasons why a document actually answers the question.
1323.a: Teach the ranking system to think through its reasoning step by step before deciding the final ranking.

1324.p: Ranking systems that read full documents take too long to respond because they process every single word.
1324.a: Combine smaller groups of words at middle stages of processing rather than at the start, so the system can skip unnecessary details.

1325.p: When a shopper searches for an ambiguous word like 'Wildflower', the search engine misses that it could mean a restaurant, a product, or a flower.
1325.a: Ground the search in the store's real inventory and instantly search the web for unknown items, then let the system suggest multiple meanings instead of forcing one answer.

1326.p: Online experiments to test website changes often give wrong answers because of differences between user groups and running too many tests at once.
1326.a: Divide users into similar groups first, watch if the test has enough power to see real effects, and separate concurrent tests to avoid interference.

1327.p: Suggesting what products to buy together is hard because items sell together due to hype, not because they truly complement each other.
1327.a: Learn true complementarity from purchase patterns while filtering out false signals from bestsellers, then spread those connections to rare and new items.

1328.p: Many search applications need compact models that understand text well but can run on simple hardware with tight resource limits.
1328.a: Shrink a large working model down to a small one while keeping its smarts intact, and make it robust against compression for storage efficiency.

1329.p: E-commerce search systems miss when a shopper wants a specific color or brand because they treat each product as one blob of meaning.
1329.a: Break down both queries and products into their separate features like color and brand, then check each feature independently before combining them.

1330.p: Research peer reviews are increasingly written with AI help, but there is no way to audit whether reviewer claims are actually supported by the paper.
1330.a: Build systems to automatically check if a reviewer's statement matches evidence in the manuscript and measure how much human reasoning versus AI text each review contains.

1331.p: Search engines must balance speed against quality, but mixing keyword search and semantic search usually creates messy inconsistencies.
1331.a: Train one model that produces both keyword and semantic matches together, regularize them to stay consistent, and combine them intelligently at ranking time.

1332.p: Building custom AI agents from scratch for every user question is expensive and wasteful, even though many questions need similar agent strategies.
1332.a: Maintain a library of pre-designed agents, retrieve the right one instantly for each question, and optionally shrink it down for cheaper inference.

1333.p: Testing a restaurant business strategy requires running expensive experiments, but simulators often miss real-world context and hidden customer habits.
1333.a: Extract decision patterns from past customer data, use them to align both human-like reasoning and statistical pattern-matching, then blend both for prediction.

1334.p: E-commerce search returns relevant products but misses what users really want, like beef steak over pork steak when searching 'steak'.
1334.a: Learn from past clicks to predict which similar products users actually prefer, rather than guessing from words alone or historical click counts.

1335.p: When a person hasn't bought or searched yet, recommender systems can't guess what they want, leaving new users with poor suggestions.
1335.a: Use an AI system to predict hidden interests before users act, then convert those predictions into product categories the system can work with.

1336.p: Online stores have product photos, text, and customer behavior data, but existing systems don't use all these signals together to rank search results.
1336.a: Build a system that processes photos and text through one AI model using multiple learning tasks at once, so rankings improve without slowing down.

1337.p: Search rankings that only optimize for clicks often promote popular items over results that truly match what someone is looking for.
1337.a: Use a lightweight AI system to rate search results as irrelevant, somewhat relevant, or highly relevant, then balance these ratings against click metrics.

1338.p: Current AI-powered search systems either plan blindly without knowing what's in stock, or take too long figuring out what went wrong and retrying.
1338.a: Check store inventory first to ground the plan in reality, then write search strategies based on what's actually available.

1339.p: Video search systems struggle to rewrite vague queries into good search terms because they can't reliably pinpoint when rewording actually helps.
1339.a: Train an AI by identifying cases where rewording is necessary, then fine-tune it to work fast enough for live streaming platforms with billions of users.

1340.p: Recommendation models treat a user's entire history as one jumbled stream, but people's interests are messy and scattered across different topics.
1340.a: Separate a user's history into multiple clean threads by topic, then analyze each thread independently so noisy data doesn't confuse the model.

1341.p: After someone buys an item, recommenders keep suggesting similar products, wasting their attention when the person already satisfied that need.
1341.a: Learn when an interest ends after a purchase, then temporarily hide related suggestions and bring them back when the person might need to rebuy.

1342.p: Recommendation systems must either retrain from scratch (slow, expensive) or update on new data (risks forgetting old patterns).
1342.a: Keep a stable older model trained on long history, lightly update it on recent data, then route newly-active users to the updated model at serving time.

1343.p: Recommender systems optimize for one behavior (clicks), but video platforms care equally about watch time and engagement metrics.
1343.a: Use an AI system that learns multiple prediction tasks together in one model, so all signals improve efficiency and accuracy at once.

1344.p: New content is posted constantly on social platforms and must be judged quality within hours, but there's almost no user interaction data to learn from.
1344.a: Use an AI that reads the text and images of new posts to estimate quality before anyone clicks, then use that guess to decide which posts to show first.

1345.p: Vague search queries lead shoppers to abandon sites because the results don't match their real needs.
1345.a: Use an AI agent that reasons about a person's purchase history to rewrite their search query to be more specific and helpful.

1346.p: Current prediction models either miss how interests evolve globally or flatten nuanced signals into crude categories that lose meaning.
1346.a: Model how a person's interests flow and change over time as a smooth path, then use movement patterns to improve predictions.

1347.p: Storing full numbers for millions of articles is slow and memory-heavy, making news retrieval expensive at scale.
1347.a: Convert article summaries into compact binary codes that still find similar articles quickly, then refine the top results with full precision.

1348.p: Enterprise AI assistants fail to find relevant documentation because users call products by informal names, nicknames, or outdated terms.
1348.a: Normalize user queries by mapping casual product names to official ones before searching, improving what the system can find.

1349.p: Music search engines fail on misspellings and phonetic variations, and learning from rare searches is difficult under strict speed limits.
1349.a: Use a neural system that learns surface-level fuzzy matches and breaks words into short chunks to handle variations without slowing down retrieval.

1350.p: Search engines rewrite messy user queries into clearer ones, but they often ignore what most people are actually searching for, leading to results that don't match what people expect.
1350.a: Track what millions of people search for to find the main patterns, then rewrite each query to match those popular patterns without needing to know each person's history.

1351.p: AI systems write things that sound perfect but are completely false, and existing methods to catch these mistakes either end up agreeing with each other even when wrong or assign fake opposing viewpoints that spread misinformation.
1351.a: Have multiple AI judges evaluate both a claim and its opposite, swapping reasoning when they disagree, so they catch false statements through genuine disagreement instead of fake conflict.

1352.p: Recommendation systems predict clicks well by one measure but give wildly wrong predictions for some products, breaking downstream systems like ad auctions that multiply predictions to set prices.
1352.a: Train the prediction system in two steps to ensure each product group gets accurate predictions, so when systems combine predictions for business decisions, the math actually works.

1353.p: Local apps treat all unknown user-item pairs as bad examples during training even though many are impossible by geography, wasting learning signal on pairs that could never happen.
1353.a: Group training data by geographic region so the system only learns from realistic examples—products users could actually see—making the learning signal much stronger.

1354.p: Online doctors need to suggest follow-up questions to patients, but clicks on suggestions don't reliably show which questions are actually good, and the system optimizes each step separately instead of for real outcomes.
1354.a: Track what the conversation is about to generate and rank suggestions together, train on what patients actually prefer, and use real user feedback to constantly improve which questions get suggested.

1355.p: When several people share one video-watching account, the app can't tell them apart in real time, so it shows the wrong videos instead of guessing which person is holding the phone right now.
1355.a: Analyze how each person holds and taps their phone as a fingerprint before the main recommendation system sees it, giving the system a clear signal about who's actually watching.

1356.p: Flight sites show one price in the search results but a higher price when you try to buy, destroying trust and turning away customers because the inventory changed between clicks.
1356.a: Check real-time seat availability before ranking flights, and let the ranking learn how sensitive each person is to price jumps so the most important flights stay at the top.

1357.p: Fuzzy flight searches like "somewhere warm in summer" are vague with low conversion rates, but the ranking system learns from precise searches and doesn't transfer that knowledge well.
1357.a: Use a precise-search teacher system to guide a fuzzy-search student system, carefully weighting what gets taught so noise doesn't hurt, and preserving the ranking order that matters most.

1358.p: E-commerce ad retrieval needs to find millions of relevant ads fast, but online latency limits how much filtering can happen, leaving many irrelevant ads reaching users.
1358.a: Do most filtering offline before the request arrives—retrieve many candidates, use a large AI system to throw out bad ones, then rank the survivors so the online system is quick and powerful.

1359.p: Local services like restaurant recommendations get worse at suggesting unpopular restaurants because geography limits where they can be shown, diluting the learning signal for smaller businesses.
1359.a: Boost how the system understands unpopular items by learning from spatial geography before the main recommendation runs, so neighborhood restaurants and shops get fairer treatment.

1360.p: High-volume e-commerce support agents waste time re-reading chat history and order details for each message, and they often break company policies or handle things inconsistently.
1360.a: Provide AI-drafted responses that rewrite the customer's question clearly, pull up company rules and order facts, and suggest on-brand replies that agents review and edit before sending.

1361.p: Phone companies want to personalize AI assistants for each customer using call history and app use, but they can't send data to public servers and the AI needs to produce reliable outputs.
1361.a: Build a system that runs entirely inside the company, turning call logs and behavior into customer profiles, then inject those profiles into the AI so responses match each person.

1362.p: Specialized search domains like law and medicine need to retrain ranking systems to work well, but it's unclear whether spending effort on domain-specific pretraining actually pays off versus simple fine-tuning.
1362.a: Test whether training with just a few hundred real domain examples beats months of domain-adaptive pretraining, showing when the expensive approach is worth the cost.

1363.p: When people shop via back-and-forth conversation, they state filters like "under $100" early on, but systems either keep every filter even after switching categories and get zero results, or forget filters entirely.
1363.a: Teach the system which constraints carry forward across category changes and which to drop by reasoning through each filter's life, then compress that reasoning into a fast model for real-time use.

1364.p: Enterprise search can't collect human relevance judgments at scale, and click signals are messy and biased, so systems trained only on AI judgments ignore how people actually behave.
1364.a: Only trust results where AI judgment and user clicks agree, filtering out noise while keeping the system grounded in real human behavior instead of just semantic correctness.

1365.p: Testing new features on social platforms gives wrong answers because users influence each other, breaking the basic math assumption that one person's result is independent.
1365.a: Map how people actually influence each other through the network, then split test groups along those real connection lines instead of randomly.

1366.p: Recommendation systems fail for brand-new users and trap people in filter bubbles because they only learn from what that individual has done.
1366.a: Borrow patterns from what similar people enjoyed to make better guesses for someone new or quiet, instead of relying on their lone history.

1367.p: Video search learns what people love for popular videos but forgets how to rank unpopular videos that too few people have watched.
1367.a: Keep the fast memory of what's popular, but add a separate system that understands what each video is actually about so unpopular ones rank fairly.

1368.p: Predicting when a user will open an app fails because most users are either always active or never active, which breaks normal statistical methods.
1368.a: Split the problem into two: first guess if someone is in the always-on or never-on group, then predict behavior separately for the middle group.

1369.p: Companies want to know which offer works best for each person, but offering many choices spreads the data so thin that it becomes unreliable.
1369.a: Let different offers share what they learn about customers, and use knowledge from past controlled experiments to guide predictions.

1370.p: AI helpers for tech support get generic instructions that don't match real work, and they never improve even when they crash.
1370.a: Build instructions from actual support tickets and past failures, then automatically watch for crashes and rewrite the instructions to fix them.

1371.p: Companies struggle to pick which recommendation change to test because manual scoring is slow and traditional scores don't match what people actually click.
1371.a: Use an AI system as a judge to quickly score recommendations the way humans would, so the best change gets picked before expensive live testing.

1372.p: Dating apps rank profiles by likes, but that signal is weak compared to whether people actually meet in person.
1372.a: Build a chain of predictions from like to matched message to real date, using the later stages as stronger proof of real interest.

1373.p: Building a working AI shopping helper is far harder in real Amazon traffic than in lab demos—it must be fast, correct, and affordable.
1373.a: Combine AI reasoning with smart fact lookup, tool coordination, and system tuning so one system handles search, answers, and buying for millions of people.

1374.p: Ranking templates for people who browse without typing queries fails because using the category name as a search query misses what they actually want.
1374.a: Learn from real users' browsing behavior what makes templates rank well, then beat the simple query-name approach with that learned ranking.

1375.p: AI systems that look up facts and write answers don't respect electrical grid rules, risking fatal mistakes from physically impossible suggestions.
1375.a: Connect retrieved facts directly to the actual grid layout and embed grid rules into the reasoning so the AI cannot suggest unsafe operations.

1376.p: When users have years of watch history, the AI model that reads it becomes too slow because it compares every item to every other item.
1376.a: Use a mathematical trick called linear attention that cuts checking time to nearly straight-line instead of squared, while keeping recommendation quality.

1377.p: Music search fails on vague requests like "songs for a road trip" because search engines only match keywords, not what the user actually means.
1377.a: Turn each song into a summary of its sound and feeling, then search by meaning instead of keywords and rank by how well matches fit intent.

1378.p: In regulated fields, some text must stay word-for-word in answers, but systems that look up and rephrase text risk accidentally changing required quotes.
1378.a: Mark which retrieved text must stay exact, pick a mode per quote (keep exact, mix, or rephrase), and double-check the final answer for violations.

1379.p: Ranking models accumulate so many input signals over time that they get bloated and slow, even though half the signals are useless noise.
1379.a: Automatically learn which signals matter by turning them on and off during training, then throw away the useless ones before the model serves customers.

1380.p: Company help systems answer questions with text alone, but employees need to see screenshots and watch videos to truly understand complex procedures.
1380.a: Find relevant images and videos hidden inside company docs, then show them in answers alongside text by matching them to related passages.

1381.p: Testing whether a change to rankings helps income is unreliable when a few sellers dominate all earnings, making it hard to trust experiment results.
1381.a: Split sellers into groups before measuring results, then use past data to reduce noise, so you can reach firm conclusions with far fewer test users.

1382.p: Pinterest struggles to recommend new posts because it has no track record of who engaged with them, so the system can't learn what's good.
1382.a: Use compact numeric codes built into each post that encode what kinds of posts similar users like, then blend that with activity data for fresh recommendations.

1383.p: Video platforms must choose between showing users what they'll watch and paying creators fairly, but these two goals often fight each other.
1383.a: Frame it as a math problem that balances both goals, then solve it with an algorithm that makes real-time choices with built-in fairness promises.

1384.p: Fashion sites suggest mismatched products because they ignore style details in text like 'mid-century' or 'oak finish' that make pairs work together.
1384.a: Teach the system to read style descriptions and use them to focus on which visual features matter for each match, combining text and images.

1385.p: Checking every new marketplace product against over a thousand rules is too slow, so problematic items slip through while safe ones get held up.
1385.a: Use an AI system to translate complex rules into searchable summaries, then filter products fast by finding which rules actually apply to each one.

1386.p: AI systems answering questions about data tables often make up facts and give wrong numbers, undermining trust in business insights.
1386.a: Show the AI not just right and wrong answers, but explain why each one is better, so it learns to reason through answers correctly.

1387.p: Customer service systems guess what customers want based only on past behavior, missing that people's next actions often reveal their true intent.
1387.a: Predict what the customer will do next, then use that prediction to understand what they really need right now.

1388.p: New e-commerce sites in developing countries lack detailed product categories, making it impossible to filter by specific attributes like color or size.
1388.a: Have an AI system write out product attributes from scratch by learning from human experts in the market, refining prompts as feedback arrives.

1389.p: Fashion apps need AI to read outfit photos and extract details, but standard AI tests don't cover the specific tasks real stores care about.
1389.a: Build a test benchmark for fashion-specific tasks like reading outfits and item features, then measure how well different AI systems actually perform.

1390.p: Reranking search results to boost seller revenue often buries relevant products, frustrating users and risking fraud.
1390.a: Swap nearby results step-by-step to raise revenue while keeping relevance and safety in bounds, doing it fast enough for live search.

1391.p: Recommending from millions of videos is slow because tracking what users watched over months strains the system and requires massive memory.
1391.a: Use compact semantic codes instead of individual IDs and compress long watch histories by folding time periods together, cutting memory by ten times.

1392.p: Recommendation ranking splits user and item data into separate towers for speed, but this prevents the system from understanding subtle matches.
1392.a: Train using full item context for better learning, then strip away that detail at serving time to stay fast, keeping both benefits.

1393.p: Recommending fresh content to retain users demands balancing relevance against diversity, but language models don't naturally learn this balance from data.
1393.a: Break novelty down into stages (what type of new thing, what topic, which items), use behavior logs to build training examples, then teach the system to optimize both goals.

1394.p: E-commerce platforms struggle to predict whether a customer will buy because discounts shift behavior in ways the system doesn't fully understand.
1394.a: Extract long-term discount patterns using math that finds cycles, correct for bias from promotion timing, and add an explicit discount-learning task to the model.

1395.p: Shopping sites must assign products to thousands of categories instantly, but rare categories get ignored because most products fit common ones.
1395.a: Use descriptions of each category and compare them to each query using semantic similarity, rather than relying only on historical product patterns.

1396.p: AI judges rate whether search results are good, but they ignore what real people actually clicked on, so their judgments drift from human reality.
1396.a: Show the AI judge a card summarizing how users historically interacted with similar queries, so it can cite real user behavior to check its own reasoning.

1397.p: When AI answer engines cite sources, some web pages get picked more often even if they're not better, which hurts visibility for overlooked sites.
1397.a: Test 252,000 pairs of pages side-by-side to measure which traits make a source more likely to be quoted first, then publish the winning formula.

1398.p: Large shopping search systems must rank products instantly, but they struggle when users have sparse behavior history and conflicting interests.
1398.a: Split user behavior into strong and weak signals, process them in parallel with a simpler attention method, and borrow patterns from crowded categories to help sparse ones.

1399.p: AI systems reason well about shopping intent but are too slow for real-time ranking, while traditional models are fast but can't explain their choices.
1399.a: Train a fast, small model to mimic an AI system's reasoning logic, so it can answer quickly and explain why—without needing human-written explanations.

1400.p: AI ranking models unfairly favor the first search result they see, even if other results are more relevant, cutting system speed in half.
1400.a: Teach the AI model itself to ignore that initial bias by using a special training method that highlights which attention signals matter for relevance.

1401.p: AI systems for ad headlines often produce samey, boring copy because they follow the most common patterns in training data.
1401.a: Automatically create diverse training examples and use multi-goal learning to teach the system to vary headlines while still driving clicks and staying truthful.

1402.p: Shopping search must understand both text and images, but text often misleads while images are accurate—and real-time systems can't use slow AI reasoning.
1402.a: Teach an AI system to explain which parts of the image or title match specific query words, then transfer that detailed reasoning to a lightweight model.

1403.p: Chatbots built into apps struggle to suggest topics because users rarely chat in them but interact heavily with regular content.
1403.a: Learn what users like from their content-viewing behavior, adapt those signals for the chatbot domain, and suggest topics that match current preferences.

1404.p: AI systems that look up facts before answering often trust irrelevant or outdated information, creating slower, worse results in live shopping systems.
1404.a: Use trial-and-reward learning to teach an AI system when to trust its own knowledge versus when to rely on looked-up facts, within a single fast answer.

1405.p: Job seekers type vague three-word queries that don't express what they really want, so search results miss their actual intent.
1405.a: Suggest refinement options—like experience level or salary range—picked from a taxonomy and ranked by a tiny AI model, in real time as users type.

1406.p: Job posting text is messy and varies wildly, but LinkedIn must extract consistent job traits for matching and products.
1406.a: Train a small AI model on synthetic job examples with reasoning steps, then use specialized adapters to extract different job attributes without retraining.

1407.p: Shopping ranking systems need richer product info to answer complex queries, but full descriptions are too slow to process when every second counts.
1407.a: Use trial-and-reward learning to create short, query-aware product summaries and cache them offline so ranking stays instant.

1408.p: Enterprise AI systems for opinion tracking must work in specific industries and low-resource languages, but retraining is expensive and risky.
1408.a: Adapt open-source AI models with instruction examples and find that skipping some expensive steps still yields strong performance for opinion graph extraction.

1409.p: Large shopping search must retrieve from billions of products but models trained on small test sets fail against such scale, and upgrading breaks domain knowledge.
1409.a: Improve training signals with better negative examples and transfer old model knowledge to a stronger new model so retrieval gains power without losing learned patterns.

1410.p: Video apps must decide what to show users when they watch, like, and comment on videos—handling all these different signals at once slows everything down.
1410.a: Use specialized mini-systems that each handle one type of signal, then combine them so they don't repeat work or conflict with each other.

1411.p: When apps predict whether you'll click an ad, one model gets stuck trying the same strategies until performance stalls—there's no way to break free and improve.
1411.a: Split the model into two parts that compete and learn from each other, taking turns as the leader and challenger, so they push each other toward better solutions.

1412.p: When an AI system learns what users want by watching their actions, clicks contain noise and lies, causing the system to chase fake patterns instead of real preferences.
1412.a: Filter out noisy clicks to keep only high-confidence user intentions, then gradually dial up the filtering strength as the model starts drifting away from its original goal.

1413.p: Websites need to turn free-form text into question-and-answer pairs so people can search for information easily, but existing methods are slow and unreliable.
1413.a: Use a code-focused AI system trained on Chinese questions and answers, which turned out to handle Chinese text better and with fewer false statements than Chinese-only systems.

1414.p: Ads run on pages with multiple slots—when one slot takes all the attention, other slots get wasted inventory and ads don't run fairly across the page.
1414.a: Treat all slots together as one optimization problem, ensuring each ad gets shown fairly without piling onto the most valuable spots.

1415.p: Live-streaming apps push popular streamers so hard that their streams crash from overload, while unknown streamers get zero viewers and revenue.
1415.a: Consider how many viewers a streamer can actually handle, then use a graph algorithm to spread viewers evenly so everyone stays happy and performs well.

1416.p: E-commerce apps need to guess what users want to search for next, but running AI systems on phones is too slow and expensive, so today they're stuck using cloud servers.
1416.a: Put a small AI system directly on phones so it can understand what users want right now and adjust recommendations instantly without waiting for a server.

1417.p: Shopping apps optimize for clicks and sales one stage at a time, never agreeing on what matters—and existing AI methods are too slow or unreliable to fix this.
1417.a: Run fast AI offline to build step-by-step reasoning instructions about what users want, then use a lightweight system online to follow those instructions instantly.

1418.p: Predicting what a user will click or buy next is hard because their interests are complex and changing—single-step guesses miss the full picture.
1418.a: Build interest predictions in layers: first guess broad categories like brand and price, then narrow down to the exact item, then predict what they'll order.

1419.p: Ads flow through multiple ranking stages where early stages show things that later stages reject anyway, wasting computing power on candidates that won't win.
1419.a: Let early and late stages talk to each other—reuse signals to skip low-value ads early and avoid wasting time ranking ads that won't perform.

1420.p: Shopping recommendations ignore rich details in product photos and descriptions, so they miss what users actually care about in complex items.
1420.a: Have an AI system read product images and text to write descriptions, then turn those descriptions into searchable features for the recommendation system.

1421.p: When people search for similar products, numeric fingerprints-based search misses context—a 'similar' laptop means something different in a gaming store versus a budget store.
1421.a: Extract structured product details from text, organize them by category, then reason over that organized structure to rank products better than raw text alone.

1422.p: Digital ads either use keywords sellers pick manually or match by similarity, but the second method fails on new items and broad searches.
1422.a: Borrow high-performing keyword-to-item pairs from manual campaigns and transfer them to similarity-based campaigns by finding semantically similar new items.

1423.p: Travel recommendation apps push popular destinations that are crowded and carbon-heavy, ignoring users' real but unstated desires for sustainable trips.
1423.a: Use multiple AI agents to ask clarifying questions about green preferences, suggest lower-impact alternatives, and explain why—letting users make sustainable choices without pressure.

1424.p: Advanced AI ranking models work well but are black boxes—nobody can see why they rank one result higher than another or how to fix them.
1424.a: Build an interactive tool that shows which parts of the model matter most for each ranking decision, and lets people test changes to understand how it works.

1425.p: People who speak Tetun, a language with few speakers and little online text, can't use AI chat systems as well as English speakers because the systems were trained mostly on English.
1425.a: They rewrote the instructions a chat system uses so it works better for Tetun, then tested it with real Tetun speakers to make sure they understand and like the answers.

1426.p: Professionals need to post constantly on LinkedIn to be seen, but AI writing tools make everyone's posts sound identical and forgettable, burying what makes each person unique.
1426.a: A system that plans what someone should post about their actual work, then looks up relevant facts before writing, so each person's voice stays distinctive instead of blending into the generic AI noise.

1427.p: Researchers need to read many papers and check many facts at once, but AI assistants process one request at a time, making large projects slow and expensive.
1427.a: Run many independent AI agents in parallel, each handling one research task, so dozens of papers or fact checks finish together instead of waiting for each one to complete.

1428.p: AI writing systems often make up facts, but adding real search results improves their accuracy; research tools have great search but aren't connected to the AI systems people use.
1428.a: Connect two research tools to AI systems through a standard plug-and-play interface, so AI writers can fetch real search results, rank them, and fact-check themselves automatically.

1429.p: Science peer reviewers often make claims that don't match what the paper actually says, but checking thousands of reviews by hand for fairness is impossible.
1429.a: Automatically pull claims from each review, find the matching parts of the paper, and flag which claims are actually supported by evidence, then show the results in an interactive tool.

1430.p: Travel ads made by AI often show wrong things or don't look like real locations, and companies can't create lots of good ads quickly without a lot of manual work.
1430.a: A system that plans what scenes a travel video should have, finds real photos of that city for each scene, expands those into detailed video instructions, and checks the final result for errors before finishing.

1431.p: Graph databases are great for storing connected data like social networks, but they can't handle complex queries about groups or communities within that data efficiently.
1431.a: A database system that adds a new query language for asking about sets and groups in a graph, plus fast storage for precomputed community structures so complex searches run quickly.

1432.p: Museums have vast collections split across photos, old paper records, and descriptions, making it hard for visitors or researchers to explore connections between objects.
1432.a: Organize all the messy museum data into one linked web of objects, people, images, and descriptions so anyone can ask natural questions and see how things relate.

1433.p: Recipe apps push popular recipes that are often unhealthy, and even when they explain why you should try a healthier dish, it doesn't change what people actually cook.
1433.a: A mobile app that recommends recipes matched to your tastes, explains in plain language why each one is healthier, and runs experiments to see what explanations actually make people cook better meals.

1434.p: Researchers reading papers often need to look up background information, but stopping to search breaks concentration and wastes time; searches also miss personalized context about what each reader knows.
1434.a: A reading tool that watches how you scroll, guesses what you want to know next based on your background, generates relevant questions, and quietly finds papers for you without interrupting.

1435.p: When companies rewrite legal rules and contracts many times, errors and contradictions sneak in that lawyers can't find by reading character-by-character differences.
1435.a: A system that reads two versions of a legal document, understands what each part actually means semantically, and flags what changed in terms of real meaning, not just word order.

1436.p: Wikipedia's knowledge base has gaps and missing connections, and humans can't manually check thousands of predicted new facts fast enough to keep it complete.
