1436.a: Suggest new facts using data patterns, retrieve Wikipedia passages to support each guess, let humans verify them with evidence in front of them, then batch-export confirmed facts.

1437.p: AI systems make up false facts in long answers, and fact-checking tools that catch this are slow, rely on expensive services, and use outdated information.
1437.a: A fast, free tool that breaks down long AI answers into smaller claims, looks up real information from Wikipedia and structured fact databases, and scores how factual the answer really is.

1438.p: Trademark lawyers must judge whether a new company name too closely resembles existing ones across spelling, sound, and meaning, but simple search rankings don't help with this nuanced decision.
1438.a: Search for similar trademark names, then simulate a back-and-forth legal debate over each one considering appearance, sound, meaning, and what goods they sell, scoring the real risk of confusion.

1439.p: People reading math-heavy PDFs often need to search for formulas or understand notation, but math tools are separate from regular PDF readers, making exploration fragmented.
1439.a: A PDF reader that recognizes all the mathematical equations on each page, lets you search and click on formulas the same way as text, and combines formula matching with word search.

1440.p: Comics are hard to search because each page mixes art, text, and timing in ways that basic text or picture search can't capture—fans need to find stories by visual style or pacing, not just words.
1440.a: Track what panels you like by watching where you look, then shift the search to match your actual taste by learning which visual and story details matter most to you.

1441.p: People have photos, videos, and audio scattered across archives, but no single place can search across all of them at once—a historian needs to find German trains in an old video, not just one kind of content.
1441.a: Build one search tool that recognizes objects, faces, sounds, and speech in any mix, so you can combine searches like 'train' plus 'Germany' plus 'audio of a whistle' in one query.

1442.p: Patent databases show titles and filing dates, but they don't help companies understand whether a patent is truly valuable, how the technology evolved, or what it means for future trends.
1442.a: Analyze the full text and how patents cite each other to spot which technologies are truly new, track how ideas evolved over time, and predict which ones will matter next.

1443.p: When you search for PDFs using visual details, the system creates so many tiny pieces to index that searching slows to a crawl—a 1000-page document becomes impossible to handle.
1443.a: Group nearby pieces together and store just a few summaries per page instead of thousands, keeping search fast without losing accuracy on what really matters.

1444.p: The tools that let AI systems look up facts before writing answers are too complicated for beginners to try without huge computing power and years of machine learning experience.
1444.a: Teach the idea layer-by-layer, starting with a simple version that borrows from search APIs, then showing three real methods that build on each other so you grasp the tradeoffs.

1445.p: Over 26 million people speak Nepali, but there's no standard test collection to measure whether search engines work well for them—researchers have nothing to benchmark against.
1445.a: Create the first public set of Nepali questions and relevant documents, including searches in Nepali, English, and mixed languages, so teams can fairly test their systems.

1446.p: AI systems can rewrite search questions or rank results in English, but it's unclear if that helps speakers of African languages like Hausa and Fongbe—or if it hurts instead.
1446.a: Test whether AI rewriting and ranking actually improve search for these languages by comparing them to simpler methods and checking where the AI fails.

1447.p: Small AI systems are fast enough to sort search results in real time, but they're almost always told how to work in English even when users are searching in Hindi or local mixed-language variants.
1447.a: Run the same system three times using three different languages, then combine the results, which lifts accuracy by a few points with no extra training needed.

1448.p: Chichewa speakers in Malawi need to ask questions in their own language to turn human-readable queries into database searches, but systems trained on English don't work well for low-resource languages.
1448.a: Add efficient training on 400 hand-made Chichewa question examples, then combine it with the look-up-facts-first trick to lift accuracy from 42% to 53%.

1449.p: Telugu-speaking farmers in drought-prone India can't access reliable crop and water advice online because no search system is built for agricultural questions in their language or tailored to their crisis.
1449.a: Collect real farming questions from phone hotlines and local guides, then build the first Telugu agricultural search benchmark so systems can be tested and improved.

1450.p: AI systems with built-in web search promise quick answers for time-sensitive questions in any language, but they often fail badly for local Marathi information despite trying to search multiple times.
1450.a: Measure how well web-search AI performs on Marathi local questions and find that shallow one-step searches work better than deep multi-step hunts, exposing design flaws.

1451.p: Summarizing multiple articles in Southeast Asian languages requires either expensive large AI systems or smaller ones that hallucinate false facts—schools and nonprofits can't afford either.
1451.a: Pull the most important sentences using a lightweight system that learns how paragraphs connect, using 28 times less training time and fitting on a single basic laptop.

1452.p: AI-written answers to farming questions in Swahili look plausible but differ measurably from human expert answers—it's unclear whether users can tell the difference or if this poses real risks.
1452.a: Compare AI and human answers by checking sentence length, word variety, and similarity patterns to show that AI writing is detectable and often longer but less diverse.

1453.p: Medical and disaster-relief workers translating into Tetun and Bislama get poor results because translation systems learned from general internet text, not domain-specific documents for their crisis.
1453.a: Let human translators build custom glossaries and memory stores, then have the AI look them up before writing—this boosts accuracy by 17-22 points while staying transparent and fast.

1454.p: Shona speakers in Southern Africa get poor search results because their language's complex word forms confound systems built for English, yet there's no test set to measure and fix the gap.
1454.a: Build the first Shona search benchmark and methods that understand how Shona words change shape, opening the door to equitable information access for 12 million people.

1455.p: Namibian schools have no internet but need to teach science with up-to-date resources; internet-based education systems don't work when the school has no reliable power or connection.
1455.a: Store a library of curriculum-matched science materials directly on computers at the school, so teachers and students can search and find resources offline without needing the cloud.

1456.p: Vietnamese lawyers waste time manually finding which laws apply to specific court cases; computers rarely work in Vietnamese, so this legal task stays mostly human-powered.
1456.a: Built a tool that learns to match court cases to applicable laws by studying Vietnamese court decisions and their citations, plus uses how laws reference each other to rank which law applies best.

1457.p: Over 120 languages exist in Tanzania but nearly all digital tools only work in English or Kiswahili, cutting off rural communities from the web and leaving most languages invisible to technology.
1457.a: Collect text and speech samples in six minority languages to begin building the data needed for search and AI systems to eventually support them, starting with Hehe and Luguru.

1458.p: AI systems are beginning to appear on search results pages above traditional links, but we don't yet know how this changes what people actually look at or how they search.
1458.a: Track where users look on their screen and what they type when an AI summary sits at the top of search results, to understand how this new layout rewires human search behavior.

1459.p: Scientists need to verify whether published claims are true or false, but the volume of papers is so huge that manual checking is becoming impossible and false findings spread unchecked.
1459.a: Build a system that automatically finds papers and evidence that support or contradict a scientific claim, tailored to the specific needs of fact-checking rather than generic search.

1460.p: Search is still mostly reactive: users type a question and wait for results, but in complex tasks they often don't know what to ask next or what information they're missing.
1460.a: Teach a conversational search system to predict what the user will want to search for next and proactively show relevant suggestions before they have to ask.

1461.p: Conversational search systems struggle because they treat every query the same, but some people need personalized results while others suffer when personalization tries to guess their intent from noisy history.
1461.a: Build a smart system with specialized agents that decide, query by query, whether personalizing the search will help or hurt, and extract real user patterns from messy long-term activity logs.

1462.p: AI systems make up facts and false sources when answering questions, creating an unsafe tool for making real decisions in science and business where wrong information causes real harm.
1462.a: Create AI question-answering that checks its own answers against actual sources, admits uncertainty, and helps users verify claims rather than trusting the AI's word alone.

1463.p: People think and search differently depending on how much they know about a topic and how deeply they're trying to understand it, but search systems use the same approach for everyone.
1463.a: Study eye-tracking and search patterns of people with different knowledge levels and thinking styles using both traditional search and AI chat, to understand how to adapt to each person.

1464.p: AI systems that generate answers are stuck with old knowledge: when they learn new documents or facts, they forget what they knew before, or they require expensive retraining of the entire system.
1464.a: Design a system that continuously learns and updates its knowledge without forgetting or requiring a complete rebuild, even as documents change and facts evolve over time.

1465.p: Recommendation systems that don't collect user data centrally work with sparse, incomplete signals, making it nearly impossible to figure out what people have in common and what they might like.
1465.a: Redesign how privacy-preserving recommenders (ones that keep data local) combine user models by recognizing that different people's preferences should be weighted differently, not all averaged equally.

1466.p: Complex questions require answers drawn from documents with text, tables, and images together, but current search treats each as separate and loses how they connect to form meaning.
1466.a: Decide how to break apart text-and-image documents into chunks for retrieval that respect how text, tables, and images work together to answer questions, not just document structure.

1467.p: AI systems in search engines slow things down and behave differently than human searches, but search engines still use the same infrastructure tuned for how people typed queries decades ago.
1467.a: Rebuild search infrastructure to handle AI-generated queries and AI-powered ranking components as first-class citizens, optimizing for their different patterns and computational costs.

1468.p: When AI agents answer questions in online discussions, they influence who trusts what, but we don't know how people's trust and conformity change when both humans and AI are offering opinions.
1468.a: Test how people's trust in information shifts when AI agents are present in group discussions, examining whether they herd toward AI opinions or maintain independence.

1469.p: Training a system to rank scientific papers requires thousands of human judgments saying which papers matter for each query, but collecting these is slow and expensive.
1469.a: Use automatic hints from the citation network, recognizing that how reliable those hints are depends on where a paper sits in the network of research connections, not globally.

1470.p: Climate research involves scattered maps, time-series data, and no standard names, which breaks current search systems built for text.
1470.a: Build search systems that track where information came from and know when a human expert is still needed to verify the answer.

1471.p: When search adapts to you, it can hide unfair choices and leak your data, and you can't tell if results suit you or just the algorithm.
1471.a: Measure hidden bias in rankings, design systems that show users the bias, and audit the whole pipeline for fairness.

1472.p: Finding text that matches your question is only half the job; real answers often need connecting facts together and checking logic.
1472.a: Map existing methods researchers use to make systems think step-by-step and show their reasoning instead of just pattern-matching.

1473.p: Current search-and-answer systems treat everyone the same and don't learn what matters to you specifically.
1473.a: Build personalization into three stages: before searching, during the search, and when writing the final answer for you.

1474.p: When testing search systems with AI-simulated users, you don't know if the sim is fair or biased against certain groups of people.
1474.a: Break the simulation into seven clear parts you can inspect: profile, rules, behavior, trace, checks, feedback, and improvements.

1475.p: Hundreds of search methods now exist (word-matching, neural networks, language models) and it's hard to experiment with them together.
1475.a: PyTerrier toolkit glues retrieval methods together so researchers can try multiple approaches in one pipeline.

1476.p: When you search for a fact, you need to know not just what's relevant but whether it's still true today or became outdated.
1476.a: Build systems that pull dates from documents, rank by when they're still valid, and reason about how facts change over time.

1477.p: Online stores need to guide customers through multi-step decisions (browse, compare, decide) but ranking a static list falls short.
1477.a: Add AI agents that can use tools, reason through steps, and talk back to the customer to help them decide.

1478.p: AI language systems answer the same way for everyone, but ideal systems should learn your values and adapt to you specifically.
1478.a: Integrate five components: memory of you, personalized system design, learning your values, adapting during conversation, and safe deployment.

1479.p: Online shopping search is fundamentally different from web search—images, carts, buying matter—yet they're treated as the same problem.
1479.a: A workshop to discuss how AI agents are changing how people browse, search, and buy online.

1480.p: Search systems are growing too complex to understand, yet laws and users demand to know why they got this result and not that one.
1480.a: A workshop to define what explainable search means, share best practices, and set a community research roadmap.

1481.p: Talking to a search system is now common, but these systems are generic—they don't know you or remember what you just said.
1481.a: A workshop focused on making conversational search personal, with a challenge track to evaluate how systems adapt to users.

1482.p: Neural search is too slow and expensive to use as the first-pass filter in real systems, blocking their adoption.
1482.a: A forum to share benchmarks, efficiency methods, and standards so the field can measure and improve speed without losing quality.

1483.p: The web now mixes human-written and AI-written content tightly, and search systems rank AI content unfairly and confuse users.
1483.a: A workshop to rethink how we evaluate search and design systems that serve both human and synthetic content fairly.

1484.p: Search systems claim to be neutral but actually shape what people see—often serving corporations and governments over individuals.
1484.a: A workshop where researchers discuss making search more democratic, transparent, and aligned with social justice and human freedom.

1485.p: AI systems used for search can be tricked by bad inputs, show bias, and change how people behave in harmful ways.
1485.a: Bring researchers from information retrieval and cybersecurity together to map vulnerabilities and develop defenses for generative systems.

1486.p: Thousands of AI tools do overlapping things; people cannot easily find or pick the right one for their specific task.
1486.a: Build search systems designed for AI tools themselves, ranking them by what they can actually do rather than keywords.

1487.p: Personalized search has always relied on user clicks and data, but this misses what people really want or need.
1487.a: Use AI systems that read language to understand preferences directly from text, without hand-coded rules or behavior tracking.

1488.p: Search systems now mix text and images together, but we lack fair, reliable ways to test whether these results are actually good.
1488.a: Gather researchers from vision and language fields to design rigorous tests for systems that combine text-and-image generation.
